items.title: #243Albany Avenue (Temple Emanuel). Local Landmark Designation
items.applicant: Congregation Emanuel of the Hudson Valley
items.owner: Congregation Emanuel of the Hudson Valley

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed local landmarking of 243 Albany Avenue (also known as Temple Emanuel 'CEHV') in the Albany Avenue neighborhood by Congregation Emanuel of the Hudson Valley, is compatible with the historic character of the city's individual landmarks and landmark districts for the following reasons: • that the proposed landmark designation was undertaken in December 2023 at the request of CEHV to ensure its protection and local recognition as historically significant house of worship and for its architectural significance. Temple Emanuel is significant as the most current house of worship owned and occupied by Congregation Emanuel - a Jewish congregation with roots in the Rondout Village dating back to the 1840s. Since its conception, CEHV has maintained is vital role to the area's Jewish residents in the form of community cohesion, education, and a support network. Temple Emanue l (243 Albany Ave) was built in 1957 by CEHV and designed by a regionally significant architect, Arthur Silver, who designed other religious structures in Long Island and Woodstock, NY. Today, CEHV leads the interfaith Council which brings various local de nominations together, along with sponsoring town halls and candidate debates, and holds world-class speakers (Jeff Greenberg, personal communication, 2024). • that Arthur Silver’s design incorporated Mid-Century Modern design elements in the form of materials, treatments, proportions, and patterns with the most significant being the blue hexagonal breeze block screen that encased the sanctuary. The inclusion of colored glass inserts into the blocks, along with them being back lit, creates a phenomenological prism effect inside the sanctuary - a design unique among religious sites in the area. While the structure has undergone some renovations (like the addition o f the chapel) to ensure its continued usability for CEHV, overall, the structure maintains a high degree of integrity across its exterior, lobby, and sanctuary. • that Temple Emanuel, located at 243 Albany Avenue is worthy of local landmark designation under Criteria C of the National Register of Historic Places, which recognizes it as "embodying the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or method of constr uction or represents the work of a master, or possesses high artistic values, or represents a significant and distinguishable entity whose components lack individual distinction." • that the Commission held a required public hearing on March 7,2024, and Joe Cohen, member, spoke in favor of the designation; • that the Commission finds that Temple Emmanuel should be listed as a Local Landmark and hereby recommends the same to the Common Council of the City of Kingston for final consideration and adoption. Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to resolve that on the 7th day of March 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, recommending that the Common Council of the City of Kingston adopt the property for listing the property at 243 Albany Avenue as a City of Kingston's Local Landmark, for reasons described herein. (KM- motion, NM-2nd; RT, AP- yes; MG- recused).

items.title: #54 West Chester Street: Local Landmark Designation
items.applicant: Brenda Seller, Trustee of the Reina Family Trust
items.owner: Brenda Seller, Trustee of the Reina Family Trust

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed local landmarking of 54 W . Chester Street in the West Chester Street neighborhood by Brenda Seller (owner), is compatible with the historic character of the city's individual landmarks and landmark districts for the following reasons: • that this local landmark designation evaluation was undertaken at the December 2023 request of Brenda Seller to ensure its protection and local recognition as an architectural ly significant dwelling at 54 W. Chester Street that retains a high degree of integrity. 54 West Chester Street was constructed circa 1895 by George M. & Anna E. Decker as their personal dwelling. It is unclear when the structure became a multi-unit dwelling but appears to have been owner occupied for much of its life. As of 2024, the structure serves as an income-producing rental property; • that 54 West Chester Street is a modest late Victorian multi -unit dwelling located on the east side of West Chester Street midway between Bond and Augusta Streets. The structure retains decorative woodwork posts and framing supporting the front porch. A two-story recessed bay supports two corbels and a street facing gable (with a multi-pane attic window is present). A circa 1890s intact multi-colored glass transom window remains over the front entrance. Evidence of the original clapboard siding beneath the existing asbestos shingle siding can be seen on the structure's southwestern corner. 54 W . Chester Street is one of a dozen contiguous late 1gth-century Victorian dwellings (and parcels) on the street, that could constitute a local historic district. One notable example being 53 W . Chester Street, the former home of Emily Hoysradt, an artist who painted murals within the Gov. Clinton Hotel (Rhoads, 2003:126). Additional research into the historical and architectural significance of these contiguous structures is warranted to determi ne, at minimum, local historic district eligibility, and potenti ally National Historic District Eligibility; • that while 54 W . Chester Street has undergone some modifications (like the replacement of most wooden sash windows with vinyl windows and the presence of asbestos shingle siding), overall, the structure maintains a high degree of integrity across its exterior and is a goo d candidate for continued preservation and data -informed restoration to free any remaining features that are presently obscured by the late addition siding; • that 54 W . Chester Street is worthy of local landmark designation under Criteria C of the National Register of Historic Places, which recognizes it as "embodying the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or method of construction or represents the work of a master, or possesses high artistic values, or represents a significant and distinguishable entity whose components lack individual distinction"; • that the Commission held a required public hearing on March 7 ,2024, and the owner spoke at said hearing in favor of listing; • that the Commission finds that 54 W . Chester Street should be listed as a Local Landmark and hereby recommends same to the Common Council of the City of Kingston for final consideration and adoption; Based on the preceding amended findings of fact, it is proposed to resolve that on the 7th day of March 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, recommending that the Common Council of the City of Kingst on adopt the property for listing the property at 54 W . Chestnut Street as a City of Kingston's Local Landmark, for reasons described herein. (MG- motion, KM- 2nd; RT, all yes).

items.title: #70 W. Union Street: Exterior rehabilitation with minor demolition and new construction

items.discussion:
Kathryn Bangs, Ryan Giuliani, and Kim Hoover, project architect, were present at the
meeting to represent the applicant, Jesse Halliburton.  The project is to rehabilitate a circa 1880 barn located
at 70 W. Union Street in the Rondout -West Strand Historic District for use as a unit within their Bed &

Breakfast Complex. R. Giuliani  presented plans to demolish the existing single entry door  bay on the
structure’s west side, install a new footing, and construct a new two -story enclosed stairwell occupying
roughly the same square footage as the existing bay. The new construction will be slightly closer to the road
such that the green entryway door (which will be reused) will be flush with the original structure’s street
face. There will be a second entryway from the new bay’s rear that will be covered with a small roof. The
proposed enclosed stairway shall be clad in roughcut beadboard and reused siding from the demo -project
that shall be painted green to match the existing beadboard on the structure. Two  existing windows on the
2nd-story shall be removed, and two 2/2 sash windows shall be installed on the new construction’s westward
face – one on the first floor toward the rear, and the other on the second floor.  It is unclear if the original
windows will be reused in the new construction.
R. Giuliani discussed the installation of a glass window in the 2 nd-story street facing doorway that formerly
served as an opening to the storage loft with a tackle and hoist. The proposed window shall be the same size
as the original opening and will not significantly alter the structure’s appearance. This approach is considered
acceptable, as it could be easily undone in the future , if desired. The applicant noted that they will not be
raising a section of the structure’s roof via a minor glass dome  as initially discussed. Lastly, the applicant
intends to modify the structure’s 2 nd-story rear windows. Presently, the  existing windows are four 2/2
windows side by side. The proposed plan is to remove the two outer windows and to shrink the two inner
2/2 windows. This component of the project will not be visible from the public right of way.

The applicant and owner of 1-5 Main Street, Sarkis Simonian, presented his plans to replace
all the wooden windows on the 2 nd and 3rd floor of the structure along Main Street and Clinton Street  with
new Pella Lifestyle 1/1 windows with an unfinished wood interior and a white aluminum -clad exterior. S.
Simonian already painted the structure, installed a new roof, and replaced the 2nd story rear windows at 1-5
Main Street. At the request of E. Dickerman, HPA, S. Simonian submitted a window condition assessment,
performed by K. Riegel, a wood window specialist, acknowledging that the existing windows are restorable
but in bad condition and would require a lot of work, making the project costly.
Staff reminded the commissioners that 1-5 Main Street is at a prominent entry point into the Kingston
Stockade National Historic District. Commissioner R. Tonner noted that cost alone is not a justifiable reason
to replace existing wood windows that were deemed restorable by a wood window specialist and approval
of such a request would set a bad precedent by running contrary to the Secretary of Interiors Standards  for
the Treatment of Historic Properties.  After debating, the Commissioners and S. Simonian co mpromised
whereby S. Simonian will restore all the wood windows on the bay facing the intersection of Main and
Clinton Street. All other 2 nd and 3rd story windows shall be replaced with Pella Architectural Series Wood
Double-Hung Window with all wood exterior and interiors  that more appropriately match the
dimensionality of the existing wood windows. The applicant also agreed to give all original wood windows
scheduled for replacement to an architectural salvage center or a wood window specialty for reuse.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR and to find as fact that the proposed exterior rehabilitation with minor demolition and new construction at 70 W - Union Street in the Rondout -West Strand Historic District by Jesse Halliburton, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures sti pulated in Section 405.26.L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the foll owing reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the two story barn structure situated on the south side of W. Union Street, 5 parcels west of the intersection of W. Union Street and Wurts Street which dates to circa 1 BB0 and is present on the Burleigh map of 1 880 and which the is one of the few remaining barn structures in the Rondout -West Strand Historic District (70 W. Union, Building Structure inventory Form, 25 October 1976); • that the applicant intends to use the structure as a Bed and Breakfast operation associated with 85 Abeel Street; • that the applicant may demolish the existing single entry door bay on the structure's west side to construct a new two -story enclosed stairwell occupying roughly same square footage, but situated slightly closer to the road; • that the new construction shall be clad in rough cut bead board and re -used siding from the demolition, along with reuse of the existing entryway door and installation of a new door at the structure's rear; • that two existing windows on the 2nd -story shall be removed, and two 212 sash windows shall be installed on the new construction's westward face - one on the 1st - floor toward the rear, and the other on the 2nd- floor; • that the applicant may install a glass window in the 2nd -story street facing doorway that formerly served as an opening to the storage loft; • that the applicant may modify the structure's 2nd -story rear windows from the existing four 2/2 windows side by side to remove the two outer windows and to shrink the two inner 2/2 windows; • Any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding amended findings of fact, it is proposed to resolve that on the 7th day of March 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG-motion; NM-2nd; all yes). 5. #1-5 Main Street: Replacement of wooden windows. SBL: 48.331-4-10. SEQR Type II. Transect Zone: T5MS, HA. Ward: 2. Sarkis Simonian, applicant; 654 Broadway, LLC., owner.

The Commission voted in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and to find as fact that the proposed original wood window replacement project at 1 -5 Main Street in the Kingston Stockade Historic District by Sarkis Simonian, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405.26.L, of t he City of Kingston's Form Based Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the 3 -story brick commercial/residential building located on the northwest corner of the intersection of Main Street and Clinton Street which dates to circa 1900 and previous business occupants in 19'15 The Women' s Exchange, Emil Kuehn's pianos, E. Osborn's chiropodist (1-5 Main St, Building Structure inventory Form, July 1987); • that the applicant contacted Staff in December of 2023 seeking to replace the structure's wood windows at which time they were informed that restoration is preferred by the HLPC and that a window condition assessment was necessary for Staff and the HLPC to evaluate any application for replacement; • that on January 18 th, 2024, the applicant submitted a window condition assessment by Kurt Riegel of Riegel Restoration which demonstrated that the street facing windows are restorable and that restoration of the windows is preferable and will result in a longer lasting window than any modern replacement; however, the assessment did acknowledge that due to costs replacement could be permissible; • that the Commission recognizes the prominent position 1 -5 Main Street occupies at the intersection of Main and Clinton Streets within the Kingston Stockade Historic District and that replacement of badly degraded original windows is permissible due to thei r poor conditions as demonstrated in the window condition assessment; • that the applicant will restore the 10 original windows, on the second and third floor of the corner bay architectural feature; • that the applicant shall donate other removed windows for re -purpose and re -use elsewhere, with notification to the city of the final donation location; • that the applicant may replace the existing windows with Pella Architectural Series Wood Double - Hung Window with all wood exterior and interiors; • Any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to resolve that on the 7th day of March 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above reference Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG-motion; NM-2nd; AP & KM – yes; RT – opposed). items.title: Financial Incentives for Preserving Your Historic Property Presenter - Marissa Marvelli, Historic Preservation Specialist and City resident. Speaker’s Background: “Marissa Marvelli is a New York City/Hudson Valley-based historic preservation professional. Her work focuses on enhancing the vibrancy o
#95 Wurts Street: Replacement of entryway door and 27 windows
items.discussion:
P. Benkert presented plans to replace the existing 6 panel wood entryway and 27 existing
windows at 95 Wurts Street in the Rondout-West Strand Historic District. He noted that after listening to
the presentation given by the speaker, M. Marvelli, he would be interested in possibly pursuing some
alternatives.  P. Benkert stated that the existing entryway door is in disrepair and that it was his opinion
that restoration and retrofitting with modern weatherstripping would not rectify the issues. He proposed
replacing the door with a modern metal door from Lowes or Home Depot. A. Puetz identified the existing
door as likely a replacement based on the gap between the door frame and the structure’s masonry walls, a
sign of an earlier and wider entryway. Commissioners were amenable to replacement but requested the

applicant research other door options made of wood that are more period appropriate for the Second
Empire row house. P. Benkert and the Commissioners agreed to table the entryway door until next month’s
meeting.
P. Benkert also discussed replacing 27 existing windows across the structure’s four faces, the majority of
which are wood windows, with Anderson 500 1/1 double hung aluminum clad wood windows. One round
window on the south face of the structure is not intended to be changed or altered in any way.  Although he
submitted a statement late, he mentioned that his tenant on the ground level had expressed concern over
safety if windows are removed to be restored and that temporary covering would be in place.  It was noted
that a restoration process would involve windows in progression.
Staff and Commissioners discussed the importance of retaining the structure’s character defining features
and integrity. The 1976 Building Structure inventory form lauded the structure for its high integrity.
P. Benkert was skeptical of the effectiveness of restoring wood windows but was amenable to doing so and
to learning if the tax credit program could assist his rehab work at this site. P. Benkert proposed restoring
the most visible windows units, those being 8 wood windows on the street face, and the 1st and 2nd floor
wood windows closest to sidewalk on the structure’s north face. P. Benkert requested the HPA to resend
him resources (initially shared with P. Benkert on March 27th) regarding wood window restoration,
retrofitting, and specialists in the area after the meeting.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed replacement of the front door and 27 windows at 95 Wurts Street in the Rondout-West Strand Historic District by Paul T. Benkert, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405.26.L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is NOT compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the circa 1870 two-story Second Empire row style house located on the west side of Wurts Street three structures north of the intersection of Wurts & W. Pierpont Street, which, "appears on the 1 870 Beers map of Rondout" and may have replaced an earlier structure shown on the 1858 French map, and which has "received no major modern alterations. It is one of the more notable residences of its style in the district" (BSIF 1976); • that the Commission shall TABLE discussion on the door replacement to allow the owner time to research woodworking and energy saving options to repair/restore, and return back with information; • that the round window on the south face of the structure will remain untouched: • that the applicant has not provided sufficient evidence that the existing 27 wood windows are in poor condition and not able to be fully restored to be made functional and efficient; • that the applicant MUST RESTORE the existing wood windows visible along the front street facing facade and the 2 windows to the street side on the north face of the building; • that the applicant MAY REPLACE the remaining windows deemed not-visible from the public right-of- way with Anderson 400 double-hung windows in white; • that all wood windows approved for replacement must be transferred to an architectural salvage supply center or to a professional historic preservationist, for future re-use, and that the applicant shall provide a record of transfer as documentation to the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to resolve that on the 4th day of April 2024, the Commission DENY the proposal as submitted, and APPROVE a Preservation Notice of Action to the recognized applicant, for the scope of work as prescribed herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG- motion, NM-2nd; KM, AP- yes).

items.title: #20 Hone Street: Minor demolition of rear addition, construction of new rear deck, windows, roof, & painting
items.discussion:
Maynor Mazariego and Joshua Holland (present owner), presented to the commission their
plans for rehabilitating 20 Hone Street. The property is currently owner occupied and contains two units. J.
Holland seeks to expand the first-floor apartment into the basement, retaining the use of the structure as a
2 family.
Exterior work includes a new in-kind EPDM roof, in-kind replacement of the existing vinyl windows,
replacement of the front balcony decking, repainting the façade in BM historic color palate, the demolition
of a minor 2-story late addition to the structure’s rear, the construction of a 1st floor rear deck, and
installation of a mini split system.  With the exception of the demolition of the rear addition, the work
described is in-kind and will be reviewed by staff as a desk level reviews.
Section 405.26.J.c of the FBC requires the HLPC to review any application for a demolition permit related
to an Individually Landmarked property or properties within Landmark Districts. J. Holland and M.
Mazariego expressed gratitude and interest in the HP tax incentives programs detailed earlier in the
meeting, and may postpone work to learn if their projects qualify.
HLPC members present reviewed the rear location of the exterior elements to be demolished and evaluated
them as to their age and contributing character to the structure.  It was determined that they are not
original to the structure, are not visible from the public right-of-way, and do not contribute to the historic
integrity of the building.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed demolition of a late, rear, two-story addition at 20 Hone Street in the Rondout-West Strand Historic District by Maynor Mazariego (applicant) and Joshua Holland (owner), if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405.26.L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the circa 1858-1870 Second Empire row house with a mansard roof, pedimented gable dormers, and a wooden paneled entrance with a transom a side lights, located on the east side of Hone Street, one structure north of the intersection of Hone and W. items.title: #601 Broadway (UPAC): Replacement of 2nd floor street-facing wood windows
items.discussion:
Chris Silva, Executive Director of the BARDAVON 1869 OPERA HOUSE, Inc, and Betsy Garthwaite,
Facilities Manager, presented plans for replacing the existing 2nd-story Broadway facing wood windows at 601
Broadway (UPAC) a local landmark. C. Silva informed the Commission that the existing windows are in severe
disrepair and prevent the 2nd-story interior space from being used due to their ineffective R-value. UPAC planned to
replace these windows for years and finally received grant funding for the project. Prior to undertaking the work,
UPAC submitted existing conditions photographs to the State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) for review who
determined that their removal would not adversely impact the structure’s integrity and that the proposed LePage
Millwork (Canadian Based manufacturer) replicas are appropriate for the structure. Staff questioned if any windows
could be saved, or portions salvaged to combine and restore some of the windows.  C. Silva explained that the age of
the windows are unknown and that they are so severely degraded that they are most likely to fall apart.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed replacement of all 2nd-story Broadway facing wood windows at 601 Broadway, a local landmark, by the owner, BARDAVON 1869 OPERA HOUSE Inc. ("UPAC"), if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the landmark for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the two-story Colonial Revival theater/commercial building situated near the corner of Broadway and Cedar Street, that according to the July 2003 Building Structure inventory Form prepared by David L. Taylor, was "erected as a movie house in 1927 by the Kingston Theater Corporation - [and known] by the 'l93Os as the Broadway Theater. - The structure's design is the result of the collaboration of Iocal architect George E. Lowe (1890-1966) and Bridgeport, Connecticut theater specialist Douglas B. Hall (d. 1945)." • that the existing 2nd-story Broadway facing wood windows are severely degraded beyond restoration capability and require immediate treatment this year; • that the 601 Broadway is subject to two preservation covenants that require the property owner to seek New York. State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) review prior to the undertaking of any visual and/or material changes that could adversely impact the structure's integrity; • that UPAC submitted photographs of the existing windows conditions along with a request for permission to replace said windows with custom made, Lepage Millwork, single hung, wood and aluminum clad windows made to match the design, operation, and color of the existing windows; • that on December 14t11,2023, SHPO Historic Site Restoration Coordinator Sara McIvor determined that the proposed project "will have NO ADVERSE IMPACT on historic and archaeological resources"; • that after reviewing the proposed project and supporting materials, the HLPC shall follow the NO ADVERSE IMPACT position taken by SHPO' and permit the replacement of the existing windows with the proposed LePage Millwork windows; • that all wood windows approved for replacement must be transferred to an architectural salvage supply center or to a professional historic preservationist, for future re-use, and that the applicant shall provide a record of transfer as documentation to the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • that the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 13th day of May 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG - Motion, NM – 2nd, AP-yes, KM-yes)

items.title: #129 Maiden Lane: Converting existing ground floor window to entryway door & adding lighting
items.discussion:
The applicant, Dorothy Pierson, RA, presented plans to modify an existing ground floor window
along Green Street into a new street-facing entryway for a 2nd-floor guest apartment. D. Pierson explained that the
window is not original to the structure and made from glass blocks. The window is situated in a 19th-century timber
framed addition to the original stone dwelling. D. Pierson also explained that the door will be a simple 1/1 panel wood
door, with no exterior storm door added.  New steps will be made of bluestone and comply with the city code. D.

Pierson, informed staff that the hardware shall be an Antique Hardware Supply (TM) Solid Brass Rectangular Full
Length Morise Entryway Set D. Pierson, RA, also proposes to install a 14-watt (100-Watt equivalent) LED Feiss
Lighting-Redding Station-small outdoor wall lantern (9” wide by 9.69” tall by 10.38” extension) in Bronze finishes. A.
Puetz, Commission Architect, noted that the side lamp height appears to be low in the drawings and will require
placement up higher for adequacy and code.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed conversion of an existing window to an entryway door at 129 Maiden Lane, a local landmark, by Aditi Goswami, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the five-bay, double pile, 2 and 112 story vernacular dwelling at the northeast corner of Maiden Lane and Green Street in the which "was built circa mid-18th-century by the McLean family and burnt in October of 1777 by the British, and which was modified to suit the changing needs of the McLeans and subsequent owners (the Schoonmaker and Fowlers) over the next 200+ years" (Marvelli,2023); • that the new owner, Aditi Goswami, seeks to convert an existing window on the timber addition along Green Street into a new entryway door leading lo a 2nd floor staircase; • that the proposed window is comprised of fixed glass blocks and not original to the structure; • that the proposed door shall be the same width as the existing window's opening and made of solid wood with 1/1 panels consistent with that of the structure's primary entrance along Maiden Lane; • that the hardware shall be an Antique Hanivare Supply (TM) Solid Brass Rectangular Full Length Morise Entryway Set; • that the applicant shall install blue stone steps leading from the sidewalk to the proposed door that meet Building Code; • that the applicant shall install a single Feiss Lighting-Redding Station small outdoor wall lantern lamp in bronze color on the door's eastward side; • that the Commission reviewed the proposed project's supporting materials and determined it conforms with the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation and the character of the individual Landmark - because it could be undone, with a fair degree of ease, at a future time, if so desired by the owners; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • that the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 13th day of May 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in the application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG- Motion, NM-2nd, KM-yes, AP – yes).

items.title: #48 (46) N. Front Street: Modifications to fenestration and adding a cornice
items.discussion:
The applicant, Paul B. Jankovitz, presented plans to modify the 2nd-floor fenestration at 48 (46/44) N.
Front Street. P. Jankovitz proposed Pella Double Hung – clad, architect series reserve with black frames and grills.
Each window will be 3’.1’ x 4’.11” to meet egress requirements. No window trim is identified. The new order and

height of the fenestration is drawn from the adjacent property that houses Stella’s. P. Jankovitz also informed staff
that the new cornice element will project 18” beyond the structure’s face and no color has been selected at this time.
P. Jankovitz informed Staff that the Everywhere Shop will resubmit an application for modified signage given the
proposed window’s impacts. Staff questioned P. Jankovitz on the proposed modifications, the 2nd-floor interior
apartment space, the roof, and code compliance. The Commission felt that 1/1 windows (without a 3 lite transom)
ordered similarly to the adjacent Stella’s building are more appropriate. The Commission also questioned the
proposed cornice’s color and Form Based Code Compliance under sections: Section 405.14 C.2. e., Section 405.14 E.2.,
and Section 405.14 G.1. Other architectural elements are with the exterior stucco treatment finish.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to TABLE the proposed project pending the applicant’s return to the commission with an updated rendering that demonstrates compliance with the City of Kingston’s Form Based Code based on feedback received from the Commission. The applicant was advised that where compliance cannot be met, there may be waivers and/or variances required. (NM-motion, KM-2nd, MG, AP-yes). RECOMMENDATIONS:

items.title: #85 (83) Broadway (Half Moon Rondout Café): Non-code conforming window signage, minor waiver request
items.discussion:
K. Grundig was present to discuss the window signage request.  Per the City’s Form Based Code,
non-conforming window signage within historic districts must be reviewed by the HLPC. The Planning
Administrator has received a request for window signage from Kaira Grundig, of Half Moon Rondout Café.  The
matter was referred to the HLPC for a recommendation on a minor waiver of Section 405.17.E: Pedestrian Oriented
Signs which limits window signage to 1 per shopfront. K. Grundig seeks a waiver to install two window signs at their
85 (83) Broadway location in the Rondout-West Strand Historic District. Both signs shall be 48” wide by 28.93” tall.
A single door window sign 12” wide by 9.45” tall will also be installed. Colors will be white and gold. The
Commission recognized that the large windows were more balanced with signage in each, and that transparency of
the design is not inhibited.  Overall, the intent of the Code is not diminished.

decisions.text: The Commission reviewed the proposed signage and determined it visually compatible with the character of the RWSHD. (MG-motion, AP-2nd, KM, NM-yes).

items.title: #311 Wall Street: Non-code conforming wall signage, minor waiver request
items.discussion:
P. Jankovitz was present to discuss the wall signage request.  Per the City’s Form Based Code, non-
conforming wall signage within historic districts must be reviewed by the HLPC. The Planning Administrator
received a request for wall mounted lettering from Paul B. Jankovitz, RA.  The matter was referred to the HLPC for a
recommendation on a waiver of Section 405.17.E: Pedestrian Oriented Signs for the installation of a new wall sign
that exceeds the max size limit at 311 Wall Street.311 Wall Street now houses Uptown Studios. Historically, F.W.
Woolworth Company occupied the structure, and the historic signage serves as the inspiration for the proposed
Uptown Studies signage. The proposed Uptown Studios sign will be backlit with a “halo” effect. The City’s FBC
permits Wall signs up to 60 square feet, and the proposed sign’s lettering is 180 square feet of the structure’s Wall
Street façade. Typical frontage in for store in this area is 20 feet wide. The Commission also recognized that the
signage was approved under a previous code review.

decisions.text: The Commission reviewed the proposed historically informed signage and determined that it is compatible with the character of the Kingston Stockade Historic District. (MG-motion, NM-2nd, KM, AP-yes).

items.title: Form Based Code Review: Section 405.26.L: Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission
items.discussion:
Staff recommended that the Commission hold a Special Meeting at either the end of May or in June
to carefully review the proposed edits to Section 405.26.L (HLPC) of the City’s Form Based Zoning Code. Careful
review of the proposed edits was deemed not possible during regular meetings and warrants the added time and
attention given the proposed edits long-term influences on the Commission and Zoning Code. Staff will send out a
Doodle Poll to the Commissioners to identify a suitable date and time for the meeting.

items.title: Local Landmarking FAQs Revisited HLPC review of updated draft to be made available for public use
items.discussion:
Staff presented the final draft of a two page “Local Landmarking FAQs” document to the
Commission. The Commission reviewed and issued its support for the document which will be distributed as needed
and posted on the HLPC webpage.

items.title: 2024 Certified Local Government Grant Application
items.discussion:
Staff informed the Commission that the 2024 Certified Local Government Grant Application Cycle
opened and will close on May 31st, 2024. Staff plans to apply for the grant to fund nominating the proposed Wilbur
Historic District to the State and National Registers of Historic Places. Staff recommends this move because of the
existing support for local landmark districting and recognizes that by securing SR and NR designation property
owners will be able to benefit from robust tax credit programs. Staff presented a draft letter of and requested the
Commission authorize the Chairman to submit on the HLPC’s behalf in support of the application.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to support the City of Kingston’s application for the 2024 Certified Local Government Grant program and for the Commission Chair to sign and send the proposed letter of support as presented. (MG-motion, KM-2nd, NM -yes, AP-yes). Next Meeting: June 6th, 2024. This meeting will be live-streamed at the City of Kingston YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/c/CityofKingstonNY

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR and recommended that the proposed fenestration modifications and cornice installation at 48 (46) N. Front Street in the Kingston Stockade Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the two story store front building on the south side of North Front Street located between Wall and Crown Streets and which the July 1 987 Building Structure inventory form prepared by the Friends of Historic Kingston states that it could date to as early as the 1 840s but that an exact date of construction would be hard to determine, and that the shop once housed H. Houghtaling ('1 894), news dealer James McIntyre (1 901 )' - subsequent businesses included painters, barbers, beverages, a tavern, Artistic Beauty Salon, and Arties Bar & Grill; • that the applicant shall modify the existing 2nd-story N. items.title: Form Based Code Review: Section 405.26.L: Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission
items.discussion:
Staff reviewed the most current draft of a document that proposed edits to Section 405.26.L: HLPC of
the City’s Form Based Zoning Code that would update the code, make it more robust, provide greater clarity, and
conform with similar landmarks preservation commission codes elsewhere in NYS and beyond. It was noted that the
document had been circulated prior to the meeting for Commission members to review and consider commenting.
This document would also call for the removal of Section 264 of the City’s Administrative Code, to avoid redundancy
and to also eliminate conflicting language.  The proposed changes are drawn from the NYS recommended HLPC law
and ordinances in Ithaca, Syracuse, and Albany, New York. Some proposed changes, like the shift from Preservation
Notice of Action to Certificate of Appropriateness, represent terminology that is recognized in historic preservation
planning nationwide. Commissioners K. McEvoy had submitted some points for discussion that were reviewed.  One
matter was to be referred to Corporation Counsel for input and staff would make changes, if needed.  This was
related to the expiration of terms.  Some discussion was had on training opportunities and quorums and in-kind
reviews.  A. Puetz provided comments that involved minor editorial corrections and others that would provide
clarity, remove repetitiveness, use comprehensive terminology and improve submissions to the HLPC.  The
comments were all discussed, and revisions were incorporated in the attached draft document.

decisions.text: Following discussion and suggested edits to Section 405.26.L of the City’s Form Based Zoning Code, the Commission voted unanimously to recommend the proposed edits for consideration by the Working Zoning Task Force. (MG-motion, KM-2nd, AP, NM, RT - yes).

items.title: Revisiting the Proposed Kingston Stockade Expansion Historic District
items.discussion:
Recognizing a communication which was submitted to the HLPC prior to the meeting, staff shared
some additional email communication to members present.  Considering the discussion, it is recommended that the
Commission revisit the 1990 Tony Opalka and Peter D. Shaver Intensive Level Survey of the Stockade Expansion
Area and Albany Avenue, which proposed two National Historic Districts: The Kingston Stockade Expansion
Historic District and the Albany Avenue Historic District.

Staff has begun some initial research and surveyed key community stakeholders with institutional knowledge this
week to learn more about the 1990 report and why the two proposed districts were not formally established.
Commissioner Grunblatt informed the commission that some pushback from former property owners along Albany
Avenue and staffing limitations resulted in a lack of inertia. K. McEvoy and E. Dickerman, HPA informed the
commission that a Stockade Expansion would envelop the Fair Street Local Landmark District, therefore Certifying
that District would no longer be necessary. Staff asked commissioners if any of them would like to participate in a
working group to restart the Stockade Expansion, which would begin with a new grant funded Intensive Level
Survey of the areas defined in the original report. Commissioners are asked to contact E. Dickerman if they want to
participate. E Dickerman will begin searching for funding opportunities for the project.

items.title: Proposed Wilbur Historic District Public Hearings
items.discussion:
Staff informed the Commissioners that the proposed Ponckhockie Historic District is taking
additional time to secure support from property owners. As such, Staff feels it is appropriate to schedule the public

1.  Creation & Purpose. The Common Council (“Council”) finds that there exist s within the City of Kingston
(“City”) places, sites, structures, and buildings of historic , cultural,  or architectural significance, antiquity,
uniqueness of exterior design or construction, which should be conserved, protected, and preserved to maintain
the architectural character of the City, to contribute to the aesthetic value of the City and to promote the general
good, welfare, health and safety of the City and its residents.
The Council hereby creates the “Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission of the City of Kingston” (“HLPC”).
The purpose of th e HLPC  is to promote the general welfare by providing for the identification, protection,
enhancement, perpetuation, and use of buildings, structures, signs, features, improvements, sites, and areas
within the city that reflect special elements of the City’s historical, architectural, cultural, economic, or aesthetic
heritage for the following reasons:

(a) To foster public knowledge, understanding, and appreciation in the beauty and character of the city and
in the accomplishments of its past.
(b) To ensure the harmonious, orderly, and efficient growth and development of the city.
(c) To enhance the visual character of the city by encouraging new design and construction that
complements the City’s historic buildings.
(d) To protect and promote the economic benefits of historic preservation to the city, its inhabitants and
visitors.
(e) To protect property values in the city.
(f) To promote and encourage continued private ownership and stewardship of historic structures.
(g) To identify as early as possible and resolve conflicts between the preservation of historic
landmarks/districts and alternative land uses.
(h) To conserve valuable material and energy resources by ongoing use and maintenance of the existing
built environment.

2. Enabling Authority. Pursuant to Article 5, § 96 ‐a*2; Article 5‐G, Article 5‐J and Article 5‐K, § 119‐dd of the
General Municipal Law; Article 14 of the Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation Law; and § 10 of the
Municipal Home Rule Law; it is hereby declared as a matter of public policy that the protection, enhancement
and perpetuation of landmarks and historic districts are necessary to promote the cultural, economic and general
welfare of the public.

3.  Commission Composition, Appointment, Terms, & Compensation.
(a) Membership:  The HLPC shall consist of seven (7) members. The City Historian shall serve the HLPC in
an advisory capacity.
(b) Appointments:  Members of the HLPC shall be appointed by the Mayor. No
2
person appointed to the commission can also serve as a member of the City’s Council or Zoning Board
of Appeals.
(c) Term of Office: Terms of office shall be three years, which shall be so arranged that approximately 1/3 of
the terms shall expire each year. Upon adoption of this article, present members shall serve until the
expiration of their terms. Members of the HLPC may be reappointed for succeeding terms.
(d) Qualifications: To the extent possible, HLPC members shall be required to have the following expertise:
i. One shall be a licensed practicing architect;
ii. One shall be an owner of a City designated building or an Owner in a City Historic District;
iii. All others shall be residents of the City of Kingston and possess a demonstrated interest in and
commitment to the field of historic preservation as evidenced by involvement in a local, state, or
national historic preservation group; employment; education; historic property ownership, or
volunteer activity in furtherance of historic preservation;
(e) Vacancies:  Vacancies occurring in the HLPC other than by expiration of term of office shall be filled by
appointment of the Mayor. Any such appointment shall be for the unexpired portion of the term of the
replaced member, and the appointment must be made in accordance with the criteria established above
for original appointments.
(f) Reappointment:  Members of the HLPC may be reappointed for succeeding terms , providing that the y
continue to meet the criteria laid out in Section 3d.
(g) Compensation:  Members shall serve without compensation.
(h) Training and attendance requirements:
i. Each member of the HLPC shall complete, at a minimum, four (4) hours of training each year
designed to enable such members to more effectively carry out their duties. Such training shall
be approved by the Planning Director and may include, but not be limited to, training provided by
a municipality, regional or county planning office or commission, county planning federation, state
agency, statewide municipal association, college or other similar entity. Training may be provided
in a variety of formats, including but not limited to, electronic media, video, distance learning and
traditional classroom training.
ii. To be eligible for reappointment to the HLPC, a member shall have completed the training
approved by the Planning Director.
iii. No decision of the HLPC shall be voided or declared invalid because of a failure to comply with
this subdivision.

4. Organization.
(a) Chairperson; designation and duties.
i. The HLPC shall designate its Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson by vote of an affirmative majority
of the members of the full HLPC membership base.
ii. All meetings of the HLPC shall be held at the call of the chairperson and at such other times as
the HLPC may determine by affirmative vote.
(b) Staff person:  The City of Kingston’s Planning Department shall employ a staff person to serve as the
HLPC Secretary and Community Liaison.
(c) Quorum:  A simple majority shall be four (4) HLPC members and shall constitute a quorum for the
transaction of business.
(d) Costs of operation; budget requests. The cost of the operation of the HLPC shall be funded by the City.
The HLPC shall submit its budget request for appropriations to the Planning Director, annually, to be
submitted to the Mayor, as part of the annual budget review process.

5. Records and Annual Report. The HLPC shall maintain a record, which shall be open to the public view, of
its resolutions, proceedings, and actions. The vote or failure to vote of each member shall be recorded. The
concurring affirmative vote of a majority of the full HLPC shall constitute approval of plans before it for review or
3
for the adoption of any resolution, motion , or other action of the HLPC. The HLPC shall make such
recommendations to the Council as it deems necessary to carry out the purposes of this Chapter.

items.title: Wilbur Historic District: Local Landmark District Designation
items.discussion:
M. Grunblatt called the hearing, noting that the purpose of the public hearing was to
solicit comments from the public on moving forward with designation of a Local Landmark District in the
hamlet of Wilbur. S. Cahill provided general background on the process that transpired to reach this point
and provided an overview of the notifications/public outreach that was undertaken.  The Commission and
Staff, along with neighborhood residents that participated in local meetings view Local Districting as a key
step toward state and national register listing. All property owners within the defined district boundary
were sent, via certified mail, a communication announcing the hearing and providing information on the
district boundaries and other associated implications.  Notice of the Public hearing was posted in the local
newspaper two weeks in advance of the meeting. Two individuals spoke at the meeting:
Ald. Michele Hirsch, Ward 9 – Stated that she supports the local designation. She participated in the
Project Advisory Committee and attended the neighborhood meetings.  As the elected representative of the
area, she spoke with some residents and property owners, and is happy to report that there is support.  She
noted that some were present at the hearing this evening in support as well.
Robert King (35 Brook Street, Kingston) – He is not an owner of property within the area to be designated
as a district but resides in the Wilbur neighborhood and served as a member of the PAC for the grant to do
the Intensive Level Survey.  He stated that Wilbur is a unique area, relatively untouched.  It has both
history and architecture that are worthy of preserving and protecting.  He is very supportive of the local
landmark designation.
No one else spoke.
Chairman Grunblatt asked the Commission members present if there were any further comments or
questions that needed to be resolved before reading through the drafted resolution which was circulated
earlier to all members.

decisions.text: Chairman Grunblatt asked for the HLPC to close the hearing. (AP – Motion, KM – 2nd – NM, MG – Yes) The Commission moved to declare the matter of the recommendation a TYPE II under SEQR, under NYCRR Part 617.5 (c) (38). Chairman Grunblatt read the following draft resolution as a motion: RESOLUTION OF THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION COMMISSION (HLPC) OF THE CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, RECOMMENDING THE COMMON COUNCIL DESIGNATE A LOCAL LANDMARK DISTRICT IN THE WILBUR NEIGHBORHOOD AREA WHEREAS, in 2021, a NYS Office of Parks Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) Certified Local Government Grant funded an Intensive-Level Historic Resources and Building Survey of the Wilbur and Ponckhockie Neighborhoods conducted by Archaeology and Historic Resource Services, LLC. (AHRS): and WHEREAS, the work completed by AHRS delineated a potential Wilbur National Historic District, and was reviewed by OPRHP in December of 2023, to further refine the proposed boundaries of the Wilbur Historic District; and WHEREAS, the OPRHP issued a formal Determination of Eligibility Document registered on the State Cultural Information System that identifies the areas as meeting Criteria A and Criteria C of the National Register of Historic Places; and WHEREAS, City Staff and HLPC Commissioners further reviewed the proposed boundaries to include 19 Dunn Street (SBL: 56.57-2-26.100), as a contributing structure to the district; and WHEREAS, the City and HLPC conducted two neighborhood meetings in Wilbur to educate, answer questions, and provide assistance to property owners in the area about the benefits of and review processes associated with historic districting; and WHEREAS, the residents supporting the establishment of the Wilbur Historic District seek designation to ensure the neighborhood's preservation and to secure access to funding opportunities set aside by the local, state, and federal governments to assist owners of historic properties; and WHEREAS, the residents of the proposed district are pursuing Local Landmark Districting as a first step towards State and National Register District listing; and WHEREAS, the HLPC in accordance with Section 405.26.L.7 (Landmark or Landmark District designation procedure) secured sufficient signatures to hold a Public Hearing on the proposed Wilbur Local Landmark District; and WHEREAS, according to Section 405.26. L notifications of the proposed Public Hearing were posted in the City’s Newspaper and sent by Certified Mail letters of notice to all property owners within the proposed district; and WHEREAS, the HLPC held a Public Hearing, on July 10, 2024, at City Hall, and the HLPC heard favorable comment from 2 speakers, to recommend to the Common Council the creation of the Wilbur Local Landmark District, as delineated (Reference Attachment A); and WHEREAS, the HLPC finds that the proposed action is considered a Type II Action under 6 NYCRR, Part 617.5 (c) (38) and is predetermined not to have a significant impact on the environment and is precluded from environmental review under Environmental Conservation Law, Article 8. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, AS FOLLOWS: SECTION 1. Recommends that the City of Kingston’s Common Council designate the area outlined in “Attachment A” of this resolution as the WILBUR LOCAL LANDMARK DISTRICT. SECTION 2. That the Common Council incorporate the following Wilbur District Description and Statement of Significance under the City of Kingston Form Based Zoning Code as Section 405.26.L.8 a. vi.: “vi. Wilbur Local Landmark District is in a low-lying area surrounded by riverine hills at the confluence of the Twaalfskill Brook (now covered) and Rondout Creek 2.5 miles west of the Hudson River. Wilbur is located on the traditional homelands of the Esopus band of the Munsee- Algonquian speaking Lenape people. In the 17th-century, Dutch settlers recognized the area as a useful port and initially named it Twaalfskill Landing. By the early 1800s, Twaalfskill Landing served as a key port for shipping locally produced flour from nearby gristmills. In 1828, the newly completed Delaware and Hudson Canal advanced Wilbur into a receiving point for goods traveling from Eddyville (to the West) via the Rondout Creek. At Twaalfskill Landing, laborers transferred export commodities to larger boats sailing out via the Hudson. By 1829, the rise of the steamboat service between Twaalfskill Landing and New York City amplified the Twaalfskill Landing’s growth. In 1836, Abijah Smith, an early landholder, laid out a formal plan for the community’s streets which remain visible today. The community adopted the name Wilbur around this time. By the mid-19th-century, bluestone quarrying emerged as a locally viable building and export material which was primarily shipped out of the port at Wilbur. In the 1840s, Wilbur businessman Ezra Fitch founded a business dedicated to shipping bluestone that later expanded to include the sale of finished bluestone products. Fitch’s Bluestone Company, on the banks of the Rondout Creek, was the hamlet’s largest employer fueling economic prosperity. By 1850, the Fitch Bluestone Company was the world’s largest bluestone exporter. Rival bluestone companies operated in Wilbur at this time, along with hotels, cement quarries, and mills. Wilbur’s commercial properties stood closer to the creek and along Wilbur Avenue, while the working-class dwellings occupied side streets. Later houses built on the hamlet’s western hill include the home of William B. Fitch, a relative of Ezra Fitch, who later led the company. In 1872, Wilbur merged with the Villages of Kingston and Rondout to form the City of Kingston. Development within the district persisted into the 1880s, with the Church of the Holy Name on Fitch Street constructed in 1885. By this time, however, the popularity of Portland cement superseded demand for bluestone. In 1890, the Fitch Bluestone Company closed extinguishing new construction in Wilbur for the next several decades. The Wilbur Local Landmark District’s historic and cultural resources exhibit the Federal, Italianate, and Gothic Revival styles and include residences, commercial buildings, a firehouse, and a church. The district’s period of significance extends from 1836 to 1890, reflecting the community’s development and peak with a distinct built environment that meets Criteria A and C of the National Register of Historic Places. The Wilbur Local Landmark District’s boundary incorporates the intact built portion of the hamlet laid out in 1836 by Abijah Smith, and as listed on the City’s Regulating Map. This includes the National Register-listed Fitch Bluestone Company Office Building; all buildings on Davis, Dunn, Burnett, Fitch, and Duflon Streets; the buildings on the west side of Abeel Street between Davis Street and parcel 56.57-2-3.100; and the buildings on Wilbur Avenue between Abeel Street and parcel 56.49-3-1.” SECTION 3. Per Section 405.26.L.7.f. of the City’s Form Based Zoning Code, the Wilbur Local Landmark District shall have interim protection under the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission. SECTION 4. This resolution shall take effect immediately and remain in full effect upon adoption by the Common Council. items.title: 35 Wurts Street: Replacement of existing wood railings with architectural salvaged wrought iron railings
items.discussion:
The applicant/owner, Thomas Kreuger, presented his plan to install a new wrought iron
front porch railing at 35 Wurts Street, a mid-18th-century 2nd-Empire Parsonage for Trinity Church. Staff
shared historical photographs to demonstrate that the structure pre-1956 (date of CoK Property Record
Card), had more elaborate balustrades for the front porch railings, however, the exact style and material
composition cannot be determined. It is likely that the early detailed railings were made of wood with
turned balusters. T. Kreuger proposes architecturally salvaged wrought iron and wood railings sourced
from a structure in Patterson, New Jersey, slated for demolition. Photos taken of these inside the current
structure to be demolished were shared.  Commissioner Tonner noted that railings are a good adaptive
reuse appropriate to the structure’s period and design. T. Krueger stated that the railing will be installed
and painted to protect it from the elements. Commissioner McEvoy asked how the bottom would be
treated, as the existing rails terminate in structural columns.  After looking at photos of the pre-existing
staircase and rail system, T. Krueger stated that he would design new wooden posts to be installed at the
base of the stairs to support the railing. S. Cahill asked if the applicant had reviewed the proposed rail with
BSD for compliance with NYS Code and T. Krueger confirmed that the proposed railing will conform with
Building Code Requirements.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2) (18) and recommended that the proposed front porch and stair railing replacement at 35 Wurts Street in the Rondout-West Strand Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the two-story brick Second Empire dwelling dating between 1858 and 1870 that stands adjacent to the Trinity Methodist Church at the corner of Wurts and Hunter St which the October 2'1st, 1971 Building-Structure Inventory Form prepared by the Friends of Historic Kingston states "was the parsonage for the neighboring Methodist church. The residence retains its original decorative features and has received no major modern alterations. lt is one of the most intact and important structures of its type and style in the district"; • that during the course of the property's rehabilitation, the property owner, identified early photographs that demonstrate the structure initially had detailed balustrades for the porch and front steps' railings, but that the exact design and material cannot be identified; • that the proposed metal and wood architectural salvage railings from the interior of a structure from Paterson, NJ, while are different materials than the existing wood railings, can be considered appropriate for the structure's period and design; • that the railings shall not be painted, but treated to preserve the wood top rail, with post at bottom, design submitted to staff for final review; • that new railings shall conform to code requirements under the NYS Building Code; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 1st day of Augusl2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (KM – motion; RT – 2nd; AP, NM - yes).

items.title: 35 Bruyn Ave (Barrel Factory): National & State Register of Historic Places Listing
items.discussion:
Dan Sirotkin of MHV Developer, LLC, owners of the “Barrel Factory”, presented their proposal to list 35
Bruyn Avenue on the State and National Register of Historic Places to allow them access to Commercial Rehabilitation
Tax Credits (40-50%). D. Sirotkin reiterated the structure’s history as an employer of over 70 people in the 1920s, a site
for bootlegging, and additional information as stated in the nomination paperwork and identified in the prepared
Statement of Significance Summary:

The Kingston Barrel Factory is a two-story brick industrial building located at 35 Bruyn Avenue in Kingston, New York that was built
ca. 1914 as a box manufacturing factory and transitioned to use as a barrel manufacturing facility in 1917. The factory is locally
significant under Criterion A in the category of INDUSTRY as a plant central to the industrial development of Kingston.
While in operation as the Kingston Barrel Factory, the building served a large New York market and employed as many as fifty to seventy
skilled workers, even during the economic downturn of the Depression years. The barrel plant functioned as a tight cooperage, meaning the
barrels manufactured there were designed to hold liquids instead of solids. Tight barrels were in demand and required more skill to make;
thus, the factory brought a successful and lucrative business to the city at a time when the United States was the top cooperage producer in
the world. The plant trained new skilled craftsmen to produce tight cooperage, which needed to be expertly finished to avoid leaks. There
were few tight cooperages on the East Coast when the Kingston Barrel Factory opened, and its strategic location in Kingston in proximity
to the railroad and the Hudson River allowed it to directly compete for the New York City market with the other large tight cooperages
from places such as Newark, New Jersey. By pivoting away from producing barrels for ale and liquor during Prohibition, the plant was
able to continue operation during these years, which also coincided with the Depression, maintaining some jobs for local workers and
contributing to the local economy. Despite its official turn from doing business related to the liquor industry, the Kingston Barrel Factory
is also significant under criterion A in the area of SOCIAL HISTORY for its association with an illegal
bootlegging operation during prohibition. The factory maintained a link to Legs Diamond, a notorious gangster and bootlegger
who bottled and stored ale at the site until federal agents seized one million dollars' worth of alcohol and equipment during a raid here in
1931. The period of significance begins ca. 1917, when it became a barrel factory, and ends in 1954, when the barrel factory closed, and the
building transitioned to use as a warehouse.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (38) and endorsed sending a Letter of Support for the nomination of 35 Bruyn Ave (the Barrel Factory) to the State & National Register of Historic Places. The letter will be sent from Acting Commission Chair McEvoy. (RT – motion; NM – 2nd; KM, AP - yes). items.title: Petition to Designate the Pike Plan Canopy (N. Front & Wall Street): Local Landmark Designation
items.discussion:
On August 6th, 2024, William Gottlieb Management Co., LLC (WGM) submitted to the Planning Office
a Section 405.26.L. 7 emergency landmarking petition containing 37 signers, of which 15 are verified as City of Kingston
residents.  The petition requested that the HLPC landmark the Pike Plan Canopy - a colonnaded canopy affixed to 44
designated structures within the Kingston Stockade National and Local Historic District.
Victoria Polidoro, Esq. (Rodenhausen, Chale, & Polidoro, LLP) representing the William Gottlieb
Management, Co., LLC, introduced to the Commission the parties present to represent the petition in addition
to herself was, Kerri Culhane, Ph.D.; Walter Wheeler, Hartgen Archeological resources; Paul Jankovitz,
Architect; and Benjamin Neidl, Attorney.  V. Polidoro summarized her clients petition to Locally Landmark the
Pike Plan Canopy. She noted that Kerri Culhane, Ph.D., and Walter R. Wheeler of Hartgen, both architectural
historians will present on their independent (and blind test) reports claiming that the Pike Plan meets the local
criteria for individual landmark status and the criteria for inclusion as a contributing feature within the
Kingston Stockade National Historic District.
PRESENTATION:
1. Kerri Culhane, Ph.D. has over two decades of experience in architectural history, planning, and NR
nominations. Her research identifies the Pike Plan as meeting the Section 405.26.L.7 of the Local
Landmarks Code and NR criteria necessary as a contributing structure to the Kingston Stockade
Historic District. Culhane posited the structure is associated with a significant period in US history
(Urban Renewal) and a significant person (John Pike), that it is 50 years old, and maintains sufficient
integrity for inclusion in the district. Culhane, PhD. announced she submitted a request to the State
Historic Preservation Office to review the City of Kingston owned Pike Plan and to render a
determination on its eligibility.
a. See Culhane, Ph.D.’s report for more information: https://kingston-
ny.gov/filestorage/8399/8491/8499/35761/63300/67265/67267/2024.8.30_PP_report_K.Culhane%
2CPh.D._%28Updated%29.pdf

2. Walter R. Wheeler (Hartgen Archaeological Associates, Inc.) informed the group that he has over
40 years of experience in architectural history, with the last 25 years working as a senior architectural

items.title: 171 Wall Street: Removal of a non-contributing garage (accessory structure)
items.discussion:
Eric Winchell, the applicant and property owner, presented plans to remove the exis ting non-
contributing garage structure in the northwest corner of his property that is severely degraded from termite
damage. Photos of the existing conditions were shared with the HLPC members. R. Tonner asked  about the
approximate age of the structure and E. Winchell noted it was constructed around 1958.  He explained that he
plans to remove the structure and will not rebuild. The site of the garage shall be returned to just the lawn.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (25) and recommended that the proposed demolition of a non -contributing and degraded garage at 171 Wall Street, a local landmark, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405 -26 L & Section 405.26.J. c, of the City of Kingsto n's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the property for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at a non -contributing accessory garage in the northwest corner of 171 Wall Street, the circa 1720 1.5 story Jacobus Masten Dutch stone house, situated on the west side of Wall Street mid-way between St. James and Warren Street; • that the existing mid-20th-century non-contributing garage is in severe disrepair due to termite damage and must be removed; • that the applicant proposes to remove the structure, with no replacement and will be returning the area to lawn; • that the applicant shall follow all legal requirements during the removal and disposal of debris; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Demolition Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 10th day of October 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Com mission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (Motion – MG; 2nd -RT; all yes)

items.title: 27 Crown Street: Construction of a new ground -floor entrance and exterior 3 rd-story ADU staircase
items.discussion:

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (2) (11) and recommended that the proposed creation of a new entryway door on the front porch and construction of an exterior staircase in the rear for a 3rd -floor ADU, with the Major Waiver authorized, at 27 Crown Street in the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that the proposed work is to take place at the 2.5 story Queen Anne Victorian dwelling situated mid-way between St. James and Warren Streets dating to the 1880s, that was occupied during this period by Noah Wolven, who worked as postmaster and a dry goods merchant, and subsequently his son William before being sold out of the family in the 1920s (SHPO Building Structure Inventory Form, 1987); • that the applicant shall construct a new basement door that matches the 1/1 panel design, composition, and color of the existing ground floor entryway door on the north side of the front porch surrounded by the same trim work, but that this new door shall have a solid wood upper panel instead of a glass panel; • that the applicant shall construct a new exterior staircase made of white painted wood in the structure's rear that shall provide access to a new 3rd-story code compliant ADU rental unit; • that a new rear facing dormer on the north gable shall be constructed following the original structure's design features, materials, and colors to allow access from the new staircase into the ADU unit; • that the 3rd-floor Crown Street-facing gable 1/1 double hung windows are late replacements and must be replaced to meet Building Code Standards for 3rd-story ADU residential spaces; • that the applicant may install new Windsor Pinnacle Wood windows with 5/8" muntins in a diamond pattern in the 3rd-story Crown Street-facing gable to meet egress code requirements; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application may be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 10th day of October 2024, the Commission grant a Preservation Notice of Action to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Com mission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion.
