items.title: Referral From Zoning Task Force: Form Based Zoning Code 1st-Floor Height Requirements
items.discussion:
Bartek Starodaj, the Director of Housing Initiatives, was not present, so Suzanne Cahill, the Planning
Director, spoke on the matter. S. Cahill stated that the City’s FBC Working Group seeks input from the HLPC on 1st-floor
height requirements for T5 and TN transects. She relayed the following message and discussed the existing height
requirements and the proposed changes:

As you might be aware, in the City’s form -based Code, each T5 and T4 Transect requires certain first floor height in any new
construction. For example, as detailed in Table 1, a new building built in the T5 Main Street transect would be required to have a first-floor
height of 16’. These requirements impact new construction in all four of the City’s Historic Districts.
Generally, the purpose of the first -floor height requirement is to ensure new buildings meet their surrounding context, that there is a
consistent building to street relationship, and that new buildings could be easily adapted to changing neighborhood conditions. For example,
a previously residential building could eventually become a commercial one.
However, the working group is reviewing these requirements to ensure they are achievable and that they accurately reflect the context
of each transect. Based on an initial review of the requirements that in effect, we propose lowering the requirements in m ost transect areas
(see Table 1).
We are currently seeking feedback on these proposed changes. Please note that the zoning working group will only recommend an y
potential changes to the Common Council, which would then decide whether to take any action.

The proposed changes extend beyond the city’s historic districts and individually listed landmarks but could
have a direct impact on the streetscapes of historic districts if the proposed new construction is not compatible
with the existing historic 1 st-floor heights. B. Starodaj submitted a rough survey of the city’s transects that is
broader than just the historic districts.

S. Cahill recommended the Commission members visit the city’s five historic districts to study the exisiting 1 st-
floor heights and identify a more nuanced approach to the new construction and 1st-floor height requirements in
historic districts. Staff identified that the Commission may wish to consider a  contextual approach in historic
districts, which may provide for increasing/decreasing a height  based on residential and commercial uses.   A.
Puetz, noted that in considering any heights, there is always consideration of mechanicals that are located in
ceilings and also the required heights with different staircases and landing positioning.

The HLPC agreed that a more contextual approach is advisable .  It was noted that HLPC members would take
the time to visit various districts to consider the impacts of first floor heights and identify existing conditions.
Staff were asked to return the proposed language, which incorporated a contextual approach for the November
7th, 2024, meeting.

decisions.vote: Motion - MG; 2nd -AP; RT, KM, NM - yes
decisions.text: The Commissioners present voted unanimously to TABLE the proposed change in favor of adding a separate line to the Form Based Zoning Code for properties that are designated as historic or are in Historic Districts. Members will make the effort to visit the various districts prior to the next meeting to specifically identify the existing first floor conditions. Staff will also work to identify language for consideration. (Motion - MG; 2nd -AP; RT, KM, NM - yes).

items.title: Petition to Designate the Pike Plan Canopy (N. Front & Wall Street): Local Landmark Designation
items.discussion:
On August 6th, 2024, William Gottlieb Management Co., LLC (WGM) submitted to the
Planning Office a Section 405.26.L. 7 emergency landmarking petition containing 37 signers, of which 15 are
verified as City of Kingston residents. The petition requested that the HLPC landmark the Pike Plan Canopy - a
colonnaded canopy affixed to 44 designated structures within the Kingston Stockade Local, State, National
Historic District. Mark Grunblatt, Esq. Chair of the HLPC began by recognizing the KSHD as the first historic
district in Kingston established before  state and national enabling legislation. He shared several important
statements from the old code that were carried over to the New Form Based Zoning Code:

Section 405.26.L.8.a.i: Landmarks and Landmark (L) Districts:
Legislative intent: The purpose of this section is to provide for the promotion of the educational, cultural, economic and
general welfare of the public through the protection, enhancement, perpetuation and preservation of landmarks and

Landmark (L) Districts. The legislative body declares that it is in the public interest to ensure that the distinctive
landmarks and Landmark (L) District shall not be injuriously affected, that the value to the community of those buildings
having architec tural and historical worth shall not be impaired and that said districts be maintained and preserved to
promote their use of the education, pleasure and welfare of the citizens of the City of Kingston and others.

Section 405.26.L.8. ii. 2: Landmarks and Landmark (L) Districts:
This area contains the architecture of the past 300 years, and new development must not be allowed to erode the best of the
architectural spaces and cultural organizations of the past.

Section 405.26.L.9 (Review Procedure):
c) All applications shall be considered by the Commission on at least the following points, these points to be used as a basis,
where relevant, for establishing relationships to the external features of buildings in the immediate neighborhood: The
building he ight in relation to surrounding buildings; the relationship to nearby roof shapes; the relationship between the
width to height of the front elevation; the size, proportion and spacing of openings within the facade and elevations exposed
to view; the rhyth m of spacing of buildings and building elements on the street; the design and placement of entrances and
projections; the relationships of materials, textures and colors; the relationship of architectural details; the continuity o f
walls; the relationship of landscape elements; the appropriateness of paving; and the effect on existing or historically
significant spaces.
d) It shall be the further duty of the Commission to exercise judgment in accord with the basis of decisions stated herein and
maintain the desirable character of the landmark or Landmark District and prevent construction, reconstruction, alteration
or demolition out of harmony with existing buildings insofar as character, material, color, line and detail are concerned, and
thus to prevent degeneration of property, to safeguard public health, promote safety and preserve the beauty of the character
of the landmark or Landmark District.
e) It shall be the further duty of the Commission to exercise judgement in accord with the guidance of the US Secretary of the
Interior Standards for Rehabilitation.
Commissioner Grunblatt shifted to the four criteria in Section 405.26.L.7.b of the FBC that the HLPC are to use
in evaluating the Pike Plan for local landmark status:
The criteria for the designation of landmarks shall particularly favor such designation where the proposed landmark or
Landmark District:
i. Exemplifies or reflects the broad cultural, political, economic or social history of the nation, state or community;
ii. Is identified with historic personages or with important events in national, state or local history;
iii. Embodies distinguishing characteristics of an architectural -type specimen, inherently valuable for a study of a
period, style, method of construction or of indigenous materials or craftsmanship; or
iv. Is representative of the notable work of a master builder, designer or architect whose individual ability has been
recognized.

At this point, Victoria Polidoro, JD presented the HLPC with commentary from one of the petitioner’s experts,
Kerri Culhane, Ph.D. responding to the Pike Plan reports by preservationist Neil Larson and Ethan Dickerman,
HPA. Copies were provided to Commission members present and M. Grunblatt summarized the statement, with

a copy transmitted to Commissioner McEvoy who was attending the meeting remotely.  K. Culhane argued N.
Larson supports Culhane and Wheeler’s  reports – recognizing the Pike Plan as  eligible as a contributing
structure on the local, state, and national registers. K. Culhane argued that E. Dickerman, HPA’s report, contains
a “number of factual errors and misrepresentations of preservation policy and practice,” therefore the commission
to place more weight on N. Larson’s conclusions.

Mr. Neil, Larson, a recognized expert in Hudson Valley history engaged by the  Kingston Historic Landmarks
Preservation Commission, agrees with the Petitioner's two independent experts on the matter at hand: The Pike P lan has
accrued historic significance for its association with the complex histories of urban renewal and preservation in Kingston,
and accordingly it should be considered a contributing resource to the local as well as State and National Register Stockade
Historic District. (Larson, 9/20/2024: 9-1 1).
ln a subsequent report compiled by Mr. Ethan Dickerman, Historic Preservation Administrator to the City
(9/2712024), Mr. Larson's report is recast as supporting an opposite conclusion: that the Pike Plan is not historic and that
it lacks integrity. Given the number of factual errors and misrepresentations of preservation policy and practice in the
Dickerman report, emphasis on this rebuttal is placed on the findings of the City's outside consultant, Mr. Larson.

THE INTEGRITY DISCUSSION

The integrity standard set by the National Register is mirrored in local evaluation. The seven (7)criteria  for
evaluating integrity are Location, Design, Setting, Material, Workmanship, Feeling and  Association. A resource does not
need to meet all of the criteria, only a majority of them; contrary  to Mr. Dickerman's assertion that a resource "should
exceed 750/o of the criteria" (Dickerman 2024:10) no percentage system is prescribed by the National Register, and in fact
only a simple majority is needed (417).
Mr. Larson argues that a case can be made for the Pike Plan meeting five (5) of the seven (7) criteria: Location, design,
setting, feeling and association (Larson 2024:9). Mr. Dickerman misreads Mr. Larson's integrity discussion, citing Larson
as stating that the Pike Plan meets only three (3) of the seven (7) criteria. (Dickerman 2024:1 0). However, Larson actually
argues for five (5) of the seven (7) criteria; Location, design, setting, feeling and association. (Larson 2024:9). To
quote Mr. Larson: "Enough qualities have been met to make a claim of historic integrity..."(Larson 2024:9)

OUT OF SCOPE ISSUES

On page 1 1 of his report, Mr. Larson states: "l would support a plan to preserve the Pike Plan but would understand if
it would be more economically prudent to remove them...". White Mr. Larson weaves into his argument topics that are
outside the scope of  the KHLPC, specifically, mixed public opinion and the City of Kingston's financial considerations,
these confuse a deliberation that must set those concerns aside. Simply stated: ln the professional opinion of the City's
outside expert, the Pike Plan is historic and worthy of preservation.

The Commission then returned  to debating the Pike Plan’s eligibility against each of Section 405.26.L.7.b ’s
criteria for landmark designation. Commissioner Grunblatt noted that the HLPC is not bound to the National
Register’s 50-year guideline for structures to become eligible for designation.

Chairman Grunblatt stated that the Pike Plan is not representative o f a common type of Urban Renewal
approach and that a better example of the process would be found in the Rondout . He further noted that he
appreciated the opinion of J. Hoyt , noting that he was present, knew the people involved an d what the
considerations were. Other Commissioners agreed that the Pike Plan did not exemplify Urban Renewal, which
was primarily associated with the wide scale destruction of neighborhoods and construction of modernist
apartment complexes, malls, and governmental facilities. Instead, the Pike Plan is recognized as a niche response
to the rise of shopping malls to give pedestrians protection from the elements. Furthermore, the HLPC did not
feel it meets the criterion for association with a person of significance at this time, no r did they feel it meets the
criterion for association with an architectural style of significance, or association with a master builder.
Commissioner Grunblatt cited the Tri-Arts Building as a better example of a structure exemplifying a significant
architectural style.

Commissioner McEvoy encouraged the other commissioners to consider N. Larson’s evaluation of integrity for
the Plan, believing that N. Larson did not fully argue that the Pike Plan of today retains sufficient integrity for
inclusion in the local, state, and national registers:

For historic resources to be considered eligible for the National Register, either individually or as contributing features in
a historic district, they first need to pass an integrity test to verify authenticity. Seven qualities form the basis for
evaluation, of which a majority is expected to be met: location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, feeling, and
association. The Pike Plan meets the first three, although its design has been compromised, but fails in materials and
workmanship as a result o f later alterations. The quality of feeling is debatable because people react both positively and
negatively to the presence of the canopies and the impact they have had on the facades of pre -existing buildings. The plan’s
association with the historic dis trict has already been demonstrated. Enough qualities have been met to make a claim of
historic integrity, but alterations to the design and questionable qualities of feeling reflect on the ongoing issue of its
authenticity. There is not a clear path here, but it appears that the very presence of the canopies over the past 50 years argue
for their preservation. They have become a character-defining feature of the Stockade. However, the Pike Plan’s structural
integrity is an important consideration. Since th eir construction in the 1970s, the canopies have created no end of
maintenance problems leading to a virtual reconstruction in 2010. This latest iteration is now in need of an overhaul. A
strict application of the integrity test, finding that authenticity has been compromised, coupled with the poor physical
conditions, and the expense of rehabilitation, which would further compromise integrity, is persuasive (Larson, 2024: 9).

Commissioners McEvoy and Grunblatt discussed the importance of the final line of N. Larson’s first paragraph
in integrity and how it differs from the statements by K. Culhane. Commissioner Grunblatt pointed out that
there is a lot of evaluation and judgement in this project  and that the authenticity of the structure has been

compromised. Commissioner Puetz felt that the matter is subjective. Commissioner Tonner mentioned that he
owned 301 Wall Street along the Pike Plan, when it was reconstructed in  2010-2011, and that resulted in a total
loss of integrity. Commissioner Tonner could not wrap his head around the Pike Plan as historic, which itself is
choking off historic buildings. Commissioner Morano pointed out that the Pike Plan’s presence in the KSHD is
minimal when compared to the area’s deeper history  of local, state, and national significance. The buildings
themselves along Wall Street are the examples to highlight and go back to.  Commissioner Grunblatt added that
elevating the Pike Plan to a local landmark is an in appropriate use of Section 405.26.L’s powers. Instead, he
worries that the canopy’s presence is causing harm to the district’s designated structures. Commissioner Tonner
concurred and referenced news articles from the 1980s that notified the Kingston residents about the structure’s
poor condition. The present buildings cannot evolve with the canopy the way they are.  He made the statement
that the reconstruction in  the 2010s was “half -assed.” Commissioner McEvoy added that the lack of integrity
weighs against the Pike Plan’s ability to meet criteria A of the local code.

Commissioner Puetz pointed out a similar canopy in Morristown, Tennessee, that differs in design, materials,
and maintenance – but felt this similar example was useful for the HLPC to be aware of at this time.
Commissioner Tonner referenced an Urban Renewal housing project in St. Louis, Missouri, that was so disliked
that the process of removing it started about a decade later and is still underway. M. Grunblatt pointed out that
some apartments, the police station, and other structures in Rondout better exemplify Urban Renewal than the
Pike Plan. He made the comment that the Pike Plan does damage to the fabric of the district, that it is now only
a “dull echo” and does not meet historic district criteria.  Commissioner Grunblatt then moved to close debate
and shifted to rendering a determination on the petition.

The Commission moved to declare the matter of the recommendation a TYPE II under SEQR, under NYCRR
Part 617.5 (c) (38). Chairman Grunblatt read the following draft resolution as a motion:

RESOLUTION OF THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION COMMISSION (HLPC) OF THE
CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, RECOMMENDING AGAINST THE DESIGNATION OF THE PIKE
PLAN CANOPY AS A LOCAL LANDMARK IN THE KINGSTON STOCKADE LOCAL, STATE, AND
NATIONAL HISTORIC DISTRICT

WHEREAS, on August 6, 2024, William Gottlieb Management Co., LLC (“WGM”) and their
representatives filed a petition with the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (“HLPC”) with 37 signers,
out of which 15 were confirmed Kingston residents, requesting the Pike Plan Canopy (“Canopy”) along portions
of North Front and Wall Streets be designated a local landmark according to Section 405.26.L. 7  of the City’s
Form Based Zoning Code (“FBC”); and

WHEREAS, the petition seeks emergency designation of the Pike Plan Canopy as a landmark on the
basis that it exemplifies the broad cultural, political, economic and social history of the City of Kingston, and the
Pike Plan is identified with historic personages or with important events; and

WHEREAS, the petition incorporated two professional preservation reports, one by Walter R. Wheeler
of Hartgen Archaeological Associates, Inc., and another by Kerri Culhane, Ph.D., which claimed the Canopy met:

1. Section 405.26.L.7 of the FBC Criteria for landmarks; and
2. Criterion A, B, C of the National Register of Historic Places (NR); and
3. the NR’s 50-year age guideline; and

WHEREAS, the HLPC engaged Neil Larson of Neil Larson and Associates: Historic Preservation and
Planning Services, Inc., an independent preservation consultant, to review the submitted materials and produce
its own report on the Canopy’s eligibility for local landmark status; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to Section 405.26.L 7 of the FBC, the HLPC notified the petitioners and affected
property owners by certified mail, and posted notice in the local newspaper on August 19, 2024, of a public
hearing to be held on September 11, 2024; and

WHEREAS, the HLPC held a public hearing on September 11, 2024, at which written comment received
prior to and at the hearing was recorded, along with the oral testimony of the public; and

WHEREAS, at the public hearing several property owners along North Front and Wall Street’s spoke
explaining reasons why the canopy would not be eligible for landmark status, including:
a) The Canopy is a new reconstruction and compromises the historic integrity of buildings.
b) The Canopy lacks integrity of design by John Pike because of previous alterations in 2010 -
2011.
c) The Canopy damages the designated structures to which it is affixed.
d) The Canopy hinders the ability for pedestrians to experience the intended design of the
district buildings and is an inappropriate structure for the character of the KSHD.

WHEREAS, at the September 11, 2024, meeting, the HLPC voted to table a decision on the petition,
pending receipt of a report by the City’s consultant, and leaving the Public Hearing open to accept additional
written comments until September 30, 2024;

WHEREAS, two additional written comments regarding the matter were received prior to close of
business on September 30, 2024, and recorded; and

WHEREAS, on September 20, 2024, the City’s preservation consultant submitted their professional
report, which was posted on the City website, concluding the following:

A. The Canopy only meets Criterion A (Exemplifies or reflects the broad cultural, political, economic or
social history of the nation, state or community) of Section 405.26.L.7.b.i of the FBC for its association
with Kingston’s Urban Renewal Era;

B. The Canopy only meets Criterion A of the National Register for its association with the Urban
Renewal Era;

C. The Kingston Stockade Historic District’s National Register nomination paperwork and local
landmark district description in Section 405.26.L.8.ii of the FBC should be updated to expand its
Statement of Significance (SOS) and the Period of Significance (POS ) up to, at least, 1975 to include
Kingston’s Urban Renewal Era and the Pike Plan Canopy as a ‘Contributing Structure’ within the
district;

D. The Canopy only meets three (3) out of the seven (7) aspects of the National Register’s Integrity Test
and acknowledges that the Pike Plan Canopy’s integrity is substantially compromised disqualifying
the structure from the National Register and local landmark designation; and

WHEREAS, the City of Kingston’s Historic Preservation Administrator prepared an independent report
dated September 27, 2024, which was posted to the City website, that concludes the following:

A. Historical and contemporary photographs of North Front and Wall Street’s demonstrate, beyond
doubt, the substantial alterations to the Canopy since its completion in 1976, including the original
structure’s temporary removal, subsequent reconstruction with new fabric, loss of character defining
features, and addition of inappropriate modern features during the City -led reconstruction between
2010-2011;

B. The New York State Historic Preservation Office, the Ulster County Planning Board, and the National
Trust for Historic Preservation’s Main Street America program all recognized the Canopy as
inappropriate in the KSHD and supported plans for its removal as recently as 2009, and that
discussions for the Canopy’s removal date back to the 1980s.

C. That the report concurs with the findings of the 1989 “HISTORIC REHABILITATION AND
STREETSCAPE DESIGN PLAN FOR THE STOCKADE AREA NATIONAL REGISTER HISTORIC DISTRICT,
KINGSTON, NEW YORK” by Crawford & Stearns, Architects, & Preservation Planners, PLLC, that the
Pike Plan Canopy’s construction and presence is a violation of standards #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, probably
#7, and#10 of the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation.

D. The majority of the property owner’s along North Front and Wall Streets were in opposition to
landmarking the Canopy.

WHEREAS, the HLPC finds that the proposed action is considered a Type II Action under 6 NYCRR,
Part 617.5 (c) (38) and is predetermined not to have a significant impact on the environment and is precluded
from environmental review under Environmental Conservation Law, Article 8.

 WHEREAS, the HLPC has considered all submissions and comments submitted in this proceeding and has
considered the criteria under FBC §405.26.L.7.b, together with all other relevant information, in making a
determination and recommendation to the Common Council.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION
COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1. The HLPC recommends to the Common Council that the August 6, 2024, petition submitted by
William Gottlieb Management Co., LLC (WGM) requesting an emergency local landmark designation for the
Pike Plan be denied based on the following findings:

A. That pursuant to Section 405.L.7.b of the FBC, the criteria under which the request should be evaluated, the
HLPC finds:

(i) “Exemplifies or reflects the broad culture, political, economic, or social history of the nation, state, or
community;” As noted in the reports by Walter R. Wheeler, Kerri Culhane, Ph.D., and
Neal Larson, the structure can be linked to Kingston’s Urban Renewal Era (Larson,
2024: 7).  However, the Urban Renewal Era on the national, state, and local level was
exemplified by seizing and demolishing large swaths of private and public property for
the purpose of modernizing and improving aging infrastructure. In contrast, the “Pike
Plan”, was a limited project seeking to promote retail business in uptown Kingston.
This limited project and goal by no means exemplifies or reflects the “broad culture,
political, economic, or social history of the nation, state, or c ommunity”. It affected
limited properties in a two-block area for the purpose of competing with retail malls.
Although the building of the canopies falls under urban renewal, it does not broadly
exemplify or reflect the Urban Renewal Era. The HLPC finds t hat there are other
building and housing projects within the City of Kingston that would be more
appropriate and better exemplify this period, should the city wish to designate a
landmark for this purpose.
(ii) “Is identified with historic personages or with important events in national, state or local history;”  –
The HLPC finds that this criterion is not met based on the report by Neal Larson,
which demonstrated that “ A far more comprehensive biography and review of his artistic and
architectural output is needed for such an evaluation” must occur to determine John Pike’s
significance and if the Canopy is an appropriate landmark to link to his contributions
to society (Larson, 2024: 7 -8). As reflected in the mate rials submitted, John Pike was
an accomplished artist who was known for his work in watercolor painting. He was
neither a resident of Kingston nor did he have any known connection to the City of
Kingston other than submitting the sketch which was picked as  the basis for the
canopy design.
(iii) “Embodies distinguishing characteristics of an architectural -type specimen, inherently valuable for a
study of a period, style, method of construction or of indigenous materials or craftsmanship; or” - The
HLPC finds that this criterion is not met based on the report by Neal Larson, which
demonstrated that the Pike Plan Canopy was “not unprecedented, but not a common solution”
as an architectural form, and that the design is not directly associated with the
American Bicentennial Celebration of 1976 (Larson, 2024: 7). The original design,

which in itself deviated from that which was submitted by John Pike, was significantly
altered when the majority of the canopies were reconstructed in 2010-2011,
(iv)  “Is representative of the notable work of a master builder, designer or architect whose individual
ability has been recognized.” - The HLPC finds that this criterion is not met based on the
report by Neal Larson, which “ …demonstrated that the Pike Plan, which no longer embodies
critical features of [John Pike’s] design, is the most appropriate resource to associate him with ”
(Larson, 2024: 7). Furthermore, John Pike was recognized as a painter and not
recognized for any works as “a master builder, designer or architect”.

B. That pursuant to Section 405.26.L.7.e of the FBC, the public commentary solicited by the HLPC from North
Front and Wall Street owners and non-owners demonstrated significant reasons, why the canopy should not
be designated a landmark, and encouraged the city to remove the Canopy and res tore the North Front and
Wall Streetscapes. These reasons included:
a. The Canopy is a new reconstruction and compromises the historic integrity of buildings.
b. The Canopy lacks integrity of design by John Pike because of previous alterations in 2010-2011.
c. The Canopy damages the designated structures to which it is affixed.
d. The Canopy hinders the beauty of the exisiting buildings and is an inappropriate structure for the
character of the KSHD.
e. “…the current structure, bears no resemblance to the former Pike Plan….it retains little to any of the
architectural integrity of the original structure…. the roof and cornices… make up 90% of what you
see. All that was removed and replaced” and “The canopies are not only a non-contributing structure
to the historic streetscape, but they are also a major detractor to the inherent architecture of the
historic buildings themselves. The canopies are physically damaging the buildings and virtually make
it impossible for the building owners to fully restore their facades.”

C. That pursuant to Section 405.26.L.7.e of the FBC, the Pike Plan reports solicited by the HLPC from the City’s
consultant and the Historic Preservation Administrator demonstrated beyond a doubt that substantial
alterations in the past to the Canopy weakened its integrity thereby disquali fying it from local landmark
designation.

SECTION 2. The HLPC concurs with the 1989 Crawford & Stearns report finding that the Pike Plan Canopy’s
construction between 1973 and 1979 violated numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, probably 7, and 10 of the Secretary of the
Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation for the indiv idual row buildings along N. Front and Wall Street and the
two streetscapes.

SECTION 3. Based on the violations of the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation, the HLPC
supports removal of the Pike Plan, but prefaces said support upon the creation of a robust historical data driven
streetscape design plan informed by the 198 9 Crawford & Stearns report that follows the Secretary of the
Interior’s Standards and the National Park Service’s Technical Preservation Briefs, and includes consultation
with the State Historic Preservation Office and all abutting property owne rs along canopy on North Front and
Wall Streets.

SECTION 4 : That pursuant to Section 405.26.L.6 of the FBC, the Commission shall review and issue
Preservation Notices of Actions for any future streetscape rehabilitation design plans and proposals for
individual properties prior to the commencement of work.

SECTION 5: That pursuant to Section 405.26.L.7.f of the FBC, a copy of this resolution shall be forwarded to the
Kingston Common Council, along with the petition and supporting documents, for final consideration and
action.

SECTION 6: Based on the findings of this resolution, Section 405.26.L.7.f of the FBC’s interim protections for
pending landmarks are not applicable to the Pike Plan Canopy.

SECTION 7. This resolution shall take effect immediately.

Chairman Grunblatt motioned to approve the foregoing resolution as read, Commissioner Morano seconded the
motion; Commissioners Puetz, McEvoy, and Tonner, also voted to approve and the motion was carried
unanimously. Staff will refer to the fully signed and certified resolution in a communication to the full Common
Council.

items.title: Letter to SHPO Defining the HLPC Position on Pike Plan Designation
items.discussion:
At the September 11 , 2024, Public Hearing for the Pike Plan Canopy , Kerri Culhane, Ph.D.
informed the HLPC and City Officials that she had submitted a 3rd -party Determination of Eligibility (DOE)
application to SHPO on the Canopy’s eligibility for inclusion in the KSHD as a contributing feature. For such an
action, the KSHD nomination paperwork must be amended again to expand the period of significance from 1965
up to, at least, 1975, to capture the Urban Renewal Era.

E. Dickerman, HPA, followed-up and spoke with Chelsea Towers, the Survey & National Register Coordinator
at SHPO, who clarified that the materials submitted will be shared with the city upon review. SHPO will permit
commentary from the City (as it is a CLG) on the Pike Plan, but all commentary must address why the Pike Plan
meets or does not meet the NR’s four Criteria and/or whether the structure retains sufficient integrity for
inclusion in the register. Staff prepared a communication for the commission to send to SHPO as formal
commentary along with the HLPC’s resolution.

Chelsea Towers, Survey & National Register Coordinator
NY Office of Parks, Recreation, & Historic Preservation
PO Box 189,
Waterford, NY 12188

RE: Kingston Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission Commentary on the Eligibility & Integrity of the Pike Plan
Canopy in the Kingston Stockade Historic District.

Dear Ms. Towers:
On behalf of the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC), I am providing our commentary on the 3 -rd
party Determination of Eligibility (DOE) application submitted to SHPO for the Pike Plan Canopy (a covered colonnade
affixed to historically desig nated row buildings) in the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District
(KSHD). Since being establish in 1966, the HLPC has advocated for the preservation and appropriate rehabilitation of
Kingston’s rich and diverse stock of historic architecture.

The KSHD is an invaluable asset to our community, NYS, and the Nation, in that it reflects the urban development of colonial
and post-colonial America. As of 2016, SHPO recognized the area’s Period of Significance as spanning the 17th-century until
1965. Constructed between 1973 and 1976 during Urban Renewal, the Canopy post-date’s the recognized POS and adversely
impacted the integrity of both the North Front and Wall Streetscapes and associated building structures. More specifically,
the 1989 Historic Rehabilitation and Streetscape Design Plan for the Stockade Area report by Crawford & Stearns identifies
that the Pike Plan violates #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, probably #7, and #10 of the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for
Rehabilitation. The HLPC additionally recognizes the Pike Plan violated #9 of the SOI’s Standards for Rehabilitation.
Further, it is understood that the 3 rd-party submittal proposed that the Pike Plan Canopy be incorporated into the
KSHD as a contributing structure, with an additional request for extending the POS to 1975. Simultaneously, a petition was
filed with the HLPC, requesting the Pike Plan Canopy be locally designated.  The HLPC has reviewed the issue, holding a
public hearing between September 11 and September 30,2024; with presentation and discussion at the September 11 and
October 10, 2024, meetings. After care ful review of the materials submitted by the Petitioners, testimony heard under the
hearing, and consideration of the structure itself, the HLPC has determined that the structure meets Criterion A of the NR
and §405.26. L. 7.b. (i) of our local code and is  nearly 50 years old (though this is not a criterion recognized under our local
code) but lacks significant integrity for landmark status.
Since being originally built, the Canopy has been subject to several periods and renditions of repairs because of its poor
design, with the most substantial episode between 2010 -2011. At this time, the Canopy was entirely removed, reconstructed
with modern materials, design changes removed character defining features, and the addition of modern mono-pitched roofs
and skylights. With exception to the form of some column’s designs, very little of the 1976 Canopy remains along North Front
and Wall Streets. As it stands, the structure barely meets three (3) of the seven (7) aspects of integrity, as defined by the
National Park Service.
Therefore, it is the position of the City of Kingston’s Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission that the Canopy
lacks the integrity necessary for historic designation on the local, state, and national levels and acknowledges its detrimen t
to the KSHD st reetscape and designated row buildings. The HLPC will support any plans for removal and a robust data
driven rehabilitation plan for both the North Front and Wall Street facades.

On behalf of the HLPC, I strongly urge the Office of Parks, Recreation, & Historic Preservation to consider the HLPC’s
determination of local eligibility and integrity for the Pike Plan Canopy, when evaluating the 3rd-party DOE application for
the Pike Plan.

Sincerely,
Mark Grunblatt, Esq., Chairman of the HLPC

decisions.vote: Motion - MG; 2nd-NM; KM, RT, AP – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to authorize Mark Grunblatt, HLPC Chair to sign the letter as presented and to send it to Chelsea Towers at the NY SHPO Office: ( Motion - MG; 2nd-NM; KM, RT, AP – yes)

items.title: Letter of Inquiry to the Summer Hill Foundation
items.discussion:
E. Dickerman, HPA, and Natalie Kikel from the Grants Management Department identified the
Summer Hill Foundation in Madison, Connecticut, as a potential funding source for Historic Preservation
projects. Earlier this year the HPA proposed updating the 1988 Stockade Expansion report and moving forward
with listing the a rea on the National Register and creating a local landmark district. Staff prepared a Letter of
Inquiry to Summer Hill requesting their application which would be tailored to hire a Preservation Consultant
to work on the Stockade Expansion District over the next two years.

Dear Mr. Johnson,

I am writing to inquire about The Summer Hill Foundation’s grant application process. The City of Kingston, New
York is a Certified Local Government with a Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) that preserves and
promotes the rich, diverse history and architecture of New York State’s First Capital.
Since its inception in 1966, the HLPC and its partner Friends of Historic Kingston have established three National
Register Historic Districts, five Local Landmark Districts, and conducted numerous resource surveys. Registered Historic
Districts preserve historic neighborhoods and structures by providing property owners with access to tax credits, federal
grants, and protection from undertakings that could harm historic properties. Beyond the HLPC’s efforts, the City also
collaborates with two nonprofits to maintain a firehouse and the Rondout Lighthouse, both listed on the State and National
Registers of Historic Places.
We are impressed by The Summer Hill Foundation’s long commitment to historic preservation in the northeast,
including initiatives led by local governments. Many of the short- and long-term objectives of the City of Kingston’s HLPC
appear to resonate with your outstanding support for historic preservation efforts. We think that many of our current and
future preservation projects will help to fulfill your foundation’s mission to preserve our region’s important history.
Thank you in advance for your time and consideration. We look forward to hearing back from you soon.

Sincerely,

Mark Grunblatt, Esq., HLPC Chair

items.title: 85 Hone Street: Abrasive Paint Removal & Exterior Painting
items.discussion:
The property owner, Dan George  and Erica Marks were present to   discuss  the work which
they and a contractor undertook to the street facing façade of 85 Hone Street the circa 1861 Rondout Rapid House
Italianate firehouse. Staff provided the following background for HLPC members.   On October 28,  2024, a
concerned resident contacted the HPA that a contractor for the owner of 85 Hone Street was grinding paint from
the structure’s Hone Street -facing facade. Staff requested that BSD investigate and Joe Naccarato , Sr. Bldg.
Inspector, visited the site and confirmed the use of a grinder and issued a stop work order. Afterward, the
property owner, Dan George, called Planning and denied that any work was done to the masonry façade – that
the work only consisted of scraping the wooden windows and trim and repain ting them in a new green color.
On Oct 31. 2024, E. Dickerman, HPA, visited the site with Inspector Naccarato, to confirm the contractor used
an electric grinder. Damage to 85 Hone Street, if left untreated, could result in severe erosion to the façade
overtime. Staff contacted the owner and asked that they submit an application to the HLPC, as no prior
authorization of work was requested.
D. George submitted documents and photos of the pre -existing, and the current conditions were provided for
the HLPC members to see.  Staff also shared some closer photos to show abrasive markings left on the stonework.
The front of the building remains with a “speckled” appearance, not all paint having been removed.  It was noted
that the sides of the structure, while also painted, are not going to be changed or touched at this time.  In addition
to the grinding work, some painting had been done on the doo rs and windows . D. George stated that the
structure was currently having water leakage, and he was trying to remove the paint on the exterior so that he
could make repairs and stop the water from doing more damage.
Chairman Grunblatt referenced abrasive cleaning to the Old Savannah building years ago which triggered an
emergency landmark designation to protect the structure from damage. Grunblatt explained that bricks have an
outer fire-hardened skin that protects them from the elements and that abrasive cleaning methods remove that
layer and expose the softer more porous interior. A brick without this skin can degrade within a few years if left
untreated.  A. Puetz confirmed that by removing the outer layer, more are a for penetration is opened and the
mortar is also damaged.  She explained that there are other means to undertake the paint removal from the older
brick that would be BMP and retain the brick’s structure.
Commissioner Grunblatt asked if D. George intends to repaint the structure or remove more paint down to bare
bricks. D. George stated he plans to leave the façade in its current state. Commissioners Grunblatt and Puetz
pointed out that if the façade is left as -is the brick may be more vulnerable and that the structure’s long -term
preservation might warrant further paint removal an d treatment with water repellents or repainting the brick.
A. Puetz also pointed out that the structure may require repointing in places because of the grinder.
HLPC discussed the need for the owner to  engage a preservation consultant and/or mason trained in historic
buildings to develop a report assessing the façade’s damage and that develops a clear and proven strategy for
sealing the damaged masonry. D. George said that he will ask his architect, Rick Alfondre, to draft a report and
treatment plan, which will be submitted  in advance of the next meeting.

decisions.vote: Motion – NM; 2nd-RT; MG, AP, KM, EW yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to TABLE the matter and required the owner to engage a professional skilled in masonry preservation techniques to evaluate the work done and provide a report to the HLPC with a clear strategy for sealing and protecting the damaged masonry and mortar. The report will be submitted in advance of the next meeting to allow adequate review time. (Motion – NM; 2nd-RT; MG, AP, KM, EW yes)

items.title: Referral From Common Council: Form Based Zoning Code Section 405.19: Affordable Housing Standards
items.discussion:
S. Cahill, the Planning Director, presented to the Commission the Common Council’s referral on
the proposed amendments to Section 405.19: Affordable Housing Standards of the Form Based Zoning Code. The
Common Council also referred the amendments to the Kingston and Ulster County Planning Boards for review.
The a mendment proposes new definitions that lower the percentage of Area Median Income  for Affordable
Housing Units (currently set at 80% AMI) and Workforce Housing Units (currently set at 12 0% AMI) to the
following:
• Affordable Housing Unit: A household whose aggregate gross annual income, including the total of all current annual
income of members residing in the household from any source whatsoever at the time of application (excluding the earnings
of working household members of 21 years o f age or younger who are full -time students, does not exceed 50% of the Area
Median income for the actual size of the household (based on the united states census and as updated by the Department of
Housing and Urban Development (HUD), and which household can afford the maximum rent specified in Table 405.19.
• Workforce Housing unit: A household whose aggregate gross annual income, including the total of all current annual
income of members residing in the household from any source whatsoever at the time of application (excluding the earnings
of working household members of 21 years o f age or younger who are full -time students, does not exceed 80% of the Area
Median income for the actual size of the household (based on the United States Census and as updated by the Department of
Housing and Urban Development (HUD), and which household can afford the maximum rent specified in Table 405.19.

S. Cahill pointed out that this change is the result of substantial increases in Ulster County’s AMI due to the
influx of higher income residents from other areas . S. Cahill pointed out that the City Code mandates that
housing projects with 7 or more units must include affordable housing units. She pointed out that the proposed
change could result in fewer multi -unit housing developments because the Affordable requ irement will reduce
the profits.  The Commissioners agreed that the proposal is not likely to adversely impact the city historic
structures or the HLPC’s ability to function.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; AP, KM, NM, EW- yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously that the proposed definition amendments to FBC Section 405.19: Affordable Housing Standards, will not impact the functioning of the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission in their review of projects which involve the city’s historic resources. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; AP, KM, NM, EW- yes).

items.title: Referral From Zoning Task Force: Form Based Zoning Code 1st-Floor Height Requirements
items.discussion:
At the October 10, 2024, HLPC meeting Suzanne Cahill, the Planning Director, spoke on the
proposed amendments by the City’s FBC Working Group to the 1 st-floor height requirements in the T5 & T4
transects. She relayed the following message and discussed the existing height requirements  and the proposed
changes:
As you might be aware, in the City’s form -based Code, each T5 and T4 Transect requires certain first floor height in any
new construction. For example, as detailed in Table 1, a new building built in the T5 Main Street transect would be required to
have a first-floor height of 16’. These requirements impact new construction in all four of the City’s Historic Districts.

Generally, the purpose of the first-floor height requirement is to ensure new buildings meet their surrounding context, that
there is a consistent building to street relationship, and that new buildings could be easily adapted to changing neighborhoo d
conditions. For example, a previously residential building could eventually become a commercial one.
However, the working group is reviewing these requirements to ensure they are achievable and that they accurately reflect
the context of each transect. Based on an initial review of the requirements that in effect, we propose lowering the requirem ents
in most transect areas (see Table 1).
We are currently seeking feedback on these proposed changes. Please note that the zoning working group will only
recommend any potential changes to the Common Council, which would then decide whether to take any action.

The proposed changes are on a citywide basis, extending beyond the city’s historic districts and individually
listed landmarks but could have a direct impact on the streetscapes of historic districts if the proposed new
construction is not compatible with the existing historic 1 st-floor heights. B. Starodaj submitted a rough survey
of the city’s transects that is broader than just the historic districts.

Commissioners Morano and Puetz visited the Stockade, Fair, Wilbur, and Rondout historic districts after the
October HLPC meeting to study the exisiting 1st-floor heights and usage. The study visits observed the
following trends:
• Corner Buildings Typically served as anchor structures with higher 1st-floor heights (14-16ft), with the
highest 1st-floor elevations observed in the heart of the Stockade Historic District.
• Structures one and two lots in from corner lots sometimes had 1st-floor height elevations above 8 and
10ft, but less than the corner lot structure – these lots are somewhat transitional to the block’s lower
elevation interior structures.
• All districts show varying 1st-floor heights. Fair Street displayed mixed used residential structures with
the greatest 1st-floor heights in the Victorian structures that were once occupied as doctor’s offices.
• Rondout and Wilbur developed as working-class neighborhoods in the 19th-century and displayed more
moderate and conventional 8-10ft 1st-floor heights even at some corner lots.

Commissioners Morano and Puetz and Dickerman, HPA agreed that a more contextual approach in historic
districts and for individually designated historic properties is appropriate. S. Cahill pointed out that corner lots
often house anchor structures and allowing a higher 1st floor elevation there might be appropriate. Staff and the
commission produced the following by bullet points for inclusion in the proposed language that shall be sent
back to the FBC Working Group:
For all properties within historic districts, or recognized individually, on the local, state, or national levels:

• Mid-block properties shall follow the underlying transect 1st-floor minimum height requirement, or for
reduced, height, the HLPC shall follow a contextual review to evaluate and determine.
• Corner lots  in historic districts shall follow the underlying transect 1st-floor minimum height
requirement or for reduced height, a Major Waiver shall be required.
• 1st-floor height shall mean floor to floor.

The Commission directed s taff to draft the final language to return to the FBC Working Group. S. Cahill
informed the commission that the final language shall be referred to the Commission again as part of the review
of the Common Council.

decisions.text: The Commissioners present voted unanimously to send to the FBC Working Group the above bullet points detailing 1 st-floor height requirements within Historic Districts and for individually designated historic sites. (Motion -MG; 2nd -AP; RT, KM, NM, EW - yes). Next Meeting: Thursday, December 5th, 2024. items.title: #9-17 & 21 N. Front Street and Fair Street Extension. Application for demolition of buildings in the Kingston Stockade Historic District and for review of the Kingstonian mixed use development proposal. SBLs 48.80-1-25.100, 48.80-1-26
items.discussion:
Andrea Puetz, AIA, recused and left the meeting room because the Kingstonian project is being
worked on  at Dutton Architecture, PLLC, her employer.

Michael Morello, Esq. and Scott Dutton, AIA were present representing Kingston Development, LLC . The
proposal before the Commission is a request  to reapprove “The Kingstonian” development previously approved
by the HLPC on March 3rd, 2022. The PNoA issued was valid for one (1) from the approval date and expired due
to several lengthy law suits regarding various aspects of the project . M. Morello, Esq. stated that there were  no
changes to the project since the original PNoA was issued. Staff informed the applicants and the Commissioners
that recently adopted amendments to Section 405.26.L (HLPC) are in effect and that all new HLPC
determinations are now Certificates of Appropriateness. The Commission was also advised that the Planning
Board recently extended their site plan/special use permit approval under their original authorizing resolution.

Chairman Grunblatt recognized that all HLPC members present, apart from E. Winchell, were part of the
original review.  He asked if any members had any questions and comments, specifically asking E. Winchell if he
had any comment on the project or wanted any information regarding the specifics of the proposal.  There were
no questions from any of the HLPC members.  E. Winchell noted that he had reviewed the documents online and
the original PNoA issued by the HLPC and had no questions.

When the project was initially reviewed, the Planning Board served as the lead SEQR agency, as the project was
determined a Type I Action. M. Morello, Esq. explained that the request for reapproval falls under Type II Actions
of SEQR. He explained his reasoning which was provided within the resubmission package to the HLPC.

decisions.text: The Commission concurred with the opinion of M. Moriello, Esq, attorney for the applicant, and identified this Application and associated Action as a Type 2 Action under the NYCRR Part 617.5 (c) (25), (26) and (32); “based upon the December 16, 2019 coordinated review, Type 1 Action Negative Declaration, issued by the City of Kingston Planning Board, as lead Agency, the Final Site Plan and Final Special Use Permit Approvals granted by said Planning Board on October 18, 2022 and Ratification/Extens ion of Approvals by the Planning Board on September 16, 2024”. Therefore, it was predetermined not to have a significant impact on the environment and no further review was required under SEQR. The Commission for the City of Kingston makes the following findings, reached in accordance with the review procedures set forth in Section 405.26.L.10 of the City of Kingston’s Form Based Zoning Code. The following determinations regarding the issuance of a Certificate of Appropriateness for the development proposal known as “The Kingstonian”, address addendum material submitted on November 20, 2024 by the applicant, as well as original submissions by consultants and interested members of the public. The HLPC further notes that the evidentiary record included material offered for consideration of the closure of Fair Street Extension, massing, scale, visual elements, fire and public health/safety issues, and uses at the project site. The aforementioned material has been thoroughly reviewed for compatibility with the historic character of the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District (KSHD). HLPC Commissioners present find as fact that The Kingstonian, located at #9- 17 & 21 North Front Street and Fair Street Extension (SBLs 48.80-1-25.100, 48.80-1-26), in the Stockade Historic District, by the Applicant and owner, Kingstonian Development LLC, if done according to the plans reviewed prior to and at this meeting, is compatible with the historic character of the KSHD for the following reasons: • The proposed work is to take place at parcels formerly occupied by a City of Kingston on grade parking lot, an abandoned portion of public roadway, including also two structures, a warehouse building and an abandoned restaurant, along with associated site improvements; • Based on the resources HLPC customarily consults, the HLPC understands that the existing warehouse structure does not appear on the 1858 Map of Ulster County by J. H. French, is depicted as a smaller structure on the 1870 Beers Map of Rondout, Kingston, and Wilbur; and it is shown on the 1914 Codwise Maps. That documentation on the NYS Cultural Resource Inventory System (CRIS) was studied and it is recognized under 2 entries that the structure was built in either the 1870’s or the 1880’s, as a 3 story frame hotel. That the structure was bricked over frame siding, removed porch, adding one story brick section to front and creating “L” shape, circa 1946. Though not an exhaustive list of reference materials, the HLPC can reasonably estimate the construction and historical transition of the building. • The proposed work will involve the demolition of existing structures, construction of a 420 vehicle parking garage, approximately 9,000 SF retail/restaurant space, a 32-room boutique hotel, 143 mixed residential units, including 14 affordable units, an ope n pedestrian plaza with public- oriented amenities, and an Americans with Disabilities (ADA)-compliant walking bridge to connect with the adjoining Kingston Plaza; • This work will cause a material change to the external appearance of the property; • that the HLPC recognizes that the project’s substance has not changed since the HLPC issued a Preservation Notice of Action for The Kingstonian project and owners on March 3, 2022, which is appended and made part hereof to this Certificate of Appropriateness; • the HLPC has examined the project in accordance with the five (5) criteria listed under §405.26.L.10 (b) of the Form Based Code as follows: 1. The effect of the proposed work in changing, destroying or affecting the exterior features of the landmark or Landmark (L) District upon which such work is to be done. • The HLPC continues its finding that the demonstrable change within the Stockade district associated with the project will not be detrimental to the district as a whole. The HLPC’s review of evidence regarding comparison scales, massing, materials, architectural features, provision for parking, and contemplated uses support the HLPC’s conclusion that the development will enhance the district. The HPLC agrees with the statement found in Brief 14, which states that “new construction should be “differentiated from the historic building(s).” Though this brief specifically applies to additions onto existing historic buildings, the Kingstonian Buildings are in essence architecturally consistent additions to the Stockade District as a whole.” 2. The relationship between the results of such work and the exterior architectural features of other neighboring improvements. • The HLPC continues its determination that the project adequately takes into consideration the immediate surrounding buildings, in addition to the various points of consideration under the first criterion as noted above. The HLPC further confirms that elements such as recessed doorways for entrances off of North Front Street are appropriately incorporated in line with the existing streetscape, along with other architectural vernacular to compliment the surrounding district.

The HLPC thus concludes, after reviewing the entirety of the administrative record, that the following statements, as made in the communication of Scott Dutton, RA, dated January 30, 2022, remain accurate: “The proposed construction on the West side of the Fair St extension will be unique, and not n

The HLPC finds that the project, as defined, will not degrade the desirable character of the KSHD, but will maintain harmony with respect to the district in so far as the character, materials, color, architectural details are concerned, and will prevent degradation of property. items.discussion:
Dan George attended the meeting remotely due to health concerns . He presented  his architect,
Rick Alfandre’s, plans for protecting 85 Hone Street’s historic masonry façade which was damaged during paint
removal by a grinder. R. Alfandre recommended applying a silane -siloxane sealer that repels water like Cover
Tec Pen50. A. Puetz, architect of the commission, was unfamiliar with this product but recognized there are
many water repellants to treat damaged historic masonry.
Chairman Grunblatt asked about any possible additional work to the exterior before the sealer is applied?  Will
the front remain as it is at present, with some paint remaining?  Will the sides of the structure remain painted,
with areas which are pealing?  D. George stated that he will leave Hone Street face in the speckled condition
because the remaining paint will be too difficult to remove and may cause additional damage. He intends to leave
the other facades painted.  A. Puetz noted that you would not typically apply the sealer where there has not been
any outward disturbance of the brick, only the front will need to be treated.  D. George noted that he only plans

to apply the product to the front.  He also noted that the space along the sides is narrow so it would be difficult
to do work without involving the adjacent property owners.
S. Cahill questioned when work will  be done and if there is  to be any preliminary cleaning to be done on the
surface before the sealer is applied.  D. George noted that he would have to clean the surface.  It would be with a
soft brush and under the architect’s guidance. Given the current temperatures, the work will be done in the
spring of 2025.
M. Grunblatt and A. Puetz pointed out that repointing mortar joints that were damaged by the grinder must be
done before Cover Tec Pen50 is applied.  D. George stated that he would ask his architect to inspect the mortar
first to determine what areas may need repointing before the sealant is applied. A suitable mortar material will
be utilized.

Filiberto Macias (owner/applicant) and Maria Parades presented  plans , drawn by John
Stinemire, PE,  to remove two exisiting ground floor entryway doors along Wilbur Avenue and install a new
ground floor entrance along Wilbur Ave in the current location of a double 6/6 living room window.
Commissioner Grunblatt also served as a Spanish translator during the meeting. M. Parades stated the proposed
door will be black, and the applicants plan to construct a covering over the entrance with two white Tuscan
columns. In addition, F. Macias plans to install khaki- colored vinyl clapboard siding on the structure’s Wilbur
Ave face on the 2nd-floor. The Commission asked if the exisiting siding is asbestos laden. F. Macias said that he
understands it is not.

Suzanne Cahill, the Planning Director, told the commission that the Common Council seeks to
serve as the Lead Agency in a coordinated SEQR review for demolishing the Pike Plan Canopy in the KSHD.
The Action has been preliminarily classified as an unlisted action, and a coordinated review will be undertaken
and the designation of a lead agency and a determination of the significance of the impact of the action on the
environment must be made in order to comply with the New York State Environmental Conservation Law
(SEQR Act) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (the Regulation) by the New York State Department
of Environmental Conservation. Upon consideration of the criteria set forth in Section 617.6 of the SEQR Act,
the Kingston Common Council believes that it should be designated lead agency and has declared intent to be
the lead agency. The HLPC is considered an Involved Agency in this project because of its Section 405.26.L role
in protecting and reviewing architectural design and material changes to structures and streetscapes within
the City’s Historic Districts. This request by the Common Council to serve as lead agency will not inhibit the
HLPC’s ability to review any proposed changes to the facades of structures along N. Front & Wall Streets
currently impacted by the Pike Plan. Chairman M. Grunblatt, spoke in favor of allowing the Common Council
to serve as the lead agency.  R. Tonner agreed that when considering the Involved Agencies, the Common
Council has the most resources to serve in that role.

Suzanne Cahill, the Planning Director, told the commission that the Common Council seeks to
serve as the Lead Agency in a coordinated SEQR review for the proposed Eminent Domain of 24 parcels in the
Rondout along R. Garraghan Drive and the construction of an Affordable Housing Development. Upon
consideration of the criteria set forth in Section 617of the SEQR Act, the Kingston Common Council believes
that it should be designated lead agency and has declared intent to be the lead agency. The HLPC is only
considered an Interested Agency in this project because the project is in close proximity the Rondout-West
Strand Historic District. This request by the Common Council to serve as lead agency will not inhibit the
HLPC’s ability to review and make recommendations on any proposed architectural plans for the proposed
affordable housing complex.   S. Cahill noted that once plans are more developed and the documents are
available, the HLPC should review and make any comments or recommendations as they feel are appropriate.

Staff went though some of the background of the project to bring all members up to date on
progress.  In the Fall of 2023, Archaeological and Historical Resource Services, Inc. (AHRS) delivered to the City
and the NY State Historic Preservation Office their final Intensive -Level Historic Building Survey report on the
Wilbur & Ponckhockie Neighborhoods. In December of 2023, the SHPO issued their determination of eligibility
(DOE) on the proposed Ponckhockie National Historic District. Following the DOE, the Planning Department
held a neighborhood meeting on February 15 th, 2024, at the Ponckhockie Congregation Church (91 Abruyn St)
to share with property owners and residents’ information on the proposed district and educate them more on
the benefits of historic districting.

At the February  meeting Staff highlighted the benefits of designating the area a local historic district before
listing it on the national register.  Also at this meeting, several property owners, New Central Baptist Church,
and Riverview Missionary Church members voiced their displeasure for the project because they were not
included in the proposed district, while also voicing opposition to historic distric ting by citing potential
gentrification. Staff continued conversations with these churches and provided them with resources on the
financial benefits of historic districting, such as the National Trust for Historic Preservation’s ‘Preserving Black
Churches’ grant. By late Spring, the churches stopped replying to the staff’s multiple emails and phone calls.
Since then, other property owners in the Ponckhockie reached out asking about the status of the project and told
Staff they would like to see it progress. S. Cahill stated that E. Dickerman has been working very diligently with
the church representatives to provide information that would be helpful to them, even without the district
designation. Although it would be preferable to have the church sign on and  be part of any forward movement,
it was noted that it might just be time to move the project along and then continue with a parallel course working
with the churches.  Chairman Grunblatt suggested the staff seek out peer organizations that may help to bridge

the understanding of the historic designation and remove any misconceptions or fears that the church groups
may have.

For the HLPC to hold a public hearing, they must secure at least 10 signatures in support of the proposed
designation. Only five (5) signatures were secured at the meeting. Three (3) more signatures were secured by the
end of April. While Section 405.26.L.7 states only 10 signatures of City residents are necessary, Staff feel that the
signatures should come from property owners within the proposed district and given the number of properties
involved, a higher number than the mandatory 10 should be on file. E. Dickerman stated there are 247 parcels
within the proposed local district and about 213 property owners. Staff encourage we secure signatures from
about 25% (or between 53 and 63 individuals) to bring the proposed district to the HLPC for a public hearing.
R. Tonner questioned if the staff are getting inquiries, why there are so few signatures which have been secured.
Staff responded that there needs to be a more progressive means to involve the residents/owners. Some were
apprehensive due to questions raised.

E. Dickerman received confirmation from Janan Cargile and Richard Stone ( former members of the Historic
Survey’s PAC) in mid-November that they are currently canvassing their street for supporters. Staff recognize
that weekends are the most effective time of the week to meet with property owners at home. To expedite the
acquisition of new signatures, Staff ask ed if any commissioners present would consider walking the proposed
district to secure additional signatures  and recognized that the time of year is d ifficult, but that we would be
looking to undertake something in the spring when the weather is nicer, and the holiday season is over.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) and recommended that the abrasive masonry cleaning of the street facing facade and painting of woodwork at 85 Hone Street in the Rondout -West Strand Historic District, as undertaken by the owner and identified within the application documentation reviewed at this meeting for compliance with the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district, with certain mitigating actions, with the following reasons and conditions: • that unauthorized work took place at the three (3) story masonry Italianate Fire House on the western side of Hone Street, midway between Spring and W. Pierpont Streets, which according to the 1977 Building Structure Inventory Form, dates to circa 1861 and served as the Rapid House Fire House, one of two firehouses in the Rondout neighborhood (BSIF, 1977); • that the owner's contractor in late October used a grinder to abrasively remove paint from the structure's Hone Street facade, and repainted the garage door, entryway door, windows, and cornice without a Certificate of Appropriateness; • that the City's Building Safety Division issued a stop work order on October 28th, 2024, identifying the contractor used incorrect equipment and unacceptable methods to remove paint on the facade, and that on the same day the property owner was notified to submit an application for HLPC review and consideration, and subsequently admitted to using a grinder on the facade in email on October 31st; • that on November 7, 2024, the Commission expressed concern that damage may have occurred to the facade by the use of said grinder, and required the property owner to secure a report from a qualified preservationist or historic preservation mason detailing the damage and providing for an appropriate course of treatment to ensure the facade's long-term preservation; • that the property owner submitted a condition assessment and treatment program by Rick Alfrandre, AIA, on November 25th, 2024 stating that the owner must apply a vapor open water repellant, such as CoverTech's CoverSeal PEN50, to the facade to prevent water from infiltrating the damaged brick; • that should the owner choose to apply a different product, that will be submitted for review and consideration prior to it being utilized; • that that property owner must also re -point any damaged mortar using historically appropriate mortar as defined in the NPS Technical Preservation Brief #2: Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings; • that any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • The Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 5th day of December 2024, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. The HLPC further motioned that the proposed rooftop solar project at 61 Spring Street in the Rondout -West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district with the following reasons and conditions: • that the proposed work is to take place at the three bay, bracketed style, two -story dwelling, with its gable end facing Spring Street and which is located on the north side of Spring mid-way between Hone and Wurts Streets, and which on the January 13th, 1 977, Building Structure Inventory Form prepared by the Friends of Historic Kingston states "that the house appears on the 1858 map of Rondout.
