items.title: #105 Abeel Street: Construction of a new 6 -unit residential building along W. Union Street

items.discussion:
Robin Gullickson of Alfandre Architecture presented on behalf of the property owners the plans
to construct a new 6 -unit residential building at the rear of 105 Abeel Street which will face W. Union Street.
The area is currently vacant.  R. Gullickson stated that the project includes a site plan under review by the
Planning Board, which will include a subdivision as well. They have the project tabled and have referred it to the
UCPB, and the rec Commission for comment.  A Coastal Consistency review will be undertaken in January 2025.
R. Gullickson also stated that she and her clients reviewed the W. Union Streetscape and other exisiting multi-
unit residential structures in the Rondout West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District to design a
structure that complemented the W. Union Street historic context. R. Gullickson shared with the commission
features a from nearby structures, including brick façade designs, fenestration designs, cornice designs, and
corner features. The proposed design represents a vision that she and h er client feel is contextual and sensitive
to the character of the historic district.

R. Gullickson stated that she and her clients are open to requests for greater conformity within the district. She
stated that the W. Union Street entrance awning will be more shed-like in design. Staff also noted that the plans
did not identify the placement of electrical and mechanical equipment, which must be screened in accordance
with the From Based Zoning Code’s Section 405.14.I.5. R. Gul lickson noted that this equipment will likely be
installed on the structure’s roof and not visible from the ROW.

Commissioners studied the proposed new construction, and the structures used to inform the design and asked
that R. Gullickson incorporate a more defined and deeper projecting cornice to conform with Section 405. 14. C.
1 (Based, Body, and Cap) of the Form Based Zoning Code. A. Puetz, Architect of the Commission, also asked that
R. Gullickson incorporate an additional expression line between the 3 rd story windows and the cornice which
would make the structure feel less massive in height.

Staff asked the applicant if any archaeological studies were done or will be done prior to the commencement of
the construction. R. Gullickson said that some shovel test pits were dug and that little was yielded. She noted
that the structure’s foundation will require an excavation of at least 10 feet. Staff shared with R. Gullickson that
there were archaeological excavations/reports conducted along Abeel Street that yielded historical and culturally
sensitive sites and that another site is recognized adjacently to the east. As such, the Commission will ask that
an archaeologist be on site to monitor the excavations during the foundation’s construction.

Alex Alaimo (Kathryn Whitman, RA’s Assistant) presented plans to  demolish an existing
carriage house/ garage and construct an Accessory Dwelling Unit(ADU) with a 700 sq/ft ground floor and
300sq/ft loft (1000 sq/ft combined) on the same site. E. Dickerman noted that he met with the property owners,
Ari Goldstein and Beth Saubermann, in October of 2024 to discuss their goals of converting the existing structure
into an ADU or demolishing the existing structure to build a new appropriately designed ADU. The owners
clarified that they wish to relocate from the primary structure into the ADU for a time so they can properly
restore the primary structure. In the future, this new ADU may become a rental or other facility of their choice.
A. Alaimo, reached out to staff in December to try and identify the structure’s age based on the 1870s Beers map,
the Sanborn Fire Insurance mops, and the assessor’s records. Due to the paucity of records on the structure, the
applicant estimates that the exisiting carriage house dates b etween 1850 and 1870 and contains wooden floors.
The Commission reviewed the photographs provided by the applicant of the structure’s exterior and interior ,
identifying late changes to the structure that include a 2ft -addition towards the driveway which allowed for a
newer overhead garage door to replace the older carriage style doors. The existing garage/carriage house is closer
to the lot line than the proposed ADU.
A. Alaimo clarified the following design features of the new structure with the Commission:
• The façade will be clad in wood cove Dutch lap with a 7” reveal that matches the dimensions of the
exisiting structure’s façade
• The ADU will have a central entrance facing the Fair Street flanked on either side by full sidelights and
faux carriage house doors. Each carriage door will be made of painted wood and have three divided lights
at their top. K. Whitman’s plans identify these carriage doors as “sliding”.
• The new windows will be wood framed 2/2 like Marvin Ultimate Wood Double Hung windows.
• The roof will be covered in architectural asphalt shingles like Certainteed Shingles in Pewterwood color.
• The structure will be painted in Benjamin Moore Essex Green HC -188 from the Historical Color
Collection.
• The proposed light fixtures will be some type of downward-facing gooseneck lamp.
• The existing wooden fence and gate that crosses the driveway and replaces it with a new wrought iron
style fencing (made of aluminum) set back from the street on the north side of the driveway near the
primary structure that will enclose the side and rear yards to prevent children and the owner’s dog from
leaving.
• On the driveway’s south side (across from the fence) the architect proposed screened enclosure for
garbage, a bike rack, and an EV charging station.
• The pavement in front of the proposed ADU will be removed to create a lawn with a stone pathway that
leads to the carriage house and that shrubbery will be planted on either side of the ADU’s entrance.

S. Cahill presented to the commission a signage and awning application from the Hudson Valley
LGBTQ Community Center for their property at 300 Wall Street which requires two minor waivers. Because the
project is within a historic district, the administrative review for the application must be reviewed and supported
by the HLPC. The Center seeks to install one (1) code conforming Wall mounted sign about the Center’s Wall
Street facing entrance. The Center also seeks to install three black fixed awnings over the Wall Street entrance
and the two entrances along John Street, which are the Center’s solution to the Uptown Canopy’s removal.

Section 405.17.E.5.e (Awning Signs) states that “A maximum of one sign is allowed per shopfront and the area
must not cover more than 75% of the awning valence.”  The Center’s proposed awning along Wall Street will
display three signs  (1 per side) and therefore requires a minor waiver and recommendation from the HLPC . A
second waiver is required to install two awnings, each with one sign, at each of the Center’s entrances along John
Street.

The Commission discussed the appropriateness of a black awning and the potential for fading or discoloration
from bird droppings but agreed that the vinyl material was sufficient for cleaning and that the dark color allows
the awning’s signage to better stand out.

RECOMMENDATION:   The Commission recommended approving the waivers requested, noting the location
is a corner business, with more than one frontage and that pre -existing door openings should be treated in a
similar fashion for symmetry and compatibility.  (Motion – MG; 2nd- RT; EW, AP, NM, KM-yes)

EXTRA NOTE  1:  Staff want to make all HLPC members aware that the newly adopted administrative code
requires that each Commissioner obtain a minimum of 4 hours of training per year. Staff have a variety of online,
on demand webinars that can be accessed, including those posted on the Department of State’s Digital Training
Courses: https://dos.ny.gov/training-courses.  Staff also stated that if commissioners a ttend outside workshops
that they believe are relevant to the HLPC they should  submit documentation to staff for review and approval.
Staff noted that Planning Courses and some continuing education programs are acceptable. Staff will track
qualified training sessions for all and will continue to make members aware as opportunities present themselves.
If commissioners have any questions, please reach out to staff for clarification. Training requirements will be part
of the CLG program’s annual reporting.

EXTRA NOTE  2:  Commissioner McEvoy informed the HLPC and Staff that the mayor is now seeking
applicants for the newly established Community Preservation Fund. K. McEvoy stated that preference is given
to Ulster County Agricultural and Farmland Protection Board, the Historic Landmarks Preservation
Commission, and/or a local conservation commission . If anyone is interested in serving on the Fund, you are
encouraged to apply via the attached link ( https://www.kingston-ny.gov/news/?FeedID=3305), which will be a
boost the preservation activities in the City of Kingston.


Next Meeting: Thursday, February 6th, 2025.

This meeting is available on  the City of Kingston YouTube channel:

decisions.text: The Commission voted to TABLE the application pending its recommendations for additional cornice details and an additional expression line between the 3rd-floor windows and the cornice. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; EW, AP, KM, NM – yes). 4. #127 Fair Street: Demolition of exisiting carriage house and construction of a new ADU. SBL: 56.107 -3-26. SEQR Type II. Transect Zone: T4N, FSHD, HA. Ward: 5. Kathryn Whitman, applicant; Ari Goldstein & Beth Saubermann, owners.

The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (2) (11) and motioned that the proposed demolition of an exisiting garage/carriage house and construction of a new ADU on the same site at 127 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Landmark District, if done according to the plans reviewed at this meeting and according to the procedures stipulated in Section 405 -26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district with the following reasons and conditions: • the proposed work is to take place at the site which contains a detached carriage house/garage structure and 2 & 1/2 story Greek Revival dwelling located on the west side of Fair St mid way between Franklin and St James St's, that the 1870 Combined Map of Rondout, Kingston, and Wilbur by Sanford & Beers, indicates may have been owned by a Mrs. E. S. Baldwin; • the owners propose to demolish the existing carriage house/garage, built circa 1858 and 1870, and has received alterations over the last century; • the project architect has provided sufficient information to the HLPC that the existing accessory structure cannot be adaptively reused as an ADU, and that demolition will not adversely impact the primary structure's integrity; • the architect provided plans, elevation drawing, and renderings of a new 1000sq/ft ADU on the same site with design features drawn from the existing accessory structure that the commission determines is appropriate for replacement construction within the FSHD; • the new ADU shall be clad in wood cove Dutch lap with a 7" reveal that matches the dimensions of the existing structure's façade; • the structure and its trim shall be painted in Benjamin Moore Essex Green HC-188; • the new structure's windows shall be 2/2 wood framed windows like Marvin Ultimate double hung wood windows; • the proposed exterior mounted wood carriage house doors shall be a design feature, with ability to close fully; • the doors and lights behind the carriage doors shall be made of a conforming material (wood or metal) with specifications to be submitted to Staff for final approval; • the new roof shall feature a jerkinhead design and shall be roofed in Certainteed Pewterwood (dark gray) architectural roofing shingles with black-painted roof trim; • the new structure shall have a union goose neck exterior wall mounted light fixtures made by Specs will be submitted to staff for final approval; • the owners may replace the existing fencing and gate with the proposed fencing and gate system detailed as submitted; • the owners may install the proposed Section 405.14.I.5 conforming garbage, bike rack, and EV charging station enclosure on the south side of the driveway as rendered; • any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 9th day of January 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Com mission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (MG – motion; 2nd – EW; KM, NM, AP, RT – yes) RECOMMENDATION: 5. 300 Wall Street: Two (2) waivers for multiple awnings and multiple awnings signs. SBL: 48.331-2-16. SEQR Type II. Transect Zone: T5MS, KSHD, HA. Ward: 2. Hudson Valley LGBTQ Community Center, Inc., applicant/owner.

items.title: #105 Abeel Street: Construction of a new 6 -unit residential building along W. Union Street

items.discussion:
Robyn Gullickson of Alfandre Architecture provided an updated rendering, with defined façade
material for the construction of a new 6 -unit residential building along W. Union Street following the HLPC’s
January 9th, 2025, request for a more defined cornice and expression line between the cornice and the 3 rd floor
window. R. Gullickson proposed a Glen Gery “Mohawk Thin Brick” façade, across the entire exterior, featuring
standard height and length sized thin bricks with varying red tones. The street face will feature  an expression
line between the ground and 2nd story following the requirement of Section 405. 14. C. 1 (Based, Body, and Cap).
The updated proposal features an additional expression line comprised of a soldier brick bond between the third
(3rd) story windows and cornice, as requested by the Commission. The FBC does not require expression lines to
wrap around the building, but only to be present along the street facing faced. The updated proposal also includes
a more defined cap/cornice as requested , which concerns Section 405. 14. C. 1 (Based, Body, and Cap).
Commissioner Grunblatt asked R. Gullickson if the proposed awning over the W. Union Street entrance if the
final proposal, which she confirmed to be accurate.

Mary Waples-Kennedy, the property owner , and her contractor Anthony Roddy, pr esented  a
plan to demolish 453/451 Abeel Street, a structure deemed eligible for listing on the State and National Registers
of Historic Places under Criteria C in 2002 , by Walter R. Wheeler (Architectural Historian)  of Hartgen
Archaeology Associated during an archaeological and cultural resource study along Abeel Street . M. Waples-
Kennedy seeks to demolish the structure due to its poor condition and the immense cost of stabilizing and
restoring v ersus demolition. E. Dickerman informed the Commission that the structure’s western half was
demolished in 1983, which compromised the structure’s integrity pr ior to W. Wheeler’s evaluation  and i t i s
unclear if W. Wheeler had this information in 2002. M. Waples -Kennedy stated that the western half was
demolished after a vehicle drove into the structure.

E. Dickerman reminded the HLPC that i n November of 2024, the City’s Common Council adopted changes to
Section 405.26.L (HLPC) of the Form Based Zoning Code, which includes Section 405.26.L.8 : Demolition of a
Non-Landmarked Historic Property & Emergency Designation.   The Code now requires that any structure

deemed “eligible” for nomination cannot be issued a permit for demolition until a review by the HLPC is
undertaken.  Staff provided the language of the code to the Commission members for their reference.   M.
Grunblatt summarized the emergency designation procedure, recalling its use in the past.  He noted that it is
important that assets be recognized and recorded if they have meaningful attributes and present themselves as a
critical historical attribute.

Staff confirmed that the  Building Inspector at the BSD and Fire Department have not provided a written
determination that the “property presents an imminent danger or hazard to public health, safety and welfare
(See Section 405.26.L.8.b.ii)” and that no court order exists for demolition.  However,  a red sign with a white X
installed on the structure’s front informs Staff and the emergency responders  not to enter the structure in the
event of a fire due to safety issues. Using  the criteria under 405.26.L.7.b, the Commission evaluated the building
to determine if the structure should be landmarked to prevent demolition.  Chairman Grunblatt read each of the
following:

1. Exemplifies or reflects the broad cultural, political, economic or social history of the nation, state or community;
2. Is identified with historic personages or with important events in national, state or local history;
3. Embodies distinguishing characteristics of an architectural-type specimen, inherently valuable for a study of a period, style,
method of construction or of indigenous materials or craftsmanship; or
4. Is representative of the notable work of a master builder, designer, or architect whose individual ability has been recognized.

Based on the materials submitted, the HLPC  determined that the deteriorated and remaining portion of the
structure does not meet the criteria laid out in the code and therefore is ineligible for local landmark status. The
HLPC further recognized that th e structure is in severe disrepair and that demolition is likely the only viable
financial option for the property owner. Commissioner Grunblatt stated that w henever demolition is the only
viable option (not local landmark protection), the HLPC directs Staff to create a package of  documentation to
preserve the structure’s history in a written record.

The applicant, Pastor Robert Sweeney of the Old Dutch Church, was not present at the meeting.
S. Cahill, the Planning Director, informed the HLPC that the Old Dutch Church  seeks approval to install four
(4) new HVAC mini split systems near the eastern wall of the 272 Wall Street (the Old Dutch Church), the City
of Kingston’s only National Historic Landmark, which also lies within the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and
National Historic District. The Old Dutch Church hired RYCOR (HVAC) to install the new units along the Fair
Street (Eastward) side of the church, who submitted a plot plan with their Building Permit application. RYCOR
works with Permit Flow (a 3 rd Party) who manages permit applications and reviews for projects. Since 2023,
HVAC installation projects are typically reviewed by Staff for conformance with Section 405.14.I.5 (Screening of
Electrical & Mechanical Equipment) of the Form Based Zoning Code.

S. Cahill and E. Dickerman opted to elevate this project for a Commission level review following three (3) plot
plan iterations that suggested the proposed HVAC units would be located near the structure’s southeastward
corner (closest to Main Street) and would be highly visible from the public street. E. Dickerman and S. Cahill
also identified a previous pair (2) of condenser units that were improperly installed to the structure’s masonry

façade that do not conform with a 2023 desk review issued by S. Cahill. Lastly, a  previous project for the
installation of a cell tower generator also appears not to conform with the 2020 HLPC PNoA, that the electrical
and mechanical equipment must be sufficiently screened. E. Dickerman, HPA, was also concerned that the past
and proposed work could interfere with exisiting gravesites in the eastern churchyard.

E. Dickerman and S. Cahill met with Pastor Sweeney at the Old Dutch Church on January 16 th, 2025, to discuss
these concerns and shared with him the concerns about past and proposed projects conformance with code and
the character of the KSHD given the structure’s significance as the only National Historic Landmark (designated
2008) and the presence of two NYS SHPO preservation Covenants. Pastor Sweeney acknowledged the NHL
status and was also aware of the deed covenants.

In his application to the HLPC, R. Sweeney stated the following about each project:
• Exisiting Wall -Mounted Condenser’s:  In the warmer weather, he intends to paint the units Sherwin
Williams (SW 7048) Urbane Bronze to match the Church’s trim work, which he feels is a more sensitive and
unobtrusive approach to screening the units.  Staff presented a color sample of the choice to the Commission
and noted that it is what has been applied to the church trim areas, and is approved by SHPO.
• Existing Generator for Steeple -Mounted Cell System:  The exisiting generator system is screened by
shrubbery, however, he recognizes that this shrubbery (which is almost 5 years old), does not fully screen
the units. In the warmer weather, he intends to also paint these units Sherwin Williams (SW 7048) Urbane
Bronze to match the Church’s trim work, which he feels is a more sensitive and unobtrusive approach to
screening the units or adding new plantings.
• 4 Proposed HVAC Mini-split Condensers: The proposed HVAC condensers will be mounted on pads (not
to the structure) atop a landscape fabric and new layer of pea-sized gravel (color matched to the surrounding
stonework) with no disturbances to the soil. All lines and electrical wiring will run into the structure’s
basement through exisiting basement portals.  Each unit is approximately W36” x H48” x D16” in size. To
address the FBC Section 405.14.I.5 screening requirements, he proposes to paint the Sherwin Williams (SW
7048) Urbane Bronze to match the Church’s trim work, which he feels is a more sensitive and unobtrusive
approach to screening the units. R. Sweeney also requested RYCOR place one pair of units behind an
exisiting buttress and another pair near another buttress (See plot plan below for more details). R. Sweeney
sees this as the most viable screening solution without planting shrubbery or installing fencing that would
attract more and present access issues for the Fire Department in the event of an emergency. Staff pointed
out and it was recognized that the installation would make use of two existing openings in the church wall
and no new penetrations are to be made for this installation.
• Burial ground Considerations: In response to E. Dickerman’s concerns about burials, he noted that most of
the stones in that area are marked with ‘Xs’ on their rear, denoting that they were removed from the church’s
basement where the burials are and replanted in their current positions in the east churchyard circa 1883. R.
Sweeney provided E. Dickerman with a written record of projects undertaken by the church authorities to
rehabilitate the structure, including the relocation of gravestones in 1883.

Selina S. Guendel, Regent for the Wiltwyck Chapter of the National Society for the Daughters
of the American Revolution, Kaaren Davis, Treasurer, and attorney, James Bacon, Esq., presented the HLPC with
the proposal to undertake the following list of work at 106-122 Green Street (the Crispell-Sleight-Tappen House)
a local landmark in the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District:
1. Replacement of all windows with historically accurate replacements. All will be double-hung, as are the
exisiting ones that were installed in 1908. The current windows have lost their integrity due to age and
weathering.
2. Repair stone, columns, and benches on the front porch, replacing wood as needed, and repaint in the
current color.
3. Repair and level the floor of the back porch, replacing wood as needed, and repaint in the current color.
4. Trim the tree in the yard on the Crown St. side of the house, as it is damaging the roof. If the roof needs
repairing, we’ll need to also address that.
5. Trim the root of a tree on Crown St. that has lifted one piece of bluestone in the sidewalk; reset the
bluestone so that it was level, eliminating any tripping hazard.

Commissioner McEvoy began addressing each of the proposed projects in reverse chronological order, starting
with project #5 regarding trees and the bluestone sidewalk. He noted that the reason for this approach was that
the matters were outside of the authority of the HLPC.  S. Guendel recognized staff already informed her that
projects 5 and 4 are outside the purview of the HLPC and that they must work with the Department of Public
Works and the Tree Commission.

S. Guendel stated that they are withdrawing their request for a review of project #3 (the rear porch) at this time
due to finances.  They prefer to focus the resources they have on the windows and front porch work needed and
will revisit the rear porch project in the future.  The Commission accepted the withdrawal from the application.

Commissioner McEvoy moved to project # 2  Repair stone, columns, and benches on the front porch, replacing wood as needed, and
repainting in the current color. S. Guendel submitted to the HLPC several photos of the conditions and then explained that the
bluestone slab beneath the front porch is cracked and the foundation for that porch (beneath the slab) must be stabilized
to ensure the feature’s long-term preservation.  At present they are unable to obtain solid understanding of what is beneath,
that will have to be examined after they begin some site work to do exploration of conditions.  She continued with the
wood columns may require minor repairs and repainting. S. Guendel stated that the Wiltwyck Chapter of the NS DAR
plans to hire a contractor to gently lift and brace the porch’s roof, temporarily remove the columns for in -kind
restoration and repaint them.  She indicated that they had the color evaluated and it is  Benjamin Moore, White-
01.  Once the initial work is complete the contractor will be able to remove the stone, inspect and repair/replace
the base upon which the bluestone slab sit s. S. Guendel clarified for the commission that they intend to reuse
the exisiting bluestone slab materials to maintain the porch’s integrity. She deferred to the various photos to
illustrate the existing damage to the column bases, the stone slab, and the area beneath.  The HLPC discussed
the photos. S. Guendel noted that she believes the front porch was a M. teller addition during the restoration in
1907-1908, it was not part of the revolutionary age.  S. Cahill asked if the organization had the M. Teller drawings
for those renovations and S. Guendel stated that they do not.

S. Cahill stated that they will need to provide both the HLPC and Building and Safety Division with
plans/elevations for the proposed work by a licensed design professional like an architect or in this case a
structural engineer. S. Guendel and J. Bacon agreed to this request. A. Puetz encouraged the HLPC to allow for
the acquisition of a demo permit  or similar authorization , pending BSD support, to allow the owners to
investigate the causes of the changes/ cracking to the bluestone porch. The applicant agreed to approach the BSD
to determine what is needed before any investigation is undertaken. The HLPC determined project #2 should be
tabled until the delivery of additional information of a design professional , recommending that a structural
engineer would be best.

Commissioner McEvoy moved on to project #1: Replacement of all windows with historically accurate replacements. All
will be double-hung, as are the exisiting ones that were installed in 1908. The current windows have lost their integrity due to age and
weather.

Chair McEvoy stated that it has been about a year and a half since the last review and  recognized that the January
2025 application does not provide any new information from the 2023 applications on the current conditions of
the existing wooden sash windows or on their age . He stated that the commission will need an update on the
current conditions.  A. Puetz asked if they had any new close -up photographs of the exisiting windows

conditions, because from the distance of the photos submitted, the HLPC cannot render a decision. S. Guendel
said no. She said that the contractor had taken some but had a medical emergency and is not available.

Puetz also pointed out that their contractor previously stated that some windows could be restored and asked if
their contractor’s position still stood. S. Guendel stated that she does not believe any can be restored. A. Puetz
stated that as it has been presented many times, in their perspective, it’s important to try and retain some form
of the historic fabric with the windows, that windows are a charter defining features of most historic structures.
While it’s understood where the applicant is coming from, the HLPC would desire to maintain some of the
historic character to demonstrate an understanding of what was  intended by past people associated with the
structure. S. Guendel stated they are replacing with windows which look identical. A. Puetz reiterated, if there
is a chance that some can be retained and restored it would be appropriate to discuss it, but more information is
needed, such as photographs and dimensions.
Puetz also asked  for documentation on the specifications and of the original windows so the HLPC can
determine how many, if any, of the windows can be restored. J. Bacon, Esq. stated that it is his legal position that
the DAR does not have to do that. He cited the court decision from November/December of 2024, which claimed
the windows are not original to the 1600s but from the early 1900s, and because the DAR’s experts advised against
replacement. He argued that the DAR custom made windows replicate exactly what is there now.

J. Bacon also stated that he reviewed the code and that the commission does not have the authority to prevent
the DAR from replacing the windows there. He argued that the even if the windows in the building were new,
they would have the ability to replace them without the HLPC’s authority to prevent the replacement. He argued
that the structure is on the local listing but is not state or federally listed. The question on the historic status was
opened and staff previously provided the applicants with the following documents demonstrating that #106-122
Green Street (SBL: 48.330 -3-19 ) was individually landmarked by the HLPC in 1969 and is a listed structure
within the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District – these materials are also posted on
the HLPC’s website under the February 6th, 2024, meeting materials for the project:

o 1966.8.1_CoK_local_law_2_HLPC_creation (Note legislation has been amended over time, and the
current Form Based Code Section 405.26 L (Amended Nov. 2024) is the Ordinance that provides the
HLPC authority.)
o 1969.8.4_106-122GreenSt_hlpc_designation_letter_history_&_architectural_integrity
o 1969.8.28_hlpc_minutes
o 1969.9.8_106-122GreenSt_hlpc_designation_&_notification
o 1975: Kingston Stockade National Historic District nomination paperwork
o 1979.2.5_106-122GreenSt_DAR_&_HLPC_plaque_agreement
o 1987.7_106-122GreenSt_BSIF drafted by Tony Opalka
o 2022.4.20: 106-122 Green St DAR & SHPO_emails
o 2022.5.26_SHPO_letter_RE_106-122GreenSt
o 2024.11.12_FBC_ss405.26.L (Adopted)

J. Bacon continued to elaborate that they researched the records provided, spoken with B. Rhoades and J. Kellar,
looked at DAR files and all the available documents from M. Teller.  That’s the evidence and if needed they would
return to court.  The code does not define window age, and when windows should be  repaired versus replaced.
The judge has stated what the statute involves, and they are willing to follow that and go back to court as they
know the ruling will be in their favor. His clients should not be delayed any longer on this matter. There had been
money expended on the windows. The court has made their position known in the decision documents. He
suggested that the HLPC go back into an attorney-client session and discuss with the city attorney. You are only
going to be provided with the reports that were previously provided, nothing more.  The Commission should
recognize that the structure will look better because the storm windows will be removed, and the new windows
are exact replicas windows.
Commissioner McEvoy motioned that the HLPC enter an attorney client session. (Motion-KM; NM-2nd; RT, AP-
Yes).
Attorney-Client Session approximately 7:55 – 8:15PM.
Commissioner McEvoy motioned that the HLPC exit an attorney client session. (Motion-KM; NM-2nd; RT, AP-
Yes).

Commissioner McEvoy stated that the HLPC would like to request a site visit to reevaluate the window’s
conditions two years since the last visit. S. Guedel stated that the HLPC members were already there. Chair.
McEvoy stated it would allow them to see current conditions and  it would assist the commission to look at the
proposed work on the front porch. After discussion with J. Bacon, S. Guendel agreed to allow the site visit, for
exterior only, and would like to have advance notice of date.  Kaaren Davis noted that one of the DAR’s members
stuck their cane through the wood of a ground floor window along Green Street.

J. Bacon reiterated his belief that the DAR have the right to replace the windows and stated that the structure is
only designated a local landmark, and not on the State and National Registers. E. Dickerman, HPA clarified that
the structure is listed in the nomination paperwork as a contributing structure to the Kingston Stockade Local,
State, and National Register Historic District (1975). E. Dickerman, stated that this information is publicly
accessible and is posted for this project on the city website, but also via the NY State Historic Preservation
Office’s Cultural Resource Information System (CRIS). J. Bacon, Esq. stated he was unaware of this designation,
and Kaaren Davis stated that SHPO told them otherwise in the past. J. Bacon stated that he thought that the
applicants should request a vote now based on what information is available, but the decision is the applicants.

There was discussion regarding separating out the individual projects or keeping them together.  It was
determined that there is additional information needed for both, so tabling them as a single matter is best at
present. The HLPC agreed to schedule a site visit the week of February 17th, 2025, and to continue with the review
of the materials to determine the application’s completeness at the March 6, 2025, HLPC meeting.

Staff informed the Commission that the State Historic Preservation Office is  reviewing
nomination paperwork for 111 Downs Street (the Charles D. & Elizabeth Lantry House) and seeks commentary
from Kingston’s HLPC. The nomination paperwork’s Statement of Significance Summary paragraph details the
structure:
The Lantry House was the first home constructed on the property. According to the Burleigh panoramic map from 1875, the lot
was enclosed by a wooden fence, presumably to support farming operations up until the land was purchased by the Lantrys.
Elizabeth purchased the property lot from Thomas Cornell in 1894 for $700, and the house was built shortly afterward. An 1899
Sanborn map shows the footprint of the Lantry House and the former carriage house at the rear of the property.

Sometime in the late nineteenth century, Charles and Elizabeth Lantry moved from Ohio to Kingston where Charles assumed
the role of superintendent of carpentry for the Hudson River division of the West Shore Railroad. An article from 1930 states
that Charles was a “pioneer railroad construction supervisor and helped construct the New York Central Lines East and West,
and his experience was wide in railroad trestle and bridge construction as well as general buildings. Given his extensive
background in carpentry, it is possible that Charles either entirely built or did some of the carpentry work on the house himself.
The architecture of the interior spaces, including the servants’ quarters and a butler’s pantry, indicates that the Lantry skep one
or more servants. Charles and Elizabeth  Lantry lived at 111 Downs Street until their deaths, having raised their two daughters
in their home.  - While the Lantry House is a fairly modest example of Queen Anne architecture compared to other high -style
residences, it is one of the most elaborate examples in the surrounding neighborhood and the only one oriented on a corner lot
with both the east and southeast elevations powerfully positioned to covey a sense of grandeur to the historically middle -class
neighborhood. Its corner lot allowed for the embellishment of two sides of the house, and the designer took special advantage of
that with the angled corner box  bay. In addition, the interior is highly intact, with original plaster walls, wood floors, and walnut
trim. The butler’s pantry, servant’s staircase, and presumed servant’s room in the attic all speak to the prosperity of the owners.
Original fixtures, doors, and windows also remain untouched. Unlike many of the ne ighboring Queen Anne -style properties,
which have since been converted into duplexes or multifamily living spaces, the Lantry House retains its original floor plan as a
single-family dwelling. The Lantry House is thus an excellent example of a Queen Anne-style residence built for an upper-middle-
class family. It features key characteristics  of the style including an asymmetrical façade, bay windows, intricate woodwork on
the interior and exterior, a steeply pitched roof, and wall surfaces of both clapboard and decorative shingles.

Staff informed the Commission that the State Historic Preservation Office is  reviewing
nomination paperwork for 80 Washington Avenue (the Home for the Aged in Ulster County) and seeks
commentary from Kingston’s HLPC. The nomination paperwork’s Statement of Significance Summary
Paragraph details the structure:

The Home for the Aged in Ulster County (Home for the Aged), located in Kingston, Ulster County, in New York's Hudson
Valley, was constructed in 1929 by the Home for the Aged in Ulster County (an incorporated charitable organization
founded in 1919) out of growing necessity to accommodate an increasing number of elderly residents in Kingston and this
county at large. The building is locally significant under National Register Criterion A in the arca of Social History as it
effectively illustrates efforts in Kingston to provide "a suitable home for the proper care, support and maintenance of
respectable aged and indigent men and women of Ulster County," as noted in the organization's meeting minutes. At the
time of construction, the Home for the Aged offered much needed additional housing for the elderly in the city, an effort that
was sorely sought after for decades. Throughout much of the twentieth century, the Home was filled, offering housing to the
less fortunate through the auspices of charitable donation , without direct financing from the city or state. The home
remained in operation in this capacity until 1974 when the building was purchased by the Hudson Valley Senior Residence,
which operated as a non -profit organization charging residents rent. The bu ilding continues to convey this significance
through its interior layout with the retention of residential units and community rooms, as well as at the exterior with the
large lawned spaces and porches utilized for resident gatherings.

The building is also locally significant under National Register Criterion C in the area of Architecture as a strong example
of the Colonial Revival style in Kingston. The building was designed by local architect George E. Lowe who was well versed
with the style in the city. Within the context of Criterion C, the Home for the Aged exemplifies its Colonial Revival style
through its symmetrical design (culminating in the one -bay wide, two -story porches at the north and south ends of the
facade), use of an entrance pediment, and use of cast stone ornamentation, particularly seen at the entrance pediment and
spandrels at the facade. While the building does feature the 1999 addition, its construction is clearly distinguishable from
the original 1929 building and does not impact the primary elevation, which is minimally visible from the street, subject
only to a small sliver of the north elevation along Washington Avenue.

The Home for the Aged in Ulster County's period of significance extends from 1929 to 1974, beginning with the construction
of the building and ending when the operation of the home shifted from charitable donations to rented rooms.

items.title: #27 W. Chestnut Street: Converting northeastward-facing ground floor entrance into a window
items.discussion:
David Smilow, owner, presented plans to convert the existing northeastward-facing (driveway
side) ground floor entryway door into a window as a component of the interior renovation/restoration of the
structure’s basement. The project will create a window in a new basement bathroom  and  is minimally visible
from the public right of way along West Chestnut Street.

D. Smilow intends to remove the existing door , retaining the existing Italianate lintel  and sill, with the portal
staying intact at  31 and ¾” width. The owner sourced 19 th-century color-matching salvaged brick from other
areas inside the home which will be mortared into the existing opening using traditional lime-based mortar. He
stated that the exterior will be painted to match the exisiting colors upon completion. D. Smilow noted that the
structure had additions constructed at the rear , and certain interior walls once served as the exterior walls, so
they contained windows and other exterior elements . He has salvaged a window from an interior wall within
the house to  install in the newly reduced -in-height portal  and he also will be sourcing brick from interior
locations as the matching infill. S. Cahill questioned if he would retain the shutters, which were not rendered on
the submitted plan. D. Smilow confirmed the shutters will stay, and will be restored as needed. He also confirmed
for the HPA that the exisiting wooden door will be stored on site.

D. Smilow  informed the commission that he intends to apply for City of Kingston’s 10 -Year Graduated
Rehabilitation Tax Abatement Program (Chapter 360, Article 5) for exterior work to historic properties which
the Common Council readopted on October 1 st, 2024. If approved, D. Smilow could be the first applicant to the
newly reestablished tax -abatement program. To qualify for the program, the work must conform with the
Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and must be reviewed by the HLPC, and given a CoA, prior to the
commencement of work. In addition to the local tax abatement program, D. Smilow is working with SHPO to
access the NYS 20% Homeowner rehabilitation tax credits.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously in favor of rendering the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) & (2) and motioned that the proposed ground floor entryway door conversion to a window at 27 W, Chestnut Street in the Chestnut Street Local, State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed, discussion had at this meeting, and according to the proce dures stipulated in Section 405 -26 L, of the City of Kingston's Form Based Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic c haracter of the district for the following reasons: • pursuant to Section 405.26.L.13.a the HLPC determined the proposed project requires a Certificate of Appropriateness prior to the issuance of a Building Permit; • pursuant to Section 405.26.L.11 the HLPC has reviewed and determined the application and its supporting materials filed by the applicant are complete for formal review of the substance of the proposed work; • the proposed work is to take place at 3 and 1/2 story brick Italianate dwelling with a low -pitched roof built into a slope on the north side of W. Chestnut Street at the southwest corner of the intersection of Welles Lane and W. Chestnut Street, which was likely built in the early 1870s and is associated with George Hutton, the son of William Hutton a locally prominent brick and lumber manufacturer (1982, SHPO, Building Structure Inventory Form); • the owner is renovating the structure's interior and proposes to remove an existing wooden basement entryway door on the structure's NE side, fill the opening with bricks salvaged from the elsewhere in the structure, raise the sill, and install a smaller (31 -3/4" wide by 28" tall) arched salvaged wood window with tempered glass in the smaller opening; • the existing arched Italianate lintel will remain undisturbed; • salvaged brick in-fill must utilize historically proportioned lime -based mortar and be painted to match the facade's existing color, and the salvaged wood window shall be painted in red to match existing window color; • the shutters must be retained in their existing places; • the owner must retain in storage the original door and frame; • the HLPC recognizes that the project will result in a change that can be undone in the future if so desired by the current or a future owner; • this Certificate of Appropriateness shall be used as a component of the property owner's application for City of Kingston's 10-Year Graduated Rehabilitation Tax Abatement Program (Chapter 360, Article 5); • any changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application will be subject to further review by our commission prior to the work being carried out; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the City of Kingston's Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, it is proposed to move that on the 6th day of March, 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Comm ission, such notice to be subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and shall be valid for one year of this date. items.title: #33 N. Front Street: Storefront restoration with modifications
items.discussion:
John Perry, the applicant/owner, presented plans to reconstruct the storefront at 33 N. Front
Street (Signature Fitness) which was damaged by a vehicle collision on November 22, 2024:
https://www.dailyfreeman.com/2024/11/22/teen-charged-after-striking-support-beam-on-north-front-street-
in-kingston/.

The new plans contain alterations that are not exact to the previous conditions but are being designed to conform
with the FBC’s architectural standards. J. Perry proposes raising the exisiting storefront windowsills to 2 feet
eight (8) inches above the sidewalk. This is slightly higher than previous, but the owner is seeking some
additional height for future protection and improved appearance, and it is conforming to the code . J. Perry
confirmed that the window height would also meet the code’s requirements. He stated that the windows will be
glass with aluminum frames and that the knee wall will be made of an architectural plastic material in black. J.
Perry stated if the Pike Plan comes down, he will be returning  for additional modifications including paint,
signage, and removing the 2nd and 3rd story aluminum façade.
