items.title: #77 Main St (Dr. Jacobus Elmendorf House): Rear Italianate Porch Demolition & Reconstruction
items.discussion:
The applicant/co-owner, Amanda LaValle, presented plans to demolish a deteriorated late Italianate rear
porch at 77 Main Street.  The work is not visible from the public ROW on Main St and is necessary to access the dwelling’s
foundation for urgent inspection and repairs. A. LaValle explained that the house was built in stages from the 1770s until
the mid-1900s and that the foundation under the rear Italianate addition is in disrepair and requires urgent attention. A.
LaValle’s mason, Derrick McNab, is a skilled historic masonry who informed her that removal of the rear would allow him
the best access to the dwelling’s foundation for repairs.

She stated that although the porch was initially original to the house, it has been significantly "remuddled ” - sometime in
the 1960s or 1970s.  T he porch was expanded  with a large brick chimney constructed (with both inside and outside
elements).  It was also enclosed with jalousie windows and partially placed on a concrete block foundation. The porch is
currently in poor condition. If allowed by the commission, they will remove the porch (saving any salvageable elements,
probably most likely flooring), do the necessary investigation and repairs to the foundation, and then restore and rebuild
the porch in a historically appropriate manner. A. LaValle plans to replicate the fascia and sofit as well as the brackets on
the new structure, but do not plan to rebuild the chimney.

E, Dickerman stated that the HLPC does not customarily review projects not visible from the public right of way. However,
77 Main St is before the HLPC, per Section 405.26.J. c  which requires the HLPC to review any application for a
demolition/construction permit related to an Individually Landmarked property or properties within Landmark Districts.
No questions or alterations to the proposed project were asked by the HLPC.

decisions.vote: Motion - MG; EW - 2nd; RT, KM, AP - yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (2)(11), and Commissioner Grunblatt introduced a motion that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed rear Italianate porch demolition and reconstruction project at 77 Main Street (the Jacobus Elmendorf House) a landmark in the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kin gston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the circa 1780s 1 and 1/2 story Dutch stone vernacular dwelling with late Gothic and Italianate influences on the north side of Main St, one (1) parcel east of the intersection of Main and Green Streets, which "according to Marius Schoonmaker - belonged to Jacobus Elmendorf. Mr. William Dewitt refers to Elmendorf as a doctor. the house may have been constructed a short time after the Revolution. From the time of publication of the 1st Kingston Directory in 1857, until 1900, (now) 77 Main was the home of Mr. & Mrs. James E. Ostrander. He was first a clerk and later treasurer of the Ulster Co. Savings Institution. In 1915, George B. Heaton, a molder, and Mrs. G.B. Hilton's Boarding House were occupants of the building. From about 1920 until after 1940, Edwin Sibley, a physician, lived in the building. Since before 1950, A. W. Hazenbush, also a doctor, has lived in the house and had his office in the new wing to the west of the old building" (NYS SHPO BSIF, 1987); • the applicant may demolish the rear Italianate porch that is not visible from the public right of way, to gain access to the dwelling's foundation to provide information needed to undertake critical repairs addressing failing structural issues; • the HLPC encourages applicant or their design professional to document the existing features, size, and orientation of the rear Italianate porch prior to demolition; • the HLCP encourages the retention and reuse of as much original building elements as feasible; • after structural repairs are completed, the applicant is encouraged to rebuild a porch according to the existing design (features, size, and orientation), but without a masonry chimney; • no other work is scheduled for the structure at this time which would impact its material and visual integrity, as viewed from the public right of way along Main Street; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 5th day of June 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion - MG; EW - 2nd; RT, KM, AP - yes)

items.title: #97 Abeel St: 2nd-story Balcony Removal & Replacement
items.discussion:
The applicant/owner, Andrew Schiff, presented plans to replace a wooden balcony that he had removed in
April without HLPC review or permits.  A. Schiff stated that he has his contractor ready to repoint the masonry façade as

needed. A. Schiff explained that he wa nts to install an expanded metal balcony with more ornate railings very similar to
the one present at 86 Abeel St (across the street). He informed the commission that he has already purchased some of the
materials for the new balcony, and he hired Ciro Interante, an architect to draft plans and elevations for the proposal. A.
Schiff proceeded to inform the commission about the design and installation process for his proposed replacement balcony.
While the balcony’s exact age of the former wooden balcony is unclear, historic photographs demonstrate the structure,
and a similar balcony was present during the following documents: 1976 SHPO blue form; 1956 Kingston property record
card; 1917 photograph of Abeel Street. A. Schiff plans to rent out the ground floor, which was served as a restaurant, most
recently, the Armadillo, and use the up stairs as two apartments, with the one closest to the street as his personal living
space. A. Schiff reviewed the 1917 and 1956 photographs and believes the balconies that were present were outliers and not
the original balcony and were put in sometime after 1917.

A. Schiff believes that installing a metal balcony makes more sense for the Victorian period and the district. He also believed
the balcony likely was larger and had some form of wooden post support. He proposed a 40 in” protrusion for the balcony
as opposed to the older smaller balcony.  To support his hypothesis, A. Schiff pointed out that there are no other wooden
balconies in the area. Staff and commissioners closely reviewed the same 1917 photograph and could not conclude that the
present balcony was larger, metal, or more ornate than the one removed by Schiff. When zoomed in 1917 the  photograph
reveals a wooden balcony generally consistent with those present in 1956 and 1976.  E. Winchell asked if there is evidence
of the previous anchor marks for a larger and metal balcony in the façade where the wooden balcony was removed from? A.
Schiff said no. Instead, he pointed out his belief that the balcony was supported with a post and cited the 1917 photograph.

E. Dickerman asked what other reasons are there for changing the balcony , other than degradation. Schiff stated his two
goals are to increase aesthetics and to use the balcony. He did not like the look of the wooden balcony  and felt that there
was no precedent for wood balconies across the city. A. Schiff stated that if permitted, the new balcony would either be
supported by either hangers or brackets below the balcony, which would also be affixed with large bolts every 16” inches
through the exisiting maso nry. A. Schiff also explained that there would be a  new interior iron beam required that will
support the mounting places from the interior. He stated that the design is strong enough – but that, “if the balcony were
to fall, it would take the whole wall with it.”

E. Dickerman asked if any masonry needs removal or addition for the installation. A. Schiff said that he does not believe so.
E. Winchell asked A. Puetz if the proposal is anachronistic for an early 20 th-century building. A. Puetz stated that “it is a
little odd – I don’t know that the style blends to what is present there. I get that other building in the neighborhood display
similar metal balconies.” A. Schiff argued that we do not know definitively that the structure dates to the 20th-century, and
argued that the city has the date wrong.

The HPA pointed out that the HLPC must review proposed work in accordance with the local code’s requirements and the
Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties , and read the following standards that
appeared to be applicable to this proposal:
#2: The historic character of a property will be retained and preserved. The removal of distinctive materials or
alteration of features, spaces and spatial relationships that characterize a property will be avoided.
#3: Each property will be recognized as a physical record of its time, place and use. Changes that create a false sense
of historical development, such as adding conjectural features or elements from other historic properties, will not be
undertaken.
#4: Changes to a property that have acquired historic significance in their own right will be retained and preserved.

The HPA asked the HLPC to evaluate the proposal under these three applicable standards.

A. Schiff then responded and drew the commission back to the 1917 photograph and his interpretation of the photograph
included a larger balcony with support. The HPA asked if he considered the alternative, which is that the 1917 photograph
shows a wooden balcony highly like the 1956 balcony. He said he does not believe that it is possible.  S. Cahill stated that
the awning referenced by A. Schiff appears to come off of the structure in the background of 97 Abeel Street. A. Shiff said
there is no other building it could come off other than 97 Abeel Street. The HPA showed the 1956 property record card and
pointed out that a structure, with an awning, might have been removed from the eastern side sometime after the 1917
photograph. S. Cahill stated that the balcony does not appear to be steel, but rather wooden. The balcony across the street
was referenced again as an explanation for why a metal balcony should be permitted at 97 Abeel Street. The HPA pointed
out that it is customary for the HLPC not only to consider the district for a while but to consider the individuality of each
structure. E. Winchell asked A. Puetz the building’s date by the 6/1 window style, but did not feel confident answering the
question.

M. Grunblatt stated he is concerned about the use of a metal plate on the structural masonry to support the balcony. A.
Schiff clarified the metal plate will be installed on the inside of the building and will not be visible from the outside. M.
Grunblatt stated that it is HLPC’s goal to preserve structure well beyond our lifetimes. S. Cahill encouraged the HLPC to
return the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards (2, 3, & 4) cited by the HPA earlier, as the proposed work appears to violate
those standards. A. Schiff expressed resistance to the proposal violating each of these standards. S. Cahill stated that she
was not convinced a metal balcony was present. Schiff argued strongly that there is no evidence for the 1917 balcony being
made of wood.

M. Grunblatt asked that A Schiff or his architect, Ciro Interannte, provide the commission with photographic evidence
that marks are present on the façade that support an earlier, larger, and metal balcony. A. Schiff was skeptical that this
approach would work, but the HLPC concurred with M. Grunblatt about the importance of seeing material evidence of
the hypothesized pre-1917 metal balcony.

decisions.vote: Motion – AP; RT -2nd; KM, EW, MG - yes
decisions.text: The HLPC voted to TABLE the proposed application pending additional information from the applicant’s architect, Ciro Interante, demonstrating that a metal balcony was present before 1917 and pending commissioner site visits (Motion – AP; RT -2nd; KM, EW, MG - yes). items.title: #110 Fair Street (The Boice House): Second Story Wood Window Replacement
items.discussion:
L. Disenhof, the father of Alex Disenhof (owner) attended the meeting via Zoom from his home in New Hampshire.
This is an application that was tabled at the June 5, 2025, meeting to all L. Disenhof to discuss with his son the possibility of installing
wooden storm windows over the vinyl windows to screen their visibility. L. Disenhof stated that he looked at other structures in the
neighborhood and observed aluminum storm windows and some had white vinyl windows. He claimed that his contractor r eceived
approval to install low -end vinyl Anderson windows  at a property in the historic district . S. Cahill requested the address that the
contractor was referring to and L. Disenhof did not have that information and said that his contractor was unable to attend in person.
Staff asked him to obtain the location and provide staff for review.  S. Cahill pointed out that the Fair Street Historic District was
established in 1989, which would explain the presence of aluminum storms on some buildings. L. Disenho f doubted that the other
windows at 110 Fair Street were replaced prior to the district.
L. Disenhof stated that his son is outside of the country and apologize d for acting without following the proper review process that
he was informed about by the HPA in November of 2024. He stated that he will follow the proper review process to restore the attic
windows in the future. L. Disenhof stated that his son will likely return by the end of November. M. Grunblatt asked in wooden inserts
were an option, and L. Disenhof stated that we would now be looking at rebuilding new inserts. It was noted by L. Disenhof that the
original windows that were illegally removed had been destroyed.  S. Cahill asked the Commission if the felt it appropriate that the
vinyl windows on the front facade be replaced with more appropriate wood windows? M. Grunblatt stated that it would be advisable.
He stated that the pattern of people asking for forgiveness than for permission is a rising problem, and the HLPC cannot permit that
to continue. L. Disenhof again referenced the installation of vinyl windows at another property (location unknown) and M. Grunblatt
stated that in his decades on HLPC, the commission has not permitted such a replacement  for original wood windows. He pointed
out it might be in the Heritage Area where the HLPC has less jurisdiction. L. Disenhof said he would get the address to the H LPC,
and S. Cahill asked that he send a copy of the reference letter.
Staff informed the HLPC that extensions could not be made to this project to accommodate A. Disenhof due to the time limits written
into the code. M. Grunblatt proposed denying the applicant and having them reapply once A. Disenhof returns from Europe. Sta ff
also informed HLPC that you cannot have them reapply with the same application, as that would imply that they would overturn the
previous decision. S. Cahill stated that the HLPC could require that the vinyl windows be removed and more historically appropriate
wood windows be installed in their place to repair the structure’s integrity. It was noted that the HLPC should have the specifications
of proposed replacements prior to purchase to ensure adequacy.  L. Disenhof said, “So you’re  asking to spend another 15K?” The
HPA then reminded the commissioners that at the previous meeting they were concerned that the work as it currently stands violates
the following components of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties:
• #2. The historic character of a property will be retained and preserved. The removal of distinctive materials or alteration of
features, spaces and spatial relationships that characterize a property will be avoided.
• #4. Changes to a property that have acquired historic significance in their own right will be retained and preserved.
• #5. Distinctive materials, features, finishes, and construction techniques or examples of craftsmanship that characterize a
property will be preserved.
• #6. Deteriorated historic features will be repaired rather than replaced. Where the severity of deterioration requires
replacement of a distinctive feature, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture and, where possible,
materials. Replacement of missing features will be substantiated by documentary and physical evidence.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; EW, NM – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2). Commissioner Grunblatt introduced the motion that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed 2nd -story street-facing window replacement project at 110 Fair Street (The Boice House) a State and Nationally Registered building in the Fair Street Local Historic Dis trict, if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is not compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a, the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is at the 2.5 story French Second Empire dwelling located on the eastern side of Fair St three (3) lot north of the intersection of Fair and John Streets that according to the State and National Register Nomination was ,"ca. 1850 by Mr. Erastus Cooke, an Ulster County attorney. He sold the house to Heweitt Boice in 1869 for $7800. Boice owned a bluestone and limestone quarry in upper Kingston. Stone from Boice's quarry as well as the Luke Noone Quarry in Kingston was used for the construction of the Brooklyn Bridge towers. Boice also served as a trustee for the First National Bank of Rondout from 1896 - 1914. The house passed from Mr. Boice to his daughter, Kathryn in 1917 and then to Richard Oliver Kuehne in 1953" (2002, NR Nom Form). • records indicate that on November 21 and 22, 2024, prior to initiating any work, the property owner engaged email exchanges with staff, providing a photograph of an original window from the interior to demonstrate condition; • on November 25, 2024, staff replied, advising the owner of review requirements, providing information on potential wood window preservationists, and noting the Homeowner tax credit programs; • the owner did not submit plans for restoration or replacement, and the city was notified of work being done which triggered the inspection of the Building Safety Division to issue a Stop Work Order, and the owner to file the appropriate paperwork and documentation for HLPC review; • under this review, the HLPC recognizes that the owner removed and destroyed the existing 1/1 wooden sash windows on the 2nd-floor facing Fair Street, and replaced them with new vinyl 1/1 double hung windows without HLPC review or permits on March 18, 2025; • that the HLPC reviewed the materials submitted and determined the window replacement project was an inappropriate treatment that violated Standards #2, 4, 5, and 6 of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Struc tures (36 CFR 67); • the HLPC hereby directs the owner to undertake the following measures to correct the inappropriate restoration work which was unauthorized: 1. Submit for HLPC review and consideration a wooden window replacement, to be installed in place of the vinyl units. 2. Submit proposed replacements to City by November 30, 2025. • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 10th day of July 2025, the Commission DENY a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work which was done without authorization and direct the applicant to return to the HLPC with an appropriate replacement wood window to more accurately reflect the historic character of the building and district within which it is a contributing asset, as noted above. (Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; EW, NM – yes)

items.title: #97 Abeel St: 2nd-story Balcony Removal & Replacement
items.discussion:
Andrew J. Schiff, the property owner, returned to HLPC with his architect, Ciro Interrante, a former HLPC member,
after his application was tabled during June 5 th, 2025, meeting. They provided the HLPC with new materials via a thumb drive that
the HLPC had not had time to review before the meeting.  At the June 5, 2025 HLPC  meeting, A. Schiff stated that he already
purchased the materials to replace the balcony with his vision. The balcony’s age is unclear, but historic photographs demons trate
the structure, and a similar wooden balcony was present in a 1917 photograph of Abeel Street, the 1956 property record card, and
the 1976 SHPO Blue Form. A. Schiff stated that he spent some time researching the structure and seeking older photographs. He
also read to the commission, only a portion of a letter from Marissa Marvelli, that discussed the history of use at the site:
82 West Union Street contributes to the history and significance of the Rondout -West Strand Historic District. It was built in
1909 by John Worf (1862-1924), a German immigrant who operated a hotel and restaurant on Abeel Street for many years.

The bustling commerce of Rondout in the nineteenth century, in particular the activity of the Delaware & Hudson Canal,
attracted a large population of immigrants, among them many German craftsmen. Together they built a community and
economy in Rondout that centered on brewing, baking, butchering, shoemaking, brickmaking, coopering, and more. Early on
Worf was a brewer and bottler in the Rondout. Glass beer bottles bearing his name can still be found. By the early 1890s he
was operating an eponymous saloon a t 103 Abeel Street, and soon thereafter a hotel above. In 1915, he commissioned a
new brick commercial building at 97 Abeel Street (Gerard W. Betz, architect) for his restaurant.
A. Schiff stated that he could not find a better photograph than the 1917 photograph. He believe s the 1917 photograph shows a
different balcony than the 1956 photograph. The HLPC, Staff, A. Schiff, and C. Interannte closely reviewed the circa 1917 photograph
that A. Schiff submitted and did not come to the same conclusion. Zooming in on the photograph reveals a wooden balcony generally
consistent with those present in 1956 and 1976. The HLPC expressed that the submitted information is insufficient to determine that
a metal balcony existed at the site.
A. Schiff and C. Interannte repeatedly pointed to metal balconies on other structures in the Rondout, but the HLPC and Staff equally
reminded the applicants that a feature that is present at one structure (e.g., 86 Abeel St, etc.) does not justify adding it to another.
Staff reminded them that there is no documentation present to verify their claims that a metal balcony once exisiting on the structure.
Even the 1956 and 1917 photograph appear to show a wood balcony. Staff also added that adding depth to a rebuilt balcony is more
appropriate than adding new design elements for which there are no data to support their presence. The HLPC and Staff reviewe d
a photograph of the structure with the balcony removed and did not see evidence of a past metal balcony, a nd the applicant
acknowledged the same.
The HPA reminded Commissioners that at the previous meeting they were concerned that the work proposed at 97 Abeel St by A.
Schiff violates the following Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation:
#2: The historic character of a property will be retained and preserved. The removal of distinctive materials or alteration of
features, spaces and spatial relationships that characterize a property will be avoided.
#3: Each property will be recognized as a physical record of its time, place and use. Changes that create a false sense of
historical development, such as adding conjectural features or elements from other historic properties, will not be undertaken.
#4: Changes to a property that have acquired historic significance in their own right will be retained and preserved.
#5: Distinctive materials, features, finishes, and construction techniques or examples of craftsmanship that characterize a
property will be preserved.
#6: Deteriorated historic features will be repaired rather than replaced. Where the severity of deterioration requires replacement
of a distinctive feature, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture and, where possible, materials. Replacement
of missing features will be substantiated by documentary and physical evidence.

The applicants pressed repeatedly about the balcony that they are proposing matches the time-period, and that we don’t know
what the original balcony looked like and what it was made of. S. Cahill stated that the commission would support reconstructing a
balcony, but that the size, material, and design are the challenging points. A. Puetz concurred and stated that the HLPC would like
to see a more simplified design that is in keeping with the historic photographs. C. Interrante stated that the tiebacks and the
supporting brackets are structurally needed, and that the changes in size were design requests. The HPA pointed out that these
new supports, which are needed for a bigger metal balcony, automatically suggest that the original balcony was lighter, especially
since there is no evidence to suggest past support structures.

A. Puetz and S. Cahill pointed out there may be new Zoning Code requirements triggered by the new construction, and that a
waiver might be required because of greater depth and proximity to the curb. Additional review is needed by Staff to determine
whether the work may trigger a minor or major waiver review. The Commission collectively felt that a metal substructure, clad in

wood, that is slightly larger and supported by brackets and tiebacks would be permissible, if it overall matched the design of the
railing removed. The Commission will allow metal railings, but not in the ornate style as proposed, but in the more simplistic ones
of the designs identified through photos, as there is insufficient evidence to fully confirm wood as the only option in 1917. Staff also
informed the applicant that once installed, the owner must list the City as coinsured because the balcony will project over the
public right of way, like projecting signs.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; AP, NM – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2). The Planning Director read to the commissioner, that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed 2nd -story street-facing balcony removal and replacement at 97 Abeel Street in the Rondout-West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application, and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is at the 2-story 3-bay masonry building with a ground-floor shop and 2nd-floor balcony on the north side of Abeel St, mid-way between the intersections with Hone and Wurts St's which dates to about 1910, and according to the 1976 NYS SHPO Blue Form, "remains intact and has received no major modern alterations since its original construction" (NYS SHPO BSIF, 1987); • the applicant/owner removed without review a 2nd- story wooden street -facing balcony that photographs demonstrated was present in some form as early as 1917; • the applicant seeks to install a new balcony made of metal that is inspired by a similar metal balcony at 86 Abeel St, but that no historical documentation exists demonstrating such a balcony was ever present; • the HLPC requires the applicant to make every effort to follow #s 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties; • the HLPC accepts using a metal frame for the base, tie backs and brackets beneath; wooden flooring; square corner posts with small caps and railings to match those depicted in photographs of 1917 and 1956 as attached; both corner posts and railings may be metal or wood; all metal surfaces shall be primed, followed by a paint color chosen from a historic palette collection and submitted to staff for approval before application; • the reconstructed balcony shall match the historic design in size and shape, with no additional ornamentation or omissions; • the HLPC recognizes and supports a Minor Waiver for the depth of the balcony to be 3'7"; • the applicant shall provide the required insurance for the balcony to overhang the public right-of-way, naming the City of Kingston as additionally insured, in accordance with Section 358-9 C. • no other work is scheduled for the building at this time which would impact its material and visual integrity; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, Commissioner Grunblatt moved that on the 10th day of July 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this da te. (Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; AP, NM – yes) RECOMMENDATION:

items.title: Proposed Amendments to Form Based Zoning Code Section 405.26.L (Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission)
items.discussion:
The HPA shared with the HLPC a series of preliminary edits to ss405.26.L (HLPC) of the Form Based Zoning Code
that addresses the Appeal process. The proposed edit will remove the ZBA as an appellate body and require property owners to file
an article 78 in the Supreme Court based on the same hardship criteria evaluated by the HLPC. The HPA also proposed adding a
HLPC Supplemental Definitions section to the code because the FBC’s master definition section does not adequately address most
of the terms within the field of historic preservation. S. Cahill, the Planning Director, also informed the commission that the Zonin g
Task force would propose some additional edits over the coming months. The Commissioners generally supported the proposal.
The HPA asked if the Commission would allow staff to further refine these edits and seek input from the SHPO CLG coordinator (a
requirement for CLG Communities) before the September meeting.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; NM, AP – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to direct staff to continue to refine the discussed amendments and to share a draft with the SHPO CLG Coordinator, pursuant to CLG requirements, so the commission can render a recommendation at its September 4, 2025, meeting. (Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; NM, AP – yes)

Proposed NAPC CAMP Virtual Training Courses
items.discussion:
The HPA informed the Commission that upon f urther review of the 2025 City Budget, they learned that the cost to
join the NAPC in 2025 was higher than anticipated. As such, th ere remains only enough funds for four (4) NAPC virtual CAMP
courses this year. Staff advised that three (3) courses are considered, CAMP Essentials , and the NAPC strongly recommends
including them in any training request to cover the fundamentals of serving on a preservation commission: Legal Basics; Standards
and Guidelines for Design Review; Meeting Procedures. After the June 5, 2025, HLPC meeting, the HPA conducted a survey of
Commissioner and related staff to learn which courses are most needed. The HPA read back to the commission that the following
non-essential courses received the highest rankings:
• TOPIC 3 – Alternate Materials
• TOPIC 8 – Enforcement & Violations
• TOPIC 12 – Community Engagement and Building Public Support

The Commission discussed these three courses and determined that Topic 12 should be requested, and Topic 3 should serve as a
back-up. Commissioners agreed that fostering a better relationship with Kingston residents and other stakeholders is critical during
the push for historic districting in Wilbur and Ponckhockie, but also at this time when so many people have relocated to King ston,
and when so many people seek to use alternative materials.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; AP, NM – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to direct staff to secure and schedule the identified NAPC CAMP trainings for the Fall of 2025. (Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; AP, NM – yes). items.title: #15 Ravine St: Basement window replacement
items.discussion:
The applicant/owner, Tara Kruse, presented plans to replace some boarded up basement portals at 15
Ravine Street in the Rondout-West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District (1970). T. Kruse, along with architect
David Murray, seek to install single fixed-pane wood windows with white trim in the three (3) boarded-up basement portals
that face Ravine Street  to allow the owner to create a basement residential unit . Close inspection of the 1956 property
record card photograph indicates that these windows were closed with wood sometime before 1956, and the applicant’s
interior photographs of the portals demonstrate that the original windows are gone. T. Kruse confirmed that the project
will not alter the exisiting portal’s size, will be installed at comparable depths into the portal as other windows across the
Ravine Street face, and will be painted white.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; AP, KM, EW – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2). Commissioner Grunblatt introduced the motion that the Commissioners present find as fact the proposed installation of new basement windows in boarded up portals at 15 Ravine Street in the Rondout-West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District (1979), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is comp atible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a, the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • work is to take place at multi -sectioned 1 to 1.5 story brick vernacular commercial building located on the west side of Ravine Street, two parcel's north of the intersection of Ravine and Abeel Streets, which dates to circa 1885 and historically served as a storage facility (see 1976, NYS SHPO BSIF); • the owner is rehabilitating the building with the intent to add a basement residential unit that requires external lighting, and the architect, David Murray, proposes installing new windows in the boarded-up basement arched portals; • the owner submitted photographs demonstrating that no windows exist behind the boards, and that historical photographs do not exist to demonstrate the original detail/design of windows previously in place; • the HLPC finds SOI Standard #6 applicable in this context: "Deteriorated historic features will be repaired rather than replaced. Where the severity of deterioration requires replacement of a distinctive feature, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture and, where possible, materials. Replacement of missing features will be substantiated by documentary and physical evidence." https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/treatment-standards-rehabilitation.htm; • the HLPC approves proposed basement windows as follows: single pane white wood trim – rectangular with central trim at top to follow the window arch; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 4th day of September, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; AP, KM, EW – yes)

items.title: #168 Fair St: Northwestward side porch construction
items.owner: Applicant, Daniel Stupple (Earthly Living Home Renovations)
items.discussion:
The applicant, Daniel Stupple of Earthly Living Home Renovations, and  Marlin Mannelly (owner)
presented plans to reconstruct the northwest side porch at 168 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Historic District. D.
Stupple described the porch as badly degraded from water coming from the gutter and downspout system off the primary
dwelling – the volume of water is significant because of the roof’s square footage. The porch had  previous repairs to
address the water damage, and a tarp is currently in place to prevent additional leaks. D. Stupple added that the columns
are compromised, and decking and railings are degraded. They propose to start with rebuilding the substructure to comply
with current code standards using pressure- treated lumber. Ideally, they plan to reuse as much original material as
possible. S. Cahill pointed out that any gutter modifications should take care to prevent water from traveling onto the
adjacent property. Additionally, S. Cahill questioned if the new substructure, which is oriented differently than the historic
structure, will be designed in a manner to retain the current porch deck board’s orientation (90 degrees from the dwelling).
D. Stupple stated that the decking orientation will stay as historically put in place.  A new shingle roof for the porch will
match the main structure’s roof  in both material and color . Commissioner Tonner noted staff comment about different
types of lattice work and questioned the decorative siding on the porch and what would happen there.  D. Stupple clarified
that the Queen Anne decorative siding at the porch’s end will be reconstructed and included in the new porch. He also

added that the lattice work beneath the porch will be recreated in-kind. He recognized that lattice work on the house is a
different style and that is not being touched under this project.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; KM, AP, EW – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2). Commissioner Grunblatt introduced the motion that the Commissioners present find as fact the proposed porch rehabilitation project at 168 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Historic District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a, the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 2.5 story Queen Anne Victorian building with a street facing gable and north facing (side porch) that is on the NE side of Fair Street one lot south of the intersection of St. James and Fair Streets, which is not present on the Beers map of Kingston from 1870, but appears to be present on the 1887 Sanborn Fire Insurance map of Kingston; • the side porch is in disrepair from water damage/neglect and requires extensive reconstruction to mitigate water infiltration and to ensure safety for the property owners; • the owner proposes reconstructing the substructure according to modern building code using pressure- treated lumber; • the applicant shall make every effort to conform with the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties ( https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/treatment-standards-rehabilitation.htm) #2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 - specifically, that the proposed porch rehabilitation shall make every effort to salvage as much historic ornamental/Queen Anne siding, railings, columns, and other character defining features as possible in their original placements; • any publicly visible materials that are non- salvageable/reusable shall be constructed out of Douglas fir lumber that matches the dimensionality of the feature its replacing; • the proposed rehabilitation shall not alter the orientation of the deck boards, or any other feature visible from the public right of way; • the porch shall be repainted / stained in matching color and that a new asphalt roof color to match the main building shall be installed; • the applicant shall install a new gutter and downspout system on the porch; • the rehabilitated porch shall feature the same lattice work beneath the porch; - no new features shall be added or removed without HLPC review; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 4th day of September 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; KM, AP, EW – yes). RECOMMENDATION:

items.title: #157 Pine St (Pine Street African Burial Ground): NY State and National Register Nomination Endorsement
items.owner: cants, Tyrone Wilson ( Executive Director Harambee) & NY SHPO
items.discussion:
Representatives of Harambee Kingston NY, Inc. and Tyrone Wilson, Exec. Dir.; were present.  The project
is the nomination of the Pine Street African Burial Grounds to the State and National Registers of Historic Places as a
cemetery site that meets criterion D (Property has yielded, or is likely to yield, information important in prehistory or history)
with a period of significance between 1750 and 1870. As is customary practice, the HLPC has been contacted by SHPO
to provide a letter of support , and any comment,  explaining why the site meets NPS criteria and is worthy of SR & NR
Listing. According to the NR Nomination, “[the Burial Ground’s] boundary was drawn to reflect the extent of the burial
ground as indicated by historical maps and archival documents, archaeological excavations, and ground penetrating
radar. Based on the collected data, approximately 60 percent of the burial ground is located within 157 Pine Street, with
further evidence of burials at 163 Pine Street, 104 Saint James Street, 106 Saint James Street, 110 Saint James Street,
114 Saint James Street, 156 Fair Street, and 160 Fair Street.”
Commissioner K. McEvoy identified some discrepancies and potential additions that would strengthen the draft national
register form. K. McEvoy attended the meeting remotely to spend additional time looking back at some of his past research
on the Pine Street burial grounds and provide the HLPC accurate information for inclusion in the LOS, and to share with
Harambe. K. McEvoy’s suggested edits and additions included the following:
• Suggest rephrasing the paperwork to state "The site is still marked as a cemetery on the 1870 and 1875 Beers
maps (Figures 4 & 5).'
• Change Maisha to Maisha Tyler throughout.
• Clarification on ownership easement situation.
• Consider mention of the 1755 Census.
• Consider brief mention of Narrative of Sojourner Truth.
• Consider including information from City Engineer A.F. Hallinan regarding remonstrance of an auction sale in
1866.
• Consider inclusion of information concerning Henry C. Rosencranse.
• Consider mention of the burial ground as described by Sylvester in 1880.
K. McEvoy stated that he has not prepared the comments in a final form but would provide a final draft of his edits to the
HPA tomorrow, Sept 5, 2025, who will finalize a draft LOS and share it with the full Commission and applicants for
feedback. The HPA reminded those in attendance that the LOS must be submitted by the city before close of business
on Friday Sept. 5, 2025, so that it is received by SHPO before the deadline.

decisions.vote: Motion MG; 2nd – RT; KM, EW, AP – yes
decisions.text: The HLPC voted unanimously to authorize Staff to finalize the attached letter of support under the process discussed, that incorporates additional information as discussed by K. McEvoy and send it to the SHPO. (Motion MG; 2nd – RT; KM, EW, AP – yes).

Adoption of HLPC Meeting Minutes of Thursday, July 10, 2025, and September 4, 2025: •
#57 N. Front St: Exterior Rehabilitation of Fire Damaged Building
items.discussion:
Paul B. Jankovitz, RA, (Architect) and Alexander and Cynthia Nyameke (Flowerhill Group, LLC),
presented their plans to modify a past rehabilitation project to address fire damage (Feb 2023) at 57 N. Front Street. P.
Jankovitz shared plans and elevation drawings that propose removing a false (western style) façade and returning to the
former street-facing gable end. S. Cahill informed P. Jankovitz that Commissioner Eric Winchell discovered just before
the meeting a circa 1900 photograph of N. Front Street on NY Heritage from Friends of Historic Kingston, that shows the
false façade was present at a much earlier time.

The photo was shared for all, and it was noted that before this early photograph was found, the earliest photograph came
from the 1956 property record card, followed by a 1976 photograph from FHK. All the photographs suggest that the false
façade was present during the mid- 20th-century and falls within the commercial district’s period of significance  which
was extended from the colonial era up to 1965 in the 2016 Stockade S/NHR update.

P. Jankovitz noted that there is precedence for a non-flat roofed row building across the street at 44 N. Front Street – the
Everywhere Shop, which had a gabled roof that ran parallel with N. Front St in 1956 and that was covered by a false
façade later. E. Winchell stated that there was also a similar scenario at the corner of John and Fair Street.

To determine the appropriateness of the project, the HLPC questioned P. Jankovitz about the condition and building
history of 57 N. Front Street. P. Jankovitz stated that the building shows multiple past fires and building episodes.
Chairman Grunblatt stated he was inside the structure years ago and can attest that the structure was heavily m odified.
With this information in hand, the HLPC evaluated the proposal against the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the
Treatment of Historic Properties: Rehabilitation as a Treatment and Standards for Rehabilitation. Going through the
standards, it was determined that numbers 1, 5, 7, 8 and 10 were not applicable in this case. Reviewing the others, the
HLPC addressed each one and determined that the street facing gable, while different than what was present in the 20th-
century is more appropriate than restoring the false façade predominantly destroyed by the fire and does not violate the
SOI Rehab Standards 2, 3, 4, 6 and 9.

P. Jankovitz also clarified for the Commission that the ground floor would remain untouched. The proposed second floor
façade would feature light grey Hardie clapboard, with white Hardie trim. The proposal featured a more elaborate corner
trim, that was deemed inappropriate for the modest structure. Architect A. Puetz proposed a more modest, simple 8” wide
corner trim board for the upper second story. The commission also requested that the window lintel trim be simplified. P.
Jankovitz and the owners agreed  to these modifications. The proposed replacement windows would be made of wood
and feature 1/1 double hung operation.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – NM; EW, AP, KM -yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Unlisted and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact. Commissioner Grunblatt introduced the motion that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed exterior rehabilitation with modifications at 57 N. Front St in the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District (1975), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, are compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 2- story wooden commercial row building three 93) lots west of the intersection of N. Front and Crown Streets that Streets that may date to the 1880s, with a commercial use for the property documented back to 1857 - over the last 100 years the property saw use as a furniture store, grocery store, shoe repair shop, watch repair shop, Dallas Hot Wieners, and a tailor shop (NYS SHPO BISF, 1987); • the structure was severely damaged by fire in early 2023 and has remained vacant since; • the project will replace the existing siding with new Hardie Board composite clapboard siding in light grey color, with modest trim in white color; • the project modifies the 2nd-story fenestration to feature two 1/1 windows with defined lintels and sills; • the project shall remove the preexisting 2nd- story faux facade and shall restore the more historically appropriate street-facing gable with Hardie board soffits and Hardie board fascia; • Based on the visual, historical, and material evidence at hand, the HLPC recognizes that the proposed alterations are appropriate for the historical context and period of significance (colonial to 1960s) for the Stockade Historic District, and conform with the Secretary of the Interiors' Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties [https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/treatment-standards-rehabilitation.htm]; • Modify the end of the 2nd-story with simplified corner molding and smaller caps as discussed, but not shown on the plans; • the ground floor storefront shall remain physically unchanged, and woodwork and windows shall be restored in-kind; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 9th day of October 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – NM; EW, AP, KM -yes)

items.title: #93 Wall Street (Van Steenburgh House): 2nd story window replacement without CoA
items.discussion:
Matha Dallis, owner and the contractor Jay Elsoffer, were present to discuss with the commission the
unauthorized work (removal and replacement of four (4) street-facing the 2nd-story windows) at 93 Wall Street (the Tobias
Van Steenburgh House) without a certificate of appropriateness or building permit. 93 Wall St is a highly significant
individual local landmark  (designated 1971) listed on the S/NHRs and is reportedly the only house not burned by the
British in 1777. One HLPC landmark plaque and another commemorating the structure’s history are affixed to the
structure’s façade along Wall St.

After the work was recognized and the owner notified, M. Dallis emailed the HPA, on August 28, 2025, that they applied
for a CoA and Building Permit stating: “ We misunderstood the window process. Our apologies. As of today, 7 of the
windows are installed, and 3 are uninstalled. 1 window, which we had purchased, will not be installed due to an air
conditioner in the old window. We have the window so in the future we have it as the mate to the other adjacent window
that was installed. Both very small windows on the back of the house.” M. Dallis later  informed the HPA on August 29th,
that they are not “…opting for any tax credit for the windows. Thank you for asking though.”

The Commission reviewed a past work review that took place in 2024. The  property owners (Martha Bear Dallis and

David Dallis) came before staff for an in-kind roof and gutter replacement project that received a desk review. J. Elsoffer,
who was the also the contractor for that work,  shared photos of the work he did to replace the roof and restore the box
gutters in-kind, and that during that work they discovered more severe wood rot than anticipated, and they added that the
sills of the windows before replacement were in poor condition too. The units that were removed were destroyed and are
no longer at the site.

E. Dickerman noted that the desk review granted states to the owners, in writing, to reconnect with Staff and/or the HLPC
if the type or scope of work changed .  It was unclear to the HLPC why the applicants did not do so. When asked about
this component of the desk review, M. Dallis, stated that “they should have read the approval more closely”.

The Commission reviewed photographs of the windows before the work was undertaken, along with those the HPA took
of the site afterwards, as a reference. The HLPC reviewed the project using the Secretary of Interiors Standards for the
Rehabilitation of Historic Properties  [https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/treatment-standards-rehabilitation.htm] and
determined that standards 1, 7, 8 and 10 are not applicable and the work as it stands violates the following standards:

#2: The historic character of a property will be retained and preserved. The removal of distinctive materials or
alteration of features, spaces and spatial relationships that characterize a property will be avoided.
#3: Each property will be recognized as a physical record of its time, place and use. Changes that create a false
sense of historical development, such as adding conjectural features or elements from other historic properties, will
not be undertaken.
#4: Changes to a property that have acquired historic significance in their own right will be retained and preserved.
#5: Distinctive materials, features, finishes, and construction techniques or examples of craftsmanship that
characterize a property will be preserved.
#6: Deteriorated historic features will be repaired rather than replaced. Where the severity of deterioration requires
replacement of a distinctive feature, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture and, where possible,
materials. Replacement of missing features will be substantiated by documentary and physical evidence.
#9: New additions, exterior alterations, or related new construction will not destroy historic materials, features, and
spatial relationships that characterize the property. The new work will be differentiated from the old and will be
compatible with the historic materials, features, size, scale and proportion, and massing to protect the integrity of
the property and its environment.

The Commission examined the south-facing gable window and found that its operation, design, and material more closely
match the window that the owner/applicant removed. However,  the three Wall Street facing windows are more
complicated. Here the work done in violation replaced original fabric, changed the window’s design from two, 8 by 8 pane;
and 1, 10 by 10 pane ; inward swinging French windows, to all 6/6 double hung windows . The Commission determined
this work inappropriate and inconsistent with preservation objectives . The HLPC did recognize that the owner and their
contractor did a substantially appropriate project for the roof and gutter restoration. However, the HLPC must evaluate
the window work as a violation in accordance with the SOI and the local code to determine appropriateness.

Chairman Grunblatt asked about the possibility of replacing the current windows with pre- made windows that match the
material, design, and operation of the original windows or making identical replacements. M. Dallis asked who will pay for
this work and questioned if the future replacement would include only single-pane windows which are less energy efficient.
Commission Puetz noted that there are exemptions for energy code matters with historic properties and while it is not

desirable in some cases, it is possible for a better restoration job. J. Elsoffer said he understood the request and was

items.title: FY25 Certified Local Government Grant Opportunity
items.discussion:
The HPA informed the Commission that SHPO announced the FY25 CLG grant opportunity is open and
accepting applications until October 31, 2025. CLG funds are available for a wide variety of projects and awards typically
range between $10,000 - $50,000. Examples of CLG grant projects may include Commission Training; Surveys/National
Register Nominations; Public Outreach programs and materials, including publications; Design Guidelines; Website
updates/web-based projects or other administrative tools. Since joining the CLG program in 1987, the cit y has received
numerous grants for preservation consultant studies of neighborhoods, recommendation, and national register listings.
Most recently, the city received a 2021 CLG for surveying Wilbur and Ponckhockie, and a 2024 CLG grant to nominate
Wilbur to the State and National Registers of Historic Places.

Based on the grant opportunity’s parameters, Staff believe that this is a timely opportunity for the city to apply for
Kingston’s 1st Historic Preservation Plan, complementing and strengthening the proposed comprehensive plan update.
Our close review of the exisiting comp plan (2015- 2025) and past CLG consultant reports from 2014, 2003, 2001, and
1987 also speak to the long-identified need for a historic preservation master plan to guide the city’s efforts to conserve
its rich stock of architectural and cul tural resources, while positioning them as critical economic incentives for local
investment. Some Commissioners and Staff learned about the importance of these plans during the 2025 Preservation
Conference’s NAPC CAMP training. Model Preservation plans exist in the Albany-NY, Syracuse-NY, Montclair-NJ, Plano-
TX, Austin-TX, and others . According to the National Alliance of Preservation Commissions (which Kingston is a new
member of), a preservation plan:

“…identifies and articulates community preservation goals, lets current and future property owners know how the
community intends to grow, helps eliminate confusion about the purpose of the local preservation ordinance, educates
the public about the community’s history and heritage, creates an agenda for future preservation work and creates a
way to measure preservation’s progress. Preservation plans also encourage economic development and strengthen
political understanding of historic preservation policies.
If funding permits, Staff also believe it is prudent to create comprehensive city-wide historic preservation design guidelines
that would clarify for the community what approaches/treatments are acceptable to the City’s Landmarks Code,
Commission, and the Secretary of the Interior. Staff shared that historic design guidelines are staples of good preservation
planning nationwide by fostering greater collaboration with property owners, respect, and support for local preservation
programs. Frances Stern (SHPO CLG Coordinator) informed staff this is a CLG fundable project and supported the city
apply for this work. Cailtin Meives (Director of Preservation at the Preservation League of NYS) also encouraged the city

to apply for this project. C. Meives shared with the HPA some consultants to learn more about scopes of work and cost
estimates for the application.

decisions.vote: Motion AP; 2nd – KM; MG, NM, EW – yes
decisions.text: The HLPC voted unanimously to authorize the Chair to sign the attached letter of support and endorse the City’s application for the OPRHP FY25 CLG grant. (Motion AP; 2nd – KM; MG, NM, EW – yes) REMINDER: The HLPC CAMP training will take place on October 23 and 24, 2025. Members are encouraged to attend in person at City Hall. The training will take place in Conference Room 1. Next Meeting: Thursday, November 6, 2025. This meeting was live-streamed at the City of Kingston YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/c/CityofKingstonNY

decisions.text: The Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) for the City of Kingston makes the following findings, reached in accordance with the review procedures set forth in Section 405.26.L.10 of the City of Kingston’s Form Based Zoning Code. The following d eterminations regarding the issuance of a Certificate of Appropriateness for the development proposal known as “The Kingstonian”, address addendum material submitted on October 22, 2025, by the applicant, as well as original submissions by consultants and interested members of the public. The HLPC further notes that the evidentiary record included material offered for consideration of the closure of Fair Street Extension, massing, scale, visual elements, fire and public health/safety issues, and uses at the project site. The aforementioned material has been thoroughly reviewed for compatibility with the historic character of the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National Historic District (KSHD). HLPC Commissioners present find as fact that The Kingstonian, located at #9-17 & 21 North Front Street and Fair Street Extension (SBLs 48.80-1-25.100, 48.80-1-26), in the Stockade Historic District, by the Applicant and owner, Kingstonian Development LLC, if done according to the plans reviewed prior to and at this meeting, is compatible with the historic character of the KSHD for the following reasons: • The proposed work is to take place at parcels formerly occupied by a City of Kingston on grade parking lot, an abandoned portion of public roadway, including also two structures, a warehouse building and an abandoned restaurant, along with associated site improvements; • Based on the resources HLPC customarily consults, the HLPC understands that the existing warehouse structure does not appear on the 1858 Map of Ulster County by J. H. French, is depicted as a smaller structure on the 1870 Beers Map of Rondout, Kingston, and Wilbur; and it is shown on the 1914 Codwise Maps. That documentation on the NYS Cultural Resource Inventory System (CRIS) was studied and it is recognized under 2 entries that the structure was built in either the 1870’s or the 1880’s, as a 3 -story frame hotel. That the structure was bricked over frame siding, removed porch, adding one story brick section to front and creating “L” shape, circa 1946. Though not an exhaustive list of reference materials, the HLPC can reasonably estimate the construction and historical transition of the building. • The proposed work will involve the demolition of existing structures, construction of a 420 vehicle parking garage, approximately 9,000 SF retail/restaurant space, a 32-room boutique hotel, 143 mixed residential units, including 14 affordable units, an open pedestrian plaza with public-oriented amenities, and an Americans with Disabilities (ADA)- compliant walking bridge to connect with the adjoining Kingston Plaza; • This work will cause a material change to the external appearance of the property; • The HLPC recognizes that the project’s substance has not changed since the HLPC issued a Preservation Notice of Action for The Kingstonian project and owners on March 3, 2022; and the subsequent 1-year extension issued by the HLPC under a Certificate of Appropriateness on December 5, 2024, both of which are appended and made part hereof to this Certificate of Appropriateness; • The HLPC has examined the project in accordance with the five (5) criteria listed under §405.26.L.10 (b) of the Form Based Code and finds as follows: 1. The effect of the proposed work in changing, destroying or affecting the exterior features of the landmark or Landmark (L) District upon which such work is to be done. • The HLPC continues its finding that the demonstrable change within the Stockade district associated with the project will not be detrimental to the district as a whole. The HLPC’s review of evidence regarding comparison scales, massing, materials, architectural features, provision for parking, and contemplated uses support the HLPC’s conclusion that the development will enhance the district. The HLPC agrees with the statement found in Brief 14, which states that “new construction should be “differentiated from the historic building(s).” Though this brief specifically applies to additions onto existing historic buildings, the Kingstonian Buildings are in essence architecturally consistent additions to the Stockade District as a whole.” 2. The relationship between the results of such work and the exterior architectural features of other neighboring improvements. • The HLPC continues its determination that the project adequately takes into consideration the immediate surrounding buildings, in addition to the various points of consideration under the first criterion as noted above. The HLPC further confirms that elements such as recessed doorways for entrances off North Front Street are appropriately incorporated in line with the existing streetscape, along with other architectural vernacular to complement the surrounding district.
