items.discussion:
Matha Dallis, owner, and her contractor Jay Elsoffer, were present.  M. Dallas restated that they wish to
retain the 6/6 double-hung windows they installed earlier this year. She recognized that they acted without the approval
of HLPC, or a Building Permit.  To justify the window  design and style, M. Dallis submitted photographs of other Dutch
stone houses across Kingston and Ulster County with dormers that had 6/6 and some 8/8 double hung windows.

Chair A. Puetz asked when the dormers on the Van Steenburg House were built and whether  the owners at the time
installed double hung or casement windows. M. Dallis stated they were likely built sometime around the 1930s, and that
they were casement style windows. M. Dallis also confirmed that the casement windows were present until this year when
the roof and gutters were replaced. A. Puetz noted that if the original installation was made it could be inferred that was
what the owners wanted and that look is what the HLPC is trying to protect.  She then asked why switch from casement
to double hung windows if they were not historically present in the dormers? J. Elsoffer stated that their opinion is the
casement windows don’t go with the historic stone section of the house but work better with the 1930s additions to the
building’s sides. He also added that the option was to restore the windows there, or replace them with double- hung
windows, which they felt in their opinion were more appropriate.

A. Puetz stated that what the HLPC is struggling with is that the person who designed and built the dormers for this house
back in the 1930s purposefully chose casement windows that were different from other Dutch stone houses. Staff also
pointed out that at the last meeting, the HLPC reviewed the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation, and
#4 states that “Changes to a property that have acquired historic significance in their own right will be retained and
preserved.” Staff also added that these changes exceed the National Register’s 50-year threshold generally required for
historic significance.

N. Morano asked the applicants to confirm the original windows were gone and not retrievable. J. Elsoffer confirmed they
were destroyed.

M. Dallas and J. Elsoffer stated that they submitted specifications for other windows which may be considered as
alternatives, even though they do not want to replace those installed.  A. Puetz asked the HLPC commissioners present
whether the proposed replacements for the 6/6 double-hung windows would sufficiently remedy the violation? She noted
that the proposed are clad casement windows and added that one proposal is for true two- panel outward opening
casements and the other is for a single panel outward open casement –  the latter has a simulated check rail.
Commissioner Morano asked if there is a photograph of the exact proposed replacement windows. M. Dallis said no, but
that they are at Williams Lumber for viewing. J. Elsoffer stated that they are energy efficient windows with wooden interiors
and clad exteriors. He also asked if the dormers were installed in the 1960s with vinyl windows, he wouldn’t want to put
back in vinyl windows. S. Cahill added that was not wh at is being discussed now. She pointed out that the front facing
windows are highly visible and critical to the building’s integrity. She pointed out that this commission had denied similar
windows before because they were deemed inappropriate.

The HLPC noted that the replacement windows should match the design, material, and operation of those that were there

before the violation took place. J. Elsoffer pointed out that they tried to do the best work possible according to historic
methods to retain as much of the original structure as possible. They attempted to do the best work possible. S. Cahill
stated that no one is disputing the care J. Elsoffer and the owner put into doing the roof and box gutters. The issue being
discussed are the windows which are an integral part of the building’s appearance. Given that the work has already been
done, the HLPC must find a suitable alternative that closely matches the former windows. S. Cahill and A P uetz agreed
that operation in this case was not as critical as design, material, and color given the rarity of inward swinging casements.
M. Dallis stated she’d lived there for 10 years and that the former windows were not inward swinging. The HLPC reviewed
an older photo, and it does appear to work with inward swing, but that is not a matter for debate, as outward would be
acceptable.

A. Puetz asked the Commission if they feel they have enough information to make a decision at this time, and whether
the proposal regarding the windows is appropriate. N. Morano asked A. Puetz’s professional opinion on the windows. A.
Puetz stated that she finds the windows that were present were a unique and active choice by previous owners, and that
they marked a specific period. Staff added that the crux of the matter is that when a structure is derelict and missing many
of its character defining features, a researcher may have greater flexibility for restoring based on what would have likely
been there. However, in this case they had material and visual evidence of what was there. In this case, we now have
replacement windows that differ in design, mater ial, and operation. A. Puetz also added that the operation is not as
important in this case.

Staff also asked if all proposed replacement casement windows are 8 by 8, but that the center gable window was 10 by
10 windows. The contractor also stated he wasn’t sure if the proposed replacement casements were vinyl, but the
commission and staff recognized that the specification sheet explicitly states clad windows. R. Tonner asked if they would
be willing to change the 6/6 double hung windows., and M. Dallis said they would prefer to keep the double hung windows
but if the HLPC forces them to replace the double hung they will do that. S. Cahill asked what the commission’s position
is on approving the double hung windows. All commissioners were opposed to approving the double hung windows.

S. Cahill stated that t he next question is whether the proposed Marvin casement windows are suitable for replacement
windows. N. Morano asked if there was an alternative. S. Cahill stated, yes – that a good first step would be working with
a wood window preservationist to determ ine a suitable replacement window. The HLPC could allow the applicant more
time – a few months - to think about and research alternatives that address the design and historical integrity concerns
raised by the double hung and the proposed casement windows. S. Cahill and the Commissioners note that this would
provide them with a good opportunity to expand upon the exceptional work they did for the roof and box gutter restoration
project. The HPA added that this is one of the city’s important structures, and that their good stewardship of the structure
is commendable. A. Puetz stated let’s complete the package. M. Dallis stated it can come of f the National Historic
Register, there is a case that when a house had something happen to it that was against its design, it can come off the
register, and that’s fine with us. She stated that it is a house.

A. Puetz stated that they went through the effort to find a replacement window, which the HLPC appreciates. If they would
go an extra step further to find an uncladded casement window that better matches what was there, we would appreciate
it. M. Dallis stated to give her 6 months, and she will see what she can do. J. Elsoffer stated that he could just remove the
cladding from the windows they proposed. A. Puetz discouraged this option because it would likely void the manufacturer’s
warranty, which could be a problem for the owner in the future. A case was made again for the double hung windows,
and A. Puetz restated HLPC’s position regarding the historic significance of the casements. Staff pointed out that the

Commission must also address the side window that was replaced, because it was also visible from the public right of
way. Staff said the HLPC  can separate this window from the others or address them all together. A. Puetz asked if the
side window is clad, and J. Elsoffer stated that it is a clad window from the same series. They also clarified that it was an
outward operating casement window. J. Elsoffer again noted that it is a viable possibility to remove the cladding, and M.
Dallis stated that she would be okay with him removing the cladding. The HLPC was not comfortable approving this
because of the likelihood of it voiding the warranty. A. Puetz stated that given the presence of cladding for the side window,
it should also be looked at the same way as the front three (3) windows.

A. Puetz asked again if they would be comfortable returning to the commission with fully wood windows in the future. M.
Dallis stated that she would investigate but she would need 6 months and that she is not sure what they would ultimately
do in the end. She also pointed out that she did what the commission asked, which was to provide some alternatives to
the double hung windows. She stated that she is unsure where to turn to for guidance, and the HPA added that there is
the Wood Window Preservation Alliance and several specialists in this area who could likely assist. Staff would provide
them with resources. M. Dallis stated she would still like 6 months –  that she is busy with her business and that her
husband is busy with his business. She asked for that courtesy from the commission. N. Morano asked what the process
now would look like. S. Cahill stated that the HLPC would essentially deny the application, and require they would come
back in 6 months, with a possible extension of 3 month s, at which time a  new application with a new fee would need to
be submitted. M. Dallis stated she wanted to avoid another application fee.

S. Cahill stated there might be one option to avoid this –  there is a mutual consent component of the code (Section
405.26.L 11.i), where “Within a reasonable time after a completed formal application is filed with the HLPC, but in any
event within 90 days  after such filing or within such further time as the applicant may, in writing, allow; the HLPC shall
conduct a public meeting to approve or deny the application or approve the application with modifications.” S. Cahill stated
to M. Dallis that she would need to provide the HLPC with a written request to table the matter so they can conduct
additional research, to which she agreed. The letter would need to be received by November 26 th, 2025. Initially, Staff
and the HLPC discussed a table with a default denial if a letter is not received. Commissioner K. McEvoy pointed out
these contingency clauses could be problematic and suggested the property owner should submit the letter now. To this
end, M. Dallis hand wrote a written letter during the meeting asking for a six (6) month extension, but no later than May
of 2026. The HLPC and Staff said that if you find something sooner, then we will gladly review and move the project
along. M. Dallis thanked the commission for this option.

Phyllis Brown, and her son, Corey Carpenter, met with the commission to discuss the history of, current
conditions, and plans for 44 Abeel Street. P. Brown stated she is trying her best to restore the building after a breach of
trust by her sibling that contributed to its condition. S. Cahill asked how long it has been since the building was occupied.
P. Brown stated it’s been a long time, and that t he sibling who was caring for it basically gutted the interior. She added
the building has a lot of sentimental value. S. Cahill asked if the HPA provided them with the rehab tax incentive programs,
and she said yes. P. Brown said this is only the 3rd year since she took over responsibility for the family’s assets. S. Cahill
said that she is aware of a recent inspection and wanted to know what the plans are for moving forward. P. Brown stated
that the BSD wants stamped plans from a structural engineer. S. Cahill said that it is probably a good start for the project.
The HPA asked A. Puetz if some soft expenses like engineering work are covered by the rehab tax credit programs.

The HPA also added that it would be good for the owner to connect with a Historic Preservationist who can clarify what
might be available to them for funding and help to identify the sequence of actionable tasks for rehabilitating the structure.
The owners and the HLPC discussed that the building has a newer roof that is watertight, but a different design than the
old roof. P. Brown noted that she is being fined for the current conditions and would like to reroof the bay window section
of the former porch. She noted that she wants to rebuild the front porch but that it will be costly. She added that the house
used to be beautiful back when her parents first purchased it years ago. Her father died when she was young, and her
mother kept this property even though they moved to another part of the city. Later, this property was under the care of
one of her siblings. This sibling did things to this building without consulting the family.

 S. Cahill asked if the property owner would now consult with a structural engineer, and they said yes. S. Cahill also
pointed out that engaging a historic preservationist would be a good idea. There are some good preservation architects
in the area who could be helpful to them. The HPA added that t he preservationist component would be critical to help
develop a robust and concise plan. The HPA will connect them with the Preservation League of NYS who might be able
to recommend some specialists. The HPA asked what the building will be used for, and she said for commercial or income
producing uses. P. Brown stated that the building will likely be returned to a two-family building, and that she might even
move back in. The HPA also shared with them information about the City of Kingston’s 10-year graduated tax abatement
program.

Commissioner McEvoy added that he did some cursory research on the building in historic maps, and he thinks it might
be the former house of Major Von Beck, the former paymaster for the D&H Canal. K. McEvoy stated that Von Beck was
a notable and interesting figure in the Rondout in the mid- 19th century. A. Puetz and S. Cahill stated that the point of
tonight’s meeting was to begin discussions on the building, and that it might be good to set a 6- month timeline for
developing a rehabilitation plan. All agreed that if plans develop sooner, we can also move that ahead. S. Cahill added
that the HLPC is only concerned with the exterior, so moving ahead with the interior would be primarily with the Building
& Safety Division. Finally, the HLPC agreed that it would be okay to allow a temporary EPDM or rubber roof on the bay
windows at the buildings front. However, staff noted that if the porch is going to be rebuilt that might mean the bay
window’s newer rubber roof might have to be removed or redone in the future. A. Puetz said that EPDM is the best option
for this because it is easily undoable. Allowing this to move forward would possibly allow the BSD to take away at least
one violation. Staff said this will be addressed in a desk review tomorrow.

decisions.text: The HLPC voted unanimously to render the recommendations Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (25) and determined that no further review is required. . The HLPC will share information on resources that may assist the property owner with rehabilitating the structure and request that a more comprehensive rehabilitation plan be developed in the next 6 months and presented to back to the HLPC for further review; no later than May 6, 2026. (Motion – AP; 2nd – NM; RT, EW, KM – yes) 5. #161 Fair St (Former First Church of Christ Science): Demolition of Fire Damaged Building and Single- Family Construction. SBL: 56.91-4-19. SEQR Type Unlisted. Transect Zones: T4N, FSHD, HA. Ward 5. Applicants, Andrew & Sonia Wright; Owners, Aaron & April Goldman. https://cityofkingstonny.municollab.com/hlpc/projects/161-fair-goldman- residence/dashboard DEMO DISCUSSION: Sonia & Andrew Wright, of Wright Architects, were present to discuss the plan to demolish the severely fire -damaged former Church of Christ Scientists building at 161 Fair Street. The Wrights explained that the property was registered under the First Church of Christ Science who then sold it in 2019 to the Christian Science Society, Kingston, New York. In 2021; it again changed owners twice in the same year to Paula Jo Allen and Fair 161 LLC. Subsequently in 2023, April and Aaron Goldman purchased the property. By early June 2025 the interior renovations were few weeks away from being completed. The client, contractor and design team met on site on the morning of June 13, 2025; colors for the walls and finishes were discussed. Unfortunately, during the early morning hours of Saturday, June 14th, a fire ravaged the premises, and the renovation work was lost along with the stability of the structure. After several months of inves tigations, the fire was deemed undeterminable and the structure deemed a total loss, so the insurance company released the site to start the process of demolition to make space for a new structure. A. Wright stated that their firm did an extensive study of the building to determine if it could be reconstructed, but it was too much of a loss. He also stated that he believes the fire was caused by an earlier electrical system in the building that was not property turned off and which resulted in a basement fire that traveled up the southern red- brick chimney and into the roof structure. Photographs of the building pre and post fire were shown the commission. Commissioners asked if any architectural elements can be salvaged, such as window, pediments, columns, doors, and trim. The Wrights were unsure and stated they could not find anyone interested in the two large columns. A Wright did state that the Douglas fir flooring inside is old growth and in good condition still and they may try to salvage those materials. DEMO DECISION: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (25) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact. Commissioner Puetz motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed demolition of a fire damaged building at 161 Fair Street (Former Church of Christ Scientists), in the Fair Street Local Landmark District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the landmark district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at two story, Greek Revival, religious structure - turned - dwelling, on the west side of Fair Street, four parcel's south of the intersection of Fair & St. James Sts, that was built by George W. Anderson circa 1914 for t he First Church of Christ Scientists - the church and Anderson chose the Greek Revival style to purposefully differentiate from Victorian churches that favored Gothic styles, which were deemed to "gloomy" and shrouded in mystery and superstition" (Rhodes & Bleeker, 2003: 72-73); • the owners purchased the property in 2023 and were renovating the interior between 2024 and 2025, when on June 14, 2025 a fire engulfed the building and resulted in a total loss; • that the HLPC reviewed the photographic evidence of the fire, and recognizes that the structure is beyond repair and that demolition is deemed the only feasible option; • the HLPC requests that the applicants/owners create a photographic record of the structure before and after the fire that must be delivered to the HLPC by December 20th, 2025 for record keeping; • the HLPC requests that any historical character defining features not damaged by the fire, such as windows, trim, columns, doors, etc., be salvaged and possibly incorporated into the new structure, or if this is not possible, be saved or transferred to an architectural salvage company for future reuse; • any new construction on the site must be compatible with the historic district setbacks, architectural theme, and the character of the Fair Street Landmark District (1988); • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 6th day of November, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – AP; 2nd – NM; RT, KM, EW – yes) NEW CONSTRUCTION DISCUSSION: The Wrights presented a proposal for a new single- family residence to be built using the foundation of the former church building, which they believe will appropriately fit the historic context of the Fair Street Local Historic District (1988). The new single-family dwelling will be 1,981 square feet with: • Habitable basement space with laundry/mechanical room and full bathroom. • First floor with front porch and rear deck along with library, reading nook, open stairs, access to basement, full bathroom, closet, dining/living area with wood burning fireplace and a large kitchen with breakfast nook. • Second floor with two bedrooms with closets, large, shared bathroom, family room and master suite with private bathroom and walk in closet. S. Wright stated that the proposed house incorporates a Classical style in mind to honor the previous structure, and added the following: • The porch’s scale and proportion are in tune with the structures from the surrounding areas. The Commission and Staff examined the streetscape via Google Maps and concurred with this statement. • The tall 9ft ceiling on the first floor and 8ft ceiling on the second floor are designed to allow proportionate windows to emulate the style of the neighboring houses. • The initial assessment of the basement walls indicates that the foundation could be used to house the new structure. • A side door and access from the outside will be added to make the basement a habitable space. • The first floor is six inches above the existing building to accommodate the new floor structure. • The gable ends have a flare detail transitioning from the shake to horizontal siding as to emulate a detail from the original structure. A. Puetz recognized that there are no formal plans or elevation drawings at this time – only renderings. A. Puetz asked whether the HLPC should table the project until the next month for the applicants to provide additional information. S. Cahill asked if the Wrights are working on a site plan. S. Wright stated they had conducted a new survey. She also stated that the exisiting structure will be largely on the same foundation. There will be no curb cut and no driveway. They will rework the walkway to the front house out of bluestone and incorporate a side walkway on the south side of the building, that will lead to a means of egress from the basement apartment. Staff asked the Wrights if there was a way to incorporate some of the features from the old church, like the Greek Revival elements that would thematically communicate the previous structure’s legacy. Staff did not see a Gothic design, but more of a late Victorian. S. Wright stated that the new structure is supposed to read completely different from what was there, which was always they and their client’s intention. Staff and the Commission reviewed the Google Streetview to determine the architectural character of Fair Street and the appropriateness of the proposed design for the district. The Wrights stated that the façade will be clad in real wood, with portions stained and other portions painted in a blue from the historic color collection. The HLPC overall felt that the proposed design was sufficiently differentiated from the historic church building but appropriately incorporated some past design elements that make it architecturally compatible with the unique and varied styles present in the FSHD. NEW CONSTRUCTION DECISION: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (25) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact. Commissioner Puetz motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed new dwelling construction project at 161 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Landmark District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the landmark district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place on the west side of Fair Street, four parcel's south of the intersection of Fair & St. James Sts, where circa 1914 George W. Anderson built the First Church of Christ Scientists - the church and Anderson chose the Greek R evival style to purposefully differentiate from Victorian churches that favored Gothic styles, which were deemed to "gloomy" and shrouded in mystery and superstition" (Rhodes & Bleeker, 2003: 72- 73), which was severely damaged by fire on June 14, 2025, dec lared a total loss, and approved for demolition by the HLPC at its November 6th, 2025 meeting; • the owner proposes a Classical Victorian style 2.5 story, single family dwelling, with a street facing gable as submitted in their application dated October 21, 2025; • the proposed structure shall be clad in both real wooden clapboard siding and wooden shake siding, and that the body will be stained in Mahogany ES -60 color (see submitted rendering) and the 3rd story body, Trim, Railings, Handrails, Stair risers & Lattice, Front Porch, Rear Deck & Front Door will be painted in Benjamin Moore Newburyport Blue HC-155 from the historic color collection; • the structure must have 6/1 double hung clad wood windows on the front elevation painted in bronze on the exterior and may have Marvin Elevate wood casement windows (as rendered) with white interiors and bronze exterior color on the sides and rear; • the roof may be clad in CertainTeed Landmark asphalt shingles in Cobblestone Gray; • the applicant may install aluminum gutters in bronze color with matching downspouts, and that the owner will be held responsible to ensure that all storm water is directed and handled on site, with no drainage directed to a public space or system; • applicants may install Arturelights Amsterdam, Vintage White Milk Glass Geometric Jar Pendant Light (Dimensions: Diameter 9.06” Height 10.63”) and a HINKLEY 44” Chisel Matte Black Damp Rated Smart Fan for the front porch. • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 6 November 2025, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. items.discussion:
3. #207 Delaware Ave (J. N. Cordts House Company Building) : Review potential for Local, State, and National Listing
Eligibility. SBL: 56.28-2-8. SEQR Type II. Transect Zone: T4N-O, HA, CZ. Ward: 8. Owner: City of Kingston-NY.

The HPA informed the commission that 207 Delaware Avenue (J. N. Cordts Hose Company Building) is
a city owned property that is scheduled for auction in January 2026. The property was identified as individual eligible for
listing on the State and National Historic Registers during the Intensive Level Survey of Ponckhockie by AHRS in 2023.
After learning about the sale and hearing from Ponckhockie residents concerned about the building’s protection, the HPA
and Commission McEvoy (absent), researched the building to provide the HLPC with some historic and cultural resource
information. The HPA read the following summary:

The J. N. Cordts Hose Company building, at 207 Delaware Avenue, is a former fire house currently owned
by the City of Kingston, in Ulster County, New York. The building falls into the category of modest Italianate
municipal buildings and is the one (1) of about eight (8) of early fire houses within the City of Kingston and is
distinct from other buildings and structures on the same block of Delaware Avenue. Members of the locally
and regionally prominent Cordts family built the fire house for the Ponckhockie neighborhood in 1894, a role
that it served until retirement in 2024. This historic and cultural resource evaluation examines the building,
company, and key individual’s history and proposes that the building meets three (3) of the four (4) criteria of
the Kingston Landmarks Code for Local Designation, and potentially individual listing on the New York State
and National Historic Registers for at least two (2) of the four (4) criteria.

Staff stated that pursuant to the Form Based Code Section 405.26. L . 7 (Landmark or Landmark District designation
procedure), “The HLPC shall consider for a Landmark or Landmark District designation real property proposed by motion
of any HLPC member or by owner of such property or by written request signed by 10 residents of the City of Kingston.”
If a member of the HLPC motions to hold a public hearing, it would be scheduled for the February 5, 2026, meeting. In

addition, FBC 405.26.L.7.K, further states that “…Once the HLPC has issued notice of a proposed designation, no building
permits or demolition permits shall be issued by the building safety officer until the HLPC has made its decision.”

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; EW, AP, NM - yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact. Commissioner that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed side door infill and porch railing extension project at 31 Stuyvesant Street in the Chestnut Street Local (2002), State, and National Historic District, if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingst on's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the local district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at 2.5 story modest Victorian building as the northeast corner of the Livingston and Stuyvesant Street intersection that was likely built circa 1890, and was at one time owned by William Roach, the owner of a "leather findings business in Rondout" (NYS BSIF, 1982); • the applicant is rehabilitating the building, which involves alterations of the interior layout and closure of a Livingston St-facing exterior door; • the HLPC recognizes that the existing door itself as non-historic, and that the proposed alteration is an action that is generally understood as reversible; • the HLPC considered three (3) proposed options as follows: 1) completely remove the side door and cover it with matching siding; 2) remove the non-historic door and replace it with a more historically appropriate wooden dummy door/non-functioning; 3) Leave the door frame in place and infill the portal with siding to retain a ghost door; • the HLPC finds that wholesale removal and infill would remove the historic portal and create a false narrative for the building's elevation along Livingston St; • the HLPC finds that option 1, completely remove the side door and cover it with matching siding, along with extending the porch railing of same material and design, closing off steps, and removing side stairs to grade is a compatible alteration that is appropriate for this feature and in this specific context; • the applicant shall replicate the existing porch railings to fill-in the former Livingston St-facing steps; • the HLPC reviewed the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Rehabilitation of Historic Properties and finds that the proposed work is substantially in conformance with the Standards; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 8th day of January 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; EW, AP, NM - yes).

items.title: Establishing in 2026, May as Historic Preservation Month in Kingston:
items.discussion:
The HPA proposed to the commission that now  may be an appropriate time for the HLPC and City to
establish the month of May as Preservation Month and to hold additional programs to foster wider support for
preservation. According to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, “Preservation Month began as National
Preservation Week in 1973. In 2005, the National Trust extended the celebration to the entire month of May and declared
it Preservation Month to provide an even greater opportunity to celebrate the diverse and unique heritage of our country’s
cities and states” ( https://savingplaces.org/stories/history-of-preservation-month). In addition, 2026 is the Semi -
Quincentennial (America250) of the Nation’s Founding and the 60th anniversary of the HLPC’s establishment. We should
capitalize on these significant anniversaries. Furthermore, outreach and educational programs are more successful (and
cost effective) in achieving positive preservation projects.

Staff shared with the Commission a draft resolution to the Common Council requesting the month of May be recognized
and designated Historic Preservation month, henceforth. The communication also stipulates that the HLPC may  issue
preservation award( s) and hold preservation related program activities  during the month. Programs could be held in
partnership with FHK (if they are amenable) and could feature some of the following:
• Historic Rehab Tax Credit Info Sessions
• Historic Rehab Specialist Talk
• Preservation Trade Workshop (e.g., wood window restoration, masonry, plaster work, etc.)
• History Talk

Any event would include sign-in sheets for the programs, thereby allowing us to collect an emailing list of interested
persons for future communications. The HPA provided the HLPC with a draft resolution for consideration and feedback.

decisions.vote: Motion – EW; 2nd – MG; AP, NM, RT – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the Action Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (25), and to approved submitting the resolution under a cover letter as a communication to the Common Council for designating the month of May as Historic Preservation Month. (Motion – EW; 2nd – MG; AP, NM, RT – yes).

items.title: Establish Committee of Three (3) to Develop a Historic Preservation Award Program:
items.discussion:
The HPA shared with the commission that it would be appropriate for the HLPC to establish a Historic
Preservation Award Program to recognize various parties that individually or collectively demonstrate stewardship of
historic value. Awards are important public relations tools that foster greater interest and support from community
members. Each community and organization have  different approaches to Preservation Awards, and it is important to
identify a framework for a Kingston specific award program. The HPA asked if three commissioners would consider joining
a working group to develop a draft framework for presentation at the February  2026 HLPC meeting. Commissioners R.
Tonner and N. Morano agreed to work on the project, Alderwoman M. Marvelli (W3) also agreed to participate. Staff will
work to coordinate a virtual meeting with the committee members in the next week or so to begin drafting a program. In
the meantime, staff provided the commissioners with the following resources and project questions for consideration:

Below are some Examples to Study:
• Cambridge Mass: https://www.cambridgema.gov/historic/aboutchc/preservationawards
• Mahwah, NJ: https://www.mahwahtwp.org/413/Historic-Preservation-Awards
• North Hampton, Mass: https://northamptonma.gov/1883/2010-Present
• Oak Park, Illinois: https://www.oak-park.us/Government/Citizen-Boards-and-Commissions/Historic-
Preservation/Historic-Preservation-Awards
• Others likely exist worth studying.

A few questions/thoughts to consider:
• What are appropriate award categories? Rehabilitation, Adaptive Reuse, Reconstruction, Restoration,
Compatible New Construction, Archaeology, Education?
• What are the criteria for evaluation?
• Would the awards be based on projects completed within the previous 1-2 calendar years?

• Who would nominate the awards –  HLPC or public through a MuniCollab recommendation portal? What is the
nomination period?
• Would the award be for the person doing the work or tied to the building?
• What would the award be? A recognition page on the website? A recognition in the mayor’s newsletter?
• In relation to the point above: Would the awards be given out in May (Preservation Month) of every year?

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; NM, RT, EW – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to establish a committee to create an historic preservation award program. (Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; NM, RT, EW – yes). items.title: Adoption of HLPC Meeting Minutes of Thursday, January 8, 2026:
#207 Delaware Ave (J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House) : Review potential for Local, State, and National Listing Eligibility
items.discussion:
Chairman Grunblatt called the hearing, noting that the purpose of the public hearing was to solicit
comments from the public on moving forward with the landmark designation of 207 Delaware Avenue (J. N. Cordts
Company Engine No. 8 House). Staff provided general background on the process that transpired to reach this point

and provided an overview of the notifications/public outreach undertaken. The City was hand-delivered notice of the public
hearing, and notice was also posted in the Daily Freeman on January 22nd, 2026, as the official  newspaper, two weeks
in advance of the meeting. No one spoke for the public hearing, and Chairman Grunblatt acknowledged a written comment
received from the Friends of Historic Kingston supporting the proposed landmark.
Mark Berthiaume, President of the Volunteer Fireman’s  Museum in Kingston, spoke to the HLPC about the historic and
cultural significance of the J. N. C ordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 D elaware Ave (SBL: 56.28 -8-8). M.
Berthiaume was a contributor, along with Commissioner McEvoy, and Alderwoman Marvelli, to the research on the Cordts
Hose building that was part of this landmark process. M Berthiaume stated that the Fireman’s Museum, located at 265
Fair Street, is the former Wiltwyck Hose building, and that the museum works to preserve, interpret, and share the written
and material firefighting history of Kingston, NY. M. Berthiaume shared that that Cordts Company was the last volunteer
company to form (1894) and the last to close. Most firehouses back in the day were very community based; therefore,
many people have memories associated with the physical firehouses. The Volunteer Fireman’s Museum maintains all the
records for the Cordts Hose Company, and some of the Museum’s current Board are relatives of those who were once
members of this fire house. He noted it was important to Ponckhockie and the City and was established primarily because
of John N. Cordts backing, even though Union Hose already existed less than a mile away in Ponckhockie. Chairman
Grunblatt acknowledged that in his hometown two of the more important social centers were laundromats and fire houses.
J. N. Cordts Company was the first motorized volunteer company. M. Berthiaume added that the architecture is consistent
with many other historic firehouses and is important to preserving the company’s history. He also noted that the original
bell remains in the tower. S. Cahill added that it should be included in the resolution that the bell be kept in the building
and the Council should make it a condition of any sale. The HPA also noted that we should include in the landmark
research that the building still has the original bell. The bell should be covered under the landmarks code because of its
visibility. Chairman Grunblatt proposed a deed restrictive covenant on the bell. Commissioner McEvoy noted a section of
the supporting document where the statement should be included about the bell and its significance.  Alderwoman Marvelli
stated that she is very excited about this landmark designation and looks forward to being a voice of support at the
Common Council.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; NM – 2nd; KM, RT, EW – yes
decisions.text: Chairman Grunblatt asked for the HLPC to close the hearing (Motion – MG; NM – 2nd; KM, RT, EW – yes). The Commission moved to declare the matter of the recommendation a TYPE II under SEQR, under NYCRR Part 617.5 (c) (38). Chairman Grunblatt read the following draft resolution as a motion: RESOLUTION OF THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION COMMISSION (HLPC) OF THE CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, RECOMMENDING THE COMMON COUNCIL DESIGNATE THE J. N. CORDTS COMPANY ENGINE NO. 8 HOUSE AT 207 DELAWARE AVENUE (SBL: 56.28-8-8): A LOCAL LANDMARK WHEREAS, in 2021, a NYS Office of Parks Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) Certified Local Government Grant funded an Intensive- Level Historic Resources and Building Survey of the Wilbur and Ponckhockie Neighborhoods conducted by Archaeology and Historic Resource Services, LLC. (AHRS): and WHEREAS, the report completed by AHRS in 2023 identified the J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 Delaware Avenue (SBL: 56.28- 8-8) as individually eligible for listing on the State and National Registers of Historic Places, and may also be a contributing resource to a future historic district in Ponckhockie; and WHEREAS, the HLPC received public comment from at least one Ponckhockie resident believing the J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 Delaware Avenue (SBL: 56.28- 8-8) is an eligible local landmark and asking the HLPC consider its designation; and WHEREAS, at the January 8, 2026 meeting, the HLPC, in accordance with Section 405.26.L.7, discussed the appropriateness of 207 Delaware Avenue being nominated for local landmark designation under the criteria established for local landmarking, and upon motion by Chairman Grunblatt, voted unanimously to hold a public landmark hearing at its February 5, 2026, meeting; and WHEREAS, according to Section 405.26. L notification of the proposed Public Hearing was posted in the Daily Freeman on January 22, 2026, and notice provided to the City Clerk as municipal owner; and WHEREAS, the HLPC held a Public Hearing, on February 5, 2026, at City Hall, and the HLPC recognized written comment from FOHK, and heard no opposition to recommending that the Common Council designate the J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 Delaware Avenue (SBL: 56.28-8-8), a local landmark; and WHEREAS, the HLPC finds that the proposed action is considered a Type II Action under 6 NYCRR, Part 617.5 (c) (38) and is predetermined not to have a significant impact on the environment and is precluded from environmental review under Environmental Conservation Law, Article 8. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE HISTORIC LANDMARKS PRESERVATION COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF KINGSTON, NEW YORK, AS FOLLOWS: SECTION 1: Recommends that the City of Kingston’s Common Council designate the J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 Delaware Avenue (SBL: 56.28-8-8), a local landmark. SECTION 2: That the historic bell remain in place and not be removed, protected by a deed restrictive covenant and/or landmark protection. SECTION 3: The attached report shall serve as the official landmark report for the building. SECTION 4: The City shall install a brass landmark plaque, at ground- level, on the building’s street-facing façade, once formal designation is completed. SECTION 5: Per Section 405.26.L.7.f. of the City’s Form Based Zoning Code, the J. N. Cordts Company Engine No. 8 House at 207 Delaware Avenue (SBL: 56.28-8-8) shall have interim protection under the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission. SECTION 6: This resolution shall take effect immediately and remain in full effect upon adoption by the Common Council. Chairman Grunblatt motioned to approve the foregoing resolution as read, Commissioner McEvoy seconded the motion; Commissioners Morano, Tonner, and Winchell also voted to approve, and the motion was carried unanimously. Staff will refer to the resolution in a communication to the full Common Council.

in May, during Historic Preservation Month. The full commission was pleased with the framework and proposed February
25, 2026, deadline for applications. Alderwoman Marvelli added that the separate Historic Preservation Month resolution
will be before the General Government Committee of the Common Council on February 25, 2026, and then go to the full
Common Council in March.

items.title: #323 Wall St: Modifying and raising the existing theater roof, installing a new metal loading door, and In- filling a rear portal with matching brick
items.owner: Wall Street Owners, LLC (William Gottlieb Real Estate)
items.discussion:
Andrew Lyon (an Architect and Principal with Lyon Studios) presented plans for an exterior rehabilitation
project with modifications to the existing rear, north, and south elevations of 323 Wall Street . Present also were the
owner’s Attorney Victoria Polidoro, the owner’s assistant, Corbin Plays, and Architect Paul Jankovitz. The building fronts
Wall Street, and the old theater portion of the building extends to Crown Street. A. Lyon pointed out the property shares
parking with 311 Wall Street, though these are recognized as separate lots with shared  licensing agreements already in
place. A. Lyon and V. Polidoro noted that updated documents would be developed with the new access and loading
doorway installed.  He also noted there is no change to the existing site plan. A. Lyons recognized the desk review issued
on February 19, 2026, for the following components of the project:
• adding new HVAC louvered vents to the building's rear tower as rendered, which shall not be visible from the public
right of way;
• retaining the existing tower roof access ladder and the existing security gate along Crown St, both as rendered on
the submitted plans;
• restoration, in-kind, of an existing Crown Street facing window with no visible changes to the design, operation, or
materials (see attached plans);
• the existing ramp and railing in the building's rear for access to the parking lot shall remain untouched;
• in-kind repairs to the existing Wall St-facing gable cornice with no design or material changes visible from the public
right of way;
• all existing murals and historic painted signage shall remain untouched;
• installation of a minimally visible new elevator shaft and bulkhead, clad with a metal panel system as rendered in the
submitted plans dated 1/22/26;

A. Lyon explained that the owner seeks to rehabilitate the former theater into a modern world class event, music, and
theater which requires the removal, modifying, and elevating the exisiting roof to accommodate contemporary artists,
equipment, and meet modern energy and sound standards. T he HLPC is reviewing the following components of the
rehabilitation project that are only visible from the public right of way along Crown Street:
• Roof Alternation: A. Lyon explained that the existing truss -based roof structure will be  removed to accommodate
most modern world-class artists and equipment. A. Lyon and their structural engineer are proposing to install new
internal walls to support a flat roof that will be approximately 9’ – 3 ¾’ taller than the existing roof at the building’s
parapet, but which is approximately 6 inches above the highest point of the current roof. The proposed roof change
will only be visible along Crown Street. The applicant proposes t hat the newly visible walls supporting the flat roof
be clad in vertically oriented metal panels that are painted in Atacama Bronze Metallic which was deemed compatible
with historic masonry.
o A. Lyon stated that their structural engineer issued a late revision that brings the extended roof’s walls to the
existing historic parapet brick wall.  This revision is proposed to ensure the historic masonry is adequately
supported by new structural members. The new walls will be acoustically rated to ensure that performances
will not adversely impact neighbors. S. Cahill asked if this change would have any impact on maintenance.
A. Lyon replied that there will still be access to the flat roof by a ladder  near the elevator bulkhead, which
was approved at desk level . Due to the expansion, approximately 2.5 feet of the new roof will extend
southward past the tower and set within the existing masonry wall.  The Commissioners had no other
questions.
• LIGHTING: A. Lyon proposed installing 11 wall-mounted Envision LED ARCY-Line 4” and 6” Architectural Cylinder
Downward-pointing lights to illuminate the existing O+ Murals on the rear, NW, and SE elevations: 4 fixtures along
the Crown Street face , 3 along the SE side, and 4 along t he NW side. He added that they are the most minimal

option available and all units will be mounted near the roof line to not be highly visible during the daytime. The units
will be painted in a bronze color, matching metal roof panels, and load doors to  blend them with the color of the
background masonry. There will be internal conduit feed. A. Lyons stated the lights will be 20 wattage, 2100 lumens,
and warm color. S. Cahill asked if there were plans to change the murals in the future and cited the customary 3-
year agreements. Attorney Polidoro added there are no plans to change them at this time.
• In-Filling Portal: M. Grunblatt noted the rear window notation and A. Lyon stated that it was part of the desk review
but explained that number two (2) on page A-201.00 identifies a small location on the rear where an existing portal
shall be filled in with new matching brick and mortar. S. Cahill asked if any of the bricks salvaged from the loading
door’s demolition and construction could be used for this component of the project. A. Lyon agreed and said they
would love to use th e salvaged material, and wi ll conduct testing to ensure the use of  historically
sensitive/proportioned mortar, consistent with the NPS Preservation Brief #2 was also noted:
https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1739/upload/preservation-brief-02-repointing.pdf
• Loading Door: A. Lyon showed elevation drawings with the proposed (22 ft tall by 40 ft wide) metal loading door on
the building’s southeast elevation. The proposed door is to allow greater access to the indoor theater facility for
arrival and departure of artists and their necessary equipment  and is acoustically rated for the theater facility. The
door will also be painted in Atacama Bronze Metallic. S. Cahill asked what the plan is for the historic brick removed.
Will it be saved, and if so, will it be saved on site? S. Cahill said that it would be nice for the material to be retained
should someone in the future remove the loading door portal  and want to restore the brick wall . A. Lyon was
amenable to retaining the material on-site but would need to consult with the owners. Attorney Polidoro asked if the
HLPC could only request a limited retention of historic masonry so that the owners have flexibility if portions of the
demolished wall are not reusable. S. Cahill said that it is reasonable but added that the work should be undertaken
with the intention of saving as much material as feasible and ke pt on-site. Corbin Plays, a representative of the
owner, said that the owners and their team have done this before.

• ARCHAEOLOGY: Commissioner McEvoy questioned the excavation that is noted for the footings  of the new support
wall for the roof.  A. Lyon stated that interior-only excavations will need to be done for the new structural walls. He added
that the excavation will include geophysical test pits and underpinning for the historic walls. He stated that there is an
existing cellar and subcellar, and at this point they do not know how deep the existing walls/footings go down. He will be
working with the structural engineer on the investigation.  Commissioner Grunblatt stated that we may finally learn if t he
local lore is true: That the former furniture store  covered the old theater seats with concrete. Attorney Polidoro asked if
that was possible. C. Plays stated that it isn’t likely but that the existing basement floor is slanted downward to the former
stage. He added that the concrete was crudely poured and at one end is about 2ft deep. S. Cahill asked if there was any
archaeological mitigation or monitoring considered due to the potential to intersect undisturbed soil in the Stockade
District. A. Lyon stated that test pits will only go as deep as the existing masonry walls, but that the underpinning and new
structural wall footings may intersect undisturbed soil. Because of the Stockade District’s local, state, and national
significance and the presence of known archaeological sites, features, and materials in proximity . Commissioners
Grunblatt and Winchell added that there were some older, potentially colonial era buildings in the parking lot that were
already demolished. A. Lyon directed the Commission to the Sanborn Fire Insurance maps which showed other structures
in the parking lot. Attorney Polidoro asked for a bit more guidance. S. Cahill added that the concern is not with the initial
test pits, but more with excavation in previously undisturbed soils. A. Lyon added that he and the client’s team want to do
the best thing for the site, project, and district.   It was recognized that the initial testing would no go beyond the existing
area that already been disturbed, but when they excavate for the new underpinnings and do work in previously
undisturbed soil, they would involve an archeological consultant.

Chairman Grunblatt shifted discussion to the Environmental Discussion to address concerns and issues and stated that
this project falls into the category of an Unlisted Action. The Chairman read through the EAF Part 2 impact questions with
the Commissioners . The only question  that fell into the category of moderate to large impact was archaeological
sensitivity, which led the HLPC to draft the EAF Part 3 explanation:

The HLPC finds that the proposed roof alterations, installation of a loading door on the SE elevation, the in-fill of an
existing portal, and installation of downward pointing wall sconces to illuminate existing murals will have no major
effect on the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1975; 2016) for the following
reason:
- ROOF: The alteration will be predominantly interior and that the exposed walls will be set back from the historic
structure and painted to minimize their impact on the building and street scape.
- LOADING DOOR: that the original fabric removed for the loading door's construction shall be retained should the
need to refill the portal ever arise. That the loading door shall be painted in a compatible color as the historic facade
thereby mitigating visibility. No historic signage or features other than the wall materials will be displaced.
- Wall SCONCE LIGHTING: The wall lights are minor in size, painted in a compatible color to the brick facade, and
elevated such that their visibility is minimal from the public right of way during daytime. Nighttime luminosity,
wattage, and light color is also capped to mitigate excessive light pollution, and will be in conformance with the city
code
- ARCHAEOLOGY: The project includes excavation of earth in the basement for footings of the new roof structure.
Because of the local, state, and national historical and cultural significance of the Stockade District, a Secretary of
the Interior 36 CRF 61 Certified Archaeologist with expertise an both native and historical archaeologist shall be
retained to monitor the project and/or ensure measures are taken to mitigate project impacts to cultural materials
and/or features, during excavation which involved digging undisturbed earth.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; EW, KM, NM – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Unlisted under SEQR and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. The Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed wall -lighting, brick in-fill, loading door, and roof alterations at 323 Wall Street (the former Keeney's Theater) in the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1975; 2016), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • the proposed work is to take place at the 2- story brick commercial building with a rear theater addition extending westward to Crown St, located on the west side of Wall Street six (6) parcels south of the intersection of N. Front & Wall Streets, that "...has been substantially altered, to the point where it is impossible to determine a construction date, but [that] documentary evidence suggests that it may date from the 3rd-quarter of the 19th-century. From 1871 through at least 1875, J. Townsend operated a millinery goods store at 13 Wall St, the original number of this parcel - followed in the 1880s by George Merritt and Company, dry goods, fancy goods, gents furnishing goods, etc. - Since 1921, uses for 323 Wall St have included McBride drug stores; part of Newberry's; V. Carpouzis confectionery; Union Fern Furniture; and Standard Furniture, present use. (SHPO BSIF, 1987)", and the building also operated as Keeney's Theater for a time; • LIGHTING: the applicant/owner shall install 11 wall-mounted Envision LED ARCY-Line 4" & 6" Architectural Cylinder Up and/or Down Lights to illuminate the existing O+ Murals as detailed in the elevation drawings to be submitted. The fixtures shall be powered by (internal / external) conduit painted to match the facade. The light fixtures shall be bronze color, shall be 20 watts, 2100 lumens, downward pointing only, and the light color shall be 2700 Kelvins. • IN-FILLING PORTAL: An existing portal (# two (2) on page A-201.00) on the Crown St elevation shall be filled in with new color matching brick and mortar, reusing brick from the demolition area. The work shall use historically sensitive/proportioned mortar, consistent with t he NPS Pres. Brief #2: https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1739/upload/preservation-brief-02-repointing.pdf • ROOF ALTERATION: They applicant shall remove the existing truss -based roof structure due to internal height limitations that would prohibit the theater's ability to perform with modern artists and equipment and shall construct internal load bearing walls to extend the roof height vertically, approximately 6 inches above the highest point of the current roof elevation. A new elevated flat roof and its supporting walls shall be clad in metal vertically oriented panels that are painted in ATACAMA BRONZE METALIC; • LOADING DOOR: the applicant/owner shall remove a portion of the southeast facing wall to install a 22ft tall by 40ft wide metal loading door to allow greater access into the theater facility - the door shall be constructed of vertically oriented metal panels, and it shall be acoustically rated. The door shall be painted in ATACAMA BRONZE METALIC to blend with the surrounding masonry. That an easement shall be secured with the adjacent property/parking lot to ensure legal right of access/egress to and from the loading door; • ARCHAEOLOGY: Based on the proposed plan and elevation drawings, the proposed new roof supporting walls require excavation in the basement for new footings. Due to the Stockade District's local, state, and national significance and the presence of known archaeological sites, features, and materials in the surrounding area, a professional 36 CFR 61 archaeologist shall be engaged to monitor and ensure the protection of any unearthed resources. Should cultural materials be unearthed, the applicant/owner shall i mmediately notify the HLPC, or representative, for additional review. • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 5th day of March 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; EW, KM, NM – yes)

items.title: #31 Stuyvesant St: Unauthorized porch demo & reconstruction
items.discussion:
P. O’Kennedy discussed the unauthorized removal of the entire historic porch, which was beyond the
scope of work of previous restoration-focused desk and Commission reviews. After the BSD issued Stop Work Order, P.
O’Kennedy explained to the HPA and Planning Director that both he and his crew realized the existing porch’s structural
damage was beyond repair and that demolition and in-kind reconstruction was the only option. He apologized for working
beyond the scope of what was authorized and stressed his commitment to salvaging whatever materials he could from
the original porch debris.  P. O’Kennedy shared images with the HLPC of the degraded porch materials, and of the
salvaged porch features that will be reused and images of r eplicated features that match the old materially and
dimensionally. He also agreed in his application to rebuild the porch’s decking in the same orientation as the original

porch.

P. O’Kennedy also noted that since he made the revised submission, he has discovered that the existing front steps are,
“not to code, with 8” risers & 11.5” treads.” He does not believe these are historically accurate steps and cite d the 1956
property record card photograph as potentially displaying evidence of an extra riser. He stated that he would like to rebuild
these steps to modern code, while simultaneously reconstructing the design and materiality of the 1956 era steps. The
HPA shared that while an exemption in NYS Building Code (Section [NY] BO109.10.2 Replacement) would allow in-kind
reconstruction, if the Building and Safety Division requires him to bring the porch and steps to the modern code –  he
would simply have to ensure that the outward appearance not change from the visually documented historic porch and
steps

DECISISON: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 (c) (1) (2) and
determined that it will have no significant environmental impact. Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed
porch reconstruction project at 31 Stuyvesant Street in the Chestnut Street Local (2002), State, and National Historic
District (1985), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section
405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with th e historic character of the Chestnut Street Landmark District
for the following reasons:
• that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting
materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness;
• the proposed work is to take place at 2.5 story modest Victorian building as the northeast corner of the Livingston
and Stuyvesant Street intersection that was likely built circa 1890, and was at one time owned by William Roach, the
owner of a "leather findings business in Rondout" (NYS BSIF, 1982);
• the owner exceeded the permission granted under previous authorizations and removed the existing porch due to
the discovery of unforeseen deterioration which made restoration impractical;
• the Building Safety Division issued a Stop Work Order, and the owner applied to the HLPC for review of the porch
removal and reconstruction project and provided the commission with existing conditions and materials demonstrating
a commitment to in-kind repairs;
• the applicant shall reconstruct the porch according to historic photographs using as much salvageable features as
possible, and shall supplement with reconstructed features that match the original in design, texture, material,
dimension, and location - rendering it a one-to-one match;
• submit lattice work for beneath porch to staff for review based on the house style and design period;
• the reconstructed porch's decking must follow the same orientation as the historic porch, regardless of the Building
and Safety Division's potential directive to bring the porch structure up to modern code requirements - should this be
done, no alterations shall be seen from the public right of way;
• the applicant shall provide the HLPC with photographs of the reconstructed porch once it is completed;
• that the criteria authorized under previous desk reviews still stand;
• any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted
application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start;
• the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any
other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies;
Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 5th day of March 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of
Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the

Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this
date. (Motion - MG; 2nd - KM; RT, EW, NM - yes)

items.title: Project Update: FFY24 CLG for the Wilbur State and National Register Nomination:
items.discussion:
The HPA and Planning Director shared the following project’s status and next steps with the
commission:
• In 2021, NYS OPRHP SHPO awarded the City a CLG grant to survey Wilbur and Ponckhockie.
• In December 2023, SHPO issued a determination Wilbur eligible for Local, State, and National Historic District
recognition.
• On September 11, 2024, the Kingston Common Council voted unanimously to establish the Wilbur Local Landmark
District (Common Council Resolution 147 of 2024).
• At the end of September 2024, NYS awarded Kingston a $15,000 CLG grant to hire a historic preservation consultant
to prepare the S/NHR Nomination for Wilbur.
• On November 12, 2025, the City awarded Gregory Dietrich Preservation (36CRF61 qualified) the contract to
research and prepare the State & National District Nomination paperwork.
• LATEST: On February 13, 2026, the WHD’s Project Advisor Committee held its 50% progress meeting with Gregory
Dietrich who presented on his draft nomination. SHPO staff noted that the district’s architectural integrity is about
30-40% may not meet NPS standards (usually 75% +), so they advised dropping the criterion C (Architecture) listing
and focusing solely on Criterion A (Community Development), which is an easier lift in terms of integrity.
• UPCOMING: An informational meeting for the Wilbur State & National Historic District Nomination is set for Tuesday,
April 21, 2026, between 5:30- 7:30pm, at 23 Fitch Street - for more information please see the attached flyer:
https://engagekingston.com/27697/widgets/94955/documents/78109 HLPC Commissioner Attendance at this

items.title: Adoption of HLPC Meeting Minutes of Thursday , March 5, 2026:
#33 N. Front St: 2nd-story Window Replacement, Signage, & Awnings for Signature Fitness
items.discussion:
The owner, John Perry, presented plans to replace the 2nd-story late vinyl replacement windows at 33 N.
Front Street. J. Perry has been working with staff and has obtained various desk review approvals for other work
associated with façade restoration. The building was formerly part of London’s Department store, which in the latter half
of the 20 th-century owned 31, 33, and 35 N. Front Street. After the canopies were put up in the early 1970s, a yellow
aluminum false façade was installed that homogenized and flattened the 2nd- and 3rd stories of these three (3) buildings.
Since January 2026, J. Perry has presented restoration plans and received two desk reviews for work that were deemed
in-kind work and conforming with the commercial area’s period of significance (~1930-1965):
• January 20, 2026: Approval for removal and in-kind repairs to the façade
March 27, 2026: Approval for reconstructing a historically inspired signboard and installing an historically inspired
awning.
J. Perry cited the historic photographs of the building and is familiar with the Secretary of the Interiors Standards for the
Rehabilitation of Historic Properties. He intends to remove the late inappropriate sized  and vinyl replacement windows
and install new wooden, with  aluminum clad exterior finish, 400 Series windows sourced from Home Depot. J. Perry
stated that window screens will be internal. The new windows are all black to match the historic design present in 1956.
They will also be appropriately recessed to match the 1956 window placement/recess. The two outermost windows shall
be 1/1 double hung windows that will match the design, material, and operation of those visible in 1956.
In the center of the section floor will be two (2) single panel square awning-style windows that will open no more than 14
inches for ventilation. The 1956 photograph and others sourced from the Friends of Historic Kingston do not clarify if the
original windows opened. Given the historic wood windows lost years ago, the HLPC generally felt that the proposed
windows and their operation were generally appropriate and more compatible than the current configuration and
materials.
In addition to the windows, J. Perry proposed adding for the signage which was approved at desk level . The proposed
lighting would be a strip style LED lighting method that would be installed in a recessed part of his signboard’s upper
trim. The proposed light strip would only cast light downwards onto the signboard and would conform with nightscape
lighting requirements. J. Perry added that the lights would be capable of producing multiple colors, but that he would only
have them produce a warm white light. The lights will turn on when his business lights turn on. The HLPC felt that the
proposed lighting would be minimally visible and not adversely impact on the historic streetscape.

decisions.vote: Motion- MG; 2nd – AP; NM, EW, RT – Yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Unlisted under SEQR and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Commissioner Grunblatt motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed window project at 33 N. Front St in the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1975; 2016), if done according to the plans reviewe d, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the Kingston Stockade Local, State, and National District for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the three story row-building located on the north side of N. Front Street two (2) parcels west of the intersection of Wall and N. Front Streets dating to the late 19th- century and which previously housed a tailor (1915), a salon (1930), Waring clothing, the Artistic Shop, and Daniel's Shoes (1940), and London's Center Junior Bazaar Clothing (1950) (1987, SHPO BSIF); • the three buildings at 31, 33, and 35 N. Front Street comprised London's Store, which around the time of the Pike Plan Canopy construction installed an inappropriate early 1970s yellow and white aluminum facade to homogenize/unify the buildings, which in turn obscured their historical facades and character defining features; • the owner has been authorized to remove the aluminum siding, and to undertake in- kind facade repair work, including masonry repairs, sign board reconstruction, awning installation, and painting, under previously issued desk reviews; • the existing 2nd- story windows are understood to be white, vinyl, double hung (all the same size) windows, smaller in size than the historic masonry portal, which adversely visually impacts the masonry facade, and which is incompatible with the commercial area's historic period of significance (~1930-1965); • the owner may replace the two (2) outermost 2nd- story windows with the proposed new Anderson 400 Series, black aluminum clad exterior, wooden double hung windows with interior screens, which must be recessed according to the historic wood windows (see 1956 PRC); • the owner may replace the two (2) innermost 2nd- story square windows with black aluminum framed single- lite awning style windows that dimensionally fill the masonry portal like the historic windows recorded in the 1956 PRC, and which must be appropriately recessed within said opening, and that the new windows may not tilt open from the base more than 18 inches; • the owner also seeks to install LED strip lighting, recessed into the upper trim panel of the sign board lighting, so as to not be visible, with downward directed lighting over sign face; • the conduit for the new lighting must be run internally, and that the light from the new lamps shall be white in color; • the criteria authorized under previous desk reviews still stand; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 13th day of April 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion- MG; 2nd – AP; NM, EW, RT – Yes).

items.title: Letter of Support for Historic Homeowner Tax Credit (S4057A Fahy/A5453 Woerner) •
items.discussion:
Chairman Grunblatt shared with the Commission that there is a proposed bill in Albany (S4057A
Fahy/A5453 Woerner) that would restore the full benefits of the On February 25, 2026, NYS Historic Homeowner
Rehabilitation Tax Credit program. Staff provided the following information from the Preservation League on the bill:

“As of January 1, 2025, the homeowner portion of the NYS Historic Rehabilitation Tax Credit Program stepped
down significantly in value from a maximum of $50,000 per project to $25,000. Additionally, the rebate provision of
the credit, which has been so helpful to those homeowners without the state tax liability to accept the full value of
the credit and instead receive it as a rebate, has been allowed to expire.

In response, there has been introduced in the NYS Legislature a bill that would restore the Homeowner Credit to its
pre-January 1, 2025, value. In the Senate it is bill S4057A sponsored by Senator Patricia Fahy and in the Assembly
it is A5453 sponsored by Assemblymember Carrie Woerner (click the links to read the full legislation and see the
current list of co-sponsors).

Because tax credits have a fiscal impact on New York State, it is likely that any fix to the tax credit program will have
to be a part of the FY27 Budget now being negotiated in Albany. For it to be included, legislators will need to sign
on as co-sponsors of the legislation and request that leadership include the bill’s language in the final FY27 Budget.”

To this end, the HPA prepared two matching letters of support to be sent to NYS Senator Michelle Hinchey (Dist. 41) &
Sarahana Shrestha (103rd Assembly Dist.) for the HLPC to review and endorse.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action a Type II, and authorized the Chairman to sign and send the letters of support for the S4057A Fahy/A5453 Woerner Bill to NYS Senator Michelle Hinchey (Dist. 41) & Sarahana Shrestha (103rd Assembly Dist.). (Motion – RT; 2nd – NM; all yes).

Chairman Grunblatt shared with the commission information on the upcoming neighborhood meeting for
the Wilbur Historic District. The meeting is an opportunity for property owners to meet and learn more about the project
and engage with the preservation consultant, Gregory District, and SHPO staff. Seating, tables, a projector, and screen

Accessibility: Anyone with mobility challenges can be dropped off at upper rear entrance on Burnett St, which
