items.title: Awning Discussion
items.discussion:
Staff shared with the commission that several projects have come for desk level review in recent weeks.
Staff base in-kind work on the commercial area’s period of significance (~1930-1965) and historical records/images of
this period (e.g., 1956 property record card, etc.). Some projects propose installing retractable awnings, some fixed
awnings, and others do not include awnings. Presently, staff encourages the use of retractable awnings when historical
records support their presence at the site in the past, and discoursed f ixed awnings. If no historical records indicate the
former presence of an awning, then staff have discouraged awnings or stated that the proposal must go before the HLPC.
While staff recognizes awnings are fixtures that can be removed in the future, we wanted to bring this topic to the
commission to determine awning types and review requirements that are satisfactory to the commissioner. The
Commissioners generally agreed with Staff on the period of significance, the preference of retractable awnings, and
sending proposals that are not based on the historic record to the HLPC for review.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; NM, RT, AP – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Unlisted under SEQR and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. The HLPC concurs with the importance of the Stockade District Commercial Area period of significance (~1930- 1965), which was delineated in update to the district's S/NHR nomination in 2016. Restoration and/or rehabilitation must conform with the US SOI Sta ndards for Rehabilitation and the Local Landmarks Code. Proposed work should be based on documentation (written, visual, or material data) from this period, rather than work that modifies buildings to time periods before or afterwards. It is generally understood that awnings of this period were retractable, and the installation of new awnings should adhere to this design. Staff may approve retractable awnings applications at desk level, providing they have documented historical basis. All future applications for fixed awnings or retractable awnings with no historical basis must be reviewed by the HLPC. (Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; NM, RT, AP – yes). NEXT MEETING: Thursday, May 7, 2026. items.title: #35 Wurts St: Construction of front masonry steps without review

decisions.vote: Motion- MG; 2nd – RT; AP, NM, KM, EW, MR – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Eqs., motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the masonry front steps at 35 Wurts Street in the Rondout West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District (1979), as shown in the plans and photos reviewed, the di scussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness (CoA); • the work has taken place at the two story brick Second Empire dwelling dating between 1858 and 1870 that stands adjacent to the Trinity Methodist Church at the corner of Wurts and Hunter St which the October 21st, 1971 Building- Structure Inventory Form prepared by the Friends of Historic Kingston states "was the parsonage for the neighboring Methodist church. The residence retains its original decorative features and has received no major modern alterations. It is one of the most intact and important structures of its type and style in the district"; • the owner is in the process of undertaking substantial rehabilitation for the building, and plans to occupy the building as a single family, once completed; • the owner mistakenly constructed concrete, brick, and bluestone front steps without a CoA from the HLPC and without a building permit, resulting in the receipt of a violation notice from the Building Safety Division; • historical photographs and other records do not provide evidence that masonry steps were formerly present at the building; • it is understood that the masonry front steps do not touch the existing structure, and could be removed without harm to the historic building, if desired in the future; • examination of the Wurts Street block reveals a mixture of masonry and wood front steps at contemporary buildings, providing a period, material, and district basis for the feature's construction; • it is the position of the HLPC that the masonry steps constructed without a CoA, are generally compatible with the character of 35 Wurts Street and the Rondout-West Strand Historic District; • that HLPC review is a requirement within Landmark districts, and that retroactive approval for previously unauthorized work is not guaranteed to any application and/or project; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the HLPC's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 7th day of May 2026, the HLPC grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the HLPC, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion- MG; 2nd – RT; AP, NM, KM, EW, MR – yes).

items.title: #161 Fair St: Amending prior CoA to authorize alternative wooden front entryway design for newly constructed dwelling
items.discussion:
Ion Trifan, of Wright Architects, represented the  property owners.  Wright Architects was before the
commission in November 2025 for the demolition and rebuilding of a single -family home at 161 Fair Street in the Fair
Street Local Historic District (1988). Prior to private ownership, the fire damaged building served as the Church of Christ

I. Trifan reviewed the proposal for a slightly different front entryway than what was authorized by the HLPC. The new door
will be made of solid mahogany - with an integrated sidelight and transom. The new unit will be painted blue and utilize
textured privacy glass. This modification seeks to improve the visual integration of the entry within the approved façade.
The HLPC examined the entryway initially proposed in Nov. 2025 and the newly proposed entryway and found the new
compatible and appropriate.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – NM; MR, AP, KM, EW, RT – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Eqs., motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed entryway modification at a new construction at 161 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Historic District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place on the west side of Fair Street, four parcel's south of the intersection of Fair and St. James Sts, where circa 1914 George W. items.title: #165 Fair St: Wood window restoration & relocation resulting from fire damage
items.discussion:
Ion Trifan, of Wright Architects, re presented the property owners. Wright Architects was contracted for
restoring 165 Fair Street, which sustained substantial fire damage of the interior, roof, and several windows in late 2024.
I. Trifan stated the proposal before the commission is a historically sensitive wood window restoration, relocation, and
replacement project for windows that were damaged by the fire. In the submission, Wright Architects provided the
following description of the proposed work:
• “The siding will stay metal and be patched because every window but two on the north side rear are single pane, so
we are suggesting white storm windows (with screens) throughout.
• To recreate what may have been the original " Eastlake Movement' upgrade of the late 1800's-early 1900's, we are
proposing to relocate original windows from the south side of the house to the 3-front 2nd-floor windows.
• We relocated the Tower window on the 3rd floor to the east façade on the same floor.
• Rebuild original 1/1 windows
• We are limited with the “egress windows” on the south face; they need to be casement to comply with code”

I. Trifan and the HLPC noted that the building’s architectural style conforms more with the Queen Anne Victorian style,
than Eastlake and going forward it was recognized to refer to the style as Queen Anne Victorian. Historical images and
material evidence at the building suggest that it was gradually expanded over the 19 th-century. The HPA stated that he
met with A. Wright on site  to review the damaged windows and the proposed plan for relocating windows to restore the
façade. It is important to note that most of the rear, rear south side, and rear, north side, are not visible or minimally from
the public right of way.
The HPA and HLPC recognized that restoration of windows is the most appropriate treatment and should be undertaken
whenever possible. Relocation of design, material, and operationally matching and usable historic windows from non-
visible locations to highly visible locations is generally another preferred treatment. I. Trifan stated that in the submission,
A. Wright recognized there are some replacement windows on the front and/or side facades that appear to be 1/1
replacements of the original windows.  In these locations, he proposed installing  historic Queen Anne Victorian style
windows sourced from other non-publicly visible parts of the building.
I. Trifan noted that two modern casement windows (one on the 3rd floor and one on the second floor) at the fire escape
are being used to meet the current  egress code . To better identify the specific windows scheduled for restoration,
relocation, and general replacement , the application includes historical photographs, existing conditions photographs,
and proposed elevations in his application, which the HLPC reviewed on the screen. All restored and/or relocated historic
wood windows will retain the late exterior mounted aluminum storm windows. Overall, the HLPC found the proposal
historically sensitive and compatible with the character of the building and Fair St Local Historic District.

decisions.vote: Motion – MR; 2nd – NM, MG, AP, KM, EW, RT – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Commissioner Ricke, motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed multicomponent window restoration, relocation, and replacement at 165 Fair Street in the Fair Street Local Historic District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 2.5 story vernacular Victorian building, which was built in stages over the 19th-century, which included Queen Anne style windows and other bracketed features, which in recent time has served as a multi-unit apartment building, which is located on the west side of Fair Street , three (3) lots south of the intersection of Fair and St. James Streets; • in late 2024, 165 Fair Street sustained a substantial fire that damaged the interior, roof, and several windows, which prompted the applicant and owners to undertake a historically sensitive wood window restoration, relocation, and minor replacement project; • the HLPC's preference is for the restoration of windows whenever possible, and that the relocation of compatible historic windows to the location of irreparably damaged portals is generally considered an appropriate treatment, over installation of modern windows; • the applicant may undertake restoration of the windows as identified on the plans dated March 26, 2026; • the applicant may undertake relocation of the historic Queen Anne style windows from this current locations to the locations proposed on the plans dated March 26, 2026; • the applicant may restore or replace the existing exterior mounted aluminum storm windows in the same overall design to ensure higher R-values at the building; • the applicant shall replace all removed windows from fire activity with 1/1 double hung wood windows along the southern face; • two egress compliant casement windows are identified on the elevation drawings for the 3rd and 2nd floor southern- facing fire escape shall be wood with aluminum covering; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the HLPC's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 7th day of May 2026, the HLPC grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the HLPC, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MR; 2nd – NM, MG, AP, KM, EW, RT – yes).

items.title: #330 Wall St: Awning, windows, rooftop elevator bulkhead and deck
items.discussion:
Ion Trifan, of Wright Architects, re presented the property owners  with a multicomponent exterior
rehabilitation and modification project. He  explained the project is an exterior restoration of the building, preserving its
original character through the installation of a shed-style awning in the facade on Fair St. that will not obscure any newly
revealed architectural details. The scope also includes the replacement of existing windows to match the existing design;
and involves interior areas that form the new spatial configuration.
AWNINGS: Staff advised that a desk review was done for a proposed Wall Street-facing awning so the owners could
apply for the Stockade Restoration Grant program. The owners will be installing a retractable awning that matches design,
operation, and placement, as the one featured in the 1956 property record card photograph of the property. I. Trifan added
that a second smaller awning is proposed along Fair Street for the rear entrance to the first-floor gallery. Although there
is no evidence of any prior awning, this is a fixture that could be easily undoable in the future. The proposed awning must
not encroach within 2ft of the sidewalk's edge and must have a minimum clearance of 8 feet. Pursuant to City Code §358-
9 the owner must provide the city with insurance naming the city as additionally for the projection over the public right of
way.
ROOFTOP BULKHEAD & TERRACE:  I. Trifan presented plans for a new non- visible rooftop terrace, accessible via a
new elevator. To accommodate the terrace, new decking to provide for a flat and useable surface and new bulkheading
are necessary. The elevator is predominantly an interior feature that will replace the existing staircase, therefore HLPC
review is unnecessary for most of the proposal. T he elevator bulkhead is sufficiently located back from the W all Street
roofline and shifted more towards the Fair Street side, but which I. Trifan explained will be minimally visible from Fair St.
I. Trifan added that rooftop bulkheads are not uncommon in uptown, and this one will have a minimal visual impact.
WINDOWS:
Wall Street-facing Windows:
• I. Trifan stated the large 2 nd-story wooden picture window, which appears to be the same as the one present
during the 1956 property record card, will be retained and restored in-kind.
• The 3 rd floor 1/1 double -hung windows will be replaced with new aluminum-clad wooden 1/1 double hung
windows. I. Trifan stated there are either late aluminum or vinyl replacement windows installed after the 1950s
era façade was removed, and the 19th-century façade was exposed.

Fair Street-facing Windows:
• 3rd floor: All the windows on the Fair Street façade are proposed for replacement. I. Trifan stated these are late
1/1 vinyl or aluminum double hung windows. The HLPC felt that replacement of these would be acceptable if the
proposed replacement is wood or aluminum clad wood of the same design and operation.
• 2nd floor: The existing set of 6/6 double hung wood windows are proposed for replacement. These appear in the
images provided to be older windows and possibly restorable.  The applicant did not demonstrate existing
conditions, and therefore Staff advised the HLPC should not approve replacement of these windows. Restoration
and retention of existing windows is considered the most appropriate treatment whenever possible.
o The windows adjacent to the right (north) are two 1/1 windows that appear to be aluminum or vinyl. I.
Trifan stated that the intention is to replace these two windows with aluminum clad wood.
• 1st floor: I. Trifan stated that three (3) 6/6 double-hung windows are present and made of vinyl. New aluminum-

clad wood windows of the same design and operation are proposed for these locations. The HPA asked if the 1st
floor transom window is proposed for replacement, too, and what the existing material is for this window. I. Trifan
stated he was unsure and would report back to staff.

Because of the presence of two (2) 6/6 wood windows on the second floor, Staff and the HLPC asked if they could be
restored and retained as some of the last existing historic window fabric. The Planning Director also asked if it was
possible to restore and relocate these windows to the ground floor  to allow them to be prominently  on display for
pedestrian traffic? The HPA also asked about the condition, material, and operation of the Fair Street transom window. I.
Trifan stated that more research is needed and he would be happy to do so and provide it to the commission after the
meeting.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – KM; MR, AP, NM, EW, RT – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Esq., motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed awning, window work, elevator bulkhead, and rooftop terrace work at 330 Wall Street in the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1975; 2016), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district with the following reasons: • pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 3-story row building, located on the east side of Wall Street 3 lots south of the intersection of Wall & N. Front Streets, which may have been initially constructed in the 1860s, but received mid- 20th-century modifications, and which by 1940 housed Nigent's National Clothing store, and by the 1950s -1960s, housed the Up-to-Date Shop" (SHOP, BSIF, 1987); • Awning: the applicant previously secured a desk review from staff for a proposed historically informed awning on the Wall St elevation. The applicant also may install, the proposed Fair St awning on the plans/elevations dated April 23, 2026, but that the awing must not encroach within 2ft of the sidewalk's edge and must have a minimum clearance of 8 feet. Pursuant to City Code §358-9 the owner must provide the city with insurance naming the city as additionally insured for all projections over the public right of way; • Rooftop Bulkhead: the proposed bulkhead is located sufficiently back from Wall St, such that it will not be visible from the public right of way. The bulkhead may be slightly visible from Fair St, N. Front St, and/or Clinton Ave, but its visibility is deemed minor and will not adversely impact the district; • Terrace: the proposed rooftop terrace appears sufficiently set back from the Wall & Fair Street roof lines such that it and the required railings will not be visible from the public right of way; • Wall St-facing Windows: the 2nd floor large picture window appears to be historical to the building's mid- 20th- century modifications and shall be restored in-kind. The 3rd floor 1/1 late1980's, vinyl replacement windows may be replaced with new 1/1 double hung wood windows installed with the same degree of recess as the historic windows; • Fair St- facing Windows: the 3rd floor windows are late vinyl replacements, which may be replaced with new 1/1 double hung wood windows; a set of existing 6/6 double hung wood windows with exterior storms must on the 2nd floor will be studied to determine if restoration is suitabl e and possibly relocated to street level to be more publicly visible along the frontage (with staff and applicant), the remaining late replacement windows on the 2nd floor shall be replaced with new 1/1 double hung wood windows; the ground floor 6/6 double hung windows are late vinyl replacement, and may be replaced with new 6/6 double hung wood windows, unless older restored windows from second floor are used to replace the set (with staff and applicant). The existing transom window above the ground floor door shall be further investigated to determine condition and shall remain/be restored, as determined by staff and applicant; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 7th day of May 2026, the HLPC grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the HLPC, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – KM; MR, AP, NM, EW, RT – yes).

items.title: #39 N. Front St: Shopfront modifications
items.discussion:
The owner, Darbie Nowatka,  and her architect, Michael Wentland, presented plans to undertake a
historically sensitive shopfront restoration/ modification project at 39 N. Front Street within the Stockade District’s
Commercial Area, which has a period of significance of ~1930- 1965. They want to make some minor changes to the
storefront facade as it exists today to bring it closer to the historical photos by installing a larger 2- pane display window,
glass store door, and transom windows above the doors. Additionally, they hope to remove the non- functional structure
around the apartment door.  During their presentation, they shared with the commission the 1956 property record card
image of the building, the later mid-century aluminum shopfront changes, the current conditions, and their proposal.

The existing shopfront is a later historically inappropriate modification from the design present during the period of
significance. The existing three windows are framed in wood and are smaller in height and contain greater divisions. The
current shop door is a late  mass-produced entryway that is inappropriate for the building and the district.  The proposed
shopfront would feature 2 larger/taller storefront windows set in wooden frames. Overall, the commission felt that the
proposed modifications are historically appropriate and more closely resemble the design and materials present during
the commercial area’s period of significance.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; MR, RT, AP, NM, KM – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Esq., motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed shop front window, door, and partition wall modifications at 39 N. Front St in the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1979), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district with the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 2- story Italianate brick row building, located on the north side of N. Front St, 5 parcels west of the intersection of N. Front & Wall Streets, likely dating to circa 1870, which formerly housed a harness & saddlery shop (1880s), a tea shop (1894), E. Hoyt Green Grocer (1910-1920s), among other businesses (SHPO, BSIF, 1987); • the applicant previously secured a desk review for reconstruction of a historically informed signboard, installation of a retractable awning, and repainting the building in historic colors; • the HLPC recognizes that the existing shop front is a late 20th- century modification undertaken likely in the late 1960s or early 1970s, outside the commercial areas period of significance; • the HLPC finds the proposed historically informed shop front window, entryway door, and partition wall modifications as rendered in the submitted plans reviewed at this meeting are appropriate for the character of the building and district; • the applicant may replace the existing three shop front windows and knee wall for the proposed larger two wooden shop front windows with lower knee wall; • the proposed wooden entryway door and transom window is considered more historically appropriate than the current features; • removal of the apartment door partition wall, which is itself a late inappropriate modification is considered an appropriate action; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the HLPC's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 7th day of May 2026, the HLPC grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the HLPC, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. items.title: #85 Broadway: Shopfront Window Modification
items.discussion:
Greg Goldstone of Still Works Architecture, presented on behalf of the owners, Middle Seat, LLC (Jesse
Kaplan, partner), plans to modify a shopfront along lower Broadway in the Rondout Historic District . He stated that the
goal of the project is to convert an unused and empty oversized foyer space into a functional commercial space to activate
the currently vacant front window as a sidewalk -facing service window for a food vendor. This conversion involves a
minimal amount of interior work to create a partition and make the space suitable for food service (workspace, sinks,
washable surfaces, etc.). It also involves the replacement of a plate glass window (itself an HLPC approved replacement
of a garage door) with a partitioned window: a fixed picture above a sliding service window. The glazing will fill the existing
opening completely and the trim and partitions will be in keeping with the historic facade of woodwork and paint colors.

The HPA reviewed the street file and confirmed that the existing wood window was authorized for replacement by this
commission in 2022. Commissioner Puetz questioned the dimensionality of the shopfront windows on the proposed
elevation relative to the current design, because the rendering contained dimensional differences.  Staff added that under
the current FBC, the shopfront language also has specific requirements.  Since the opening size is not being changed
dimensionally the lower height is not an issue  at present.  Any extensions outward which are projected over the public
right-of-way will require additional insurance to be provided, naming the city as additionally insured. Staff also added that
with the proposed nature of the window opening, the owner must be aware and comply with window signage limitations
at 25%. This would also include items and goods being offered. The limitation should be a stipulation of any approval and
if additional signage is to be permanently affixed, the owner must submit for signage review under a Planning review.

• the proposed sliding service window is considered an appropriate design/operation for the character of the building and block; • the existing window must be kept on-site should it ever need to be reinstalled in the same location; items.title: #91 W. Union St: Reconfiguring existing windows for interior renovation
items.discussion:
The owner, Rian Bradley, presented plans to relocate existing vinyl windows at 91 W. Union Street. The
project initially called for relocating side windows and installation of HVAC mini split systems , however, after discussion,
the owner confirmed with staff that the condenser units will be in the rear where they will not be visible from the W. Union
right-of-way. This modification brought their project into Section 405.14.I.5 and Landmarks compliance and allowed staff
to authorize them to proceed with securing a permit for the HVAC work only and the HLPC is only reviewing the proposed
relocation of existing windows.

R. Bradley noted the building had sat vacant for some time.  He explained his plans to relocate an existing sliding glass
window on the 1 st floor western-facing elevation and reinstall it on the eastern- facing elevation toward the rear. This
window appears to be approximately the same distance back from the street just on the building’s opposite side and
entered over a kitchen sink area. A window in the 1956 property record card appears to be removed from the kitchen area
and will be sealed over with solid wall . On the 2nd floor, it appears that one western-facing window will be relocated and
another window added. The plans state the added window will be an Anderson TW3046. The design and operation of
these windows is not clear to staff and from Google searches. Two new Anderson TW3046 windows are proposed on the
eastern elevation. The windows will match the same design, material, and 2/2 operation as the current windows in the
building. The applicant also proposed to remove the 2 nd-floor’s western (left) most 1/1 window on the street -facing
elevation.

The HPA stated that the building underwent extensive modifications made to the structure over time, including after the
1979 district nomination. It is not clear whether previous owners undertook these projects without HLPC review.  In its
current state, the building is considered “Non-contributing” to the historic district. Commissioner Puetz and others stated
that the use of wood windows in this location is unrealistic and inappropriate given the substantial alterations and lack of
historic integrity across all elevations reviewed. Installation of wood window would be akin to placing diamonds on a tin
car. Alternatives to removing the 2nd story street-facing window were discussed, such as creating a faux interior backing.
Commissioner Puetz also felt this was inappropriate and could result in a more visually obtrusive feature. Ultimately, it
was determined that removal is an appropriate ac tion to ensure sufficient reuse of the structure. It was also understood
that the removal and relocation of the windows within this project could be undone in the future if ever desired.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – RT; MR, AP, NM, KM, EW – yes

items.title: Letter of Support for White Elephant Historic Tax Credit Enhancement Act (S.6021A Baskin/A10366 Hunter)
items.discussion:
In early April 2026, the Preservation League of NYS announces the proposal of new legislation focused
on supporting the rehabilitation of White Elephant buildings. This legislation, introduced by NYS Senator April Baskin
(Buffalo) and Assemblymember Pamela Hunter (Syracuse), would enhance the NYS Rehabilitation Tax Credit to
incentivize the redevelopment of “White Elephant” properties throughout New York State. Here are some of the details:

• White Elephant Buildings are defined as very large, difficult to develop, vacant structures having $50M or more
in Qualified Rehabilitation Costs that have been vacant at least 10 of the last 15 years.
• The proposed legislation would increase the per -project cap on the NYS Rehabilitation Tax Credit from $5M to
$15M for these buildings.
• The proposed legislation also extends the entire Tax Credit Program from 2030 to 2037, to allow time to plan
and implement these larger projects.
• We would anticipate no fiscal impacts to NYS in the upcoming fiscal year due to the time it will take to complete
these large and complex White Elephant Projects.
• https://www.preservenys.org/advocacy-updates/2026-white-elephant?blm_aid=117677
• https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S6021/amendment/A

On March 30, 2026, Senator Baskin held a press conference at Buffalo’s Central Terminal, to promote the legislation.
You can see coverage of the event via WGRZ. While there is a chance that this legislation is included in the NYS Budget
currently being negotiated, it is more likely that passage would occur in the remaining legislative session ending in June.

To that end, PLNYS encouraged readers to reach out to your legislators now and ask them to co-sponsor White Elephant
Historic Tax Credit Enhancement Act (S.6021A Baskin/A10366 Hunter) To this end, the HPA prepared two matching
letters of support to be sent to NYS Senator Michelle Hinchey (Dist. 41) & Sarahana Shrestha (103rd Assembly Dist.) for
the HLPC to review and endorse.

items.title: #150 Fair St: HVAC installed in the front of a building without review
items.discussion:
The owners, Marisa K. and Patchin Podes , were present to remedy a violation for installation of  HVAC
equipment on the front porch roof and front yard  at 150 Fair Street ( Fair Street Local Historic District  (1988)). The
installation took place sometime after the Form Based Code’s passage in August of 2023 and March of 2024 and thereby
violates Section 405.26.L (HLPC) and Section 405.14.I.5 (Screening of Mechanical Equipment & Service Areas).

To mitigate the impact and remedy, M Podes proposes to move the one (1) HVAC compressor from the roof to the ground
in the front yard area, alongside the existing pad-mounted compressor. Screening was proposed as shrubbery.  M. Podes
stated the ground-mounted condenser would need to be shifted to accommodate the other condenser, formerly mounted
on the roof.
The HLPC confirmed that the units cannot be located on the side of the building due to spac e limitations and cannot be
relocated to the rear due to the length of the lines needed for such placement.  While placement in front of screening is
feasible, the owners must still conform to setback requirements. Any unit would need to be placed on pads or stands, not
mounted via brackets to the building. The photo provided indicates that these are to be located directly in front of the large
picture window. The height of the top of the unit should be below the window area, so it does not interfere with the feature.
Staff stated that if the units are placed along the front, a combination of a lattice screening which  should be painted to
match the color of the lower section, and shrubbery planted in front of that would be more appropriate given the proximity
of the public sidewalk and high visibility.  At a minimum, the vegetation type should be specified to ensure year -round
coverage. P. Podes also added that the lines leading to the 2 nd story would be in the small space along the north side.
The Commission requested th at any unpainted line hides be painted to match the façade’s existing colors  to mitigate
visibility.

decisions.vote: Motion - MG; 2nd - KM; RT, MR, AP - yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Eqs., motion that the Commissioners present find as fact that the HVAC mini split relocation project at 150 Fair St in the Fair Street Local Landmark District (1988), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • that pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the two story Neo- Greek Revival building, which was converted into a multi - unit rental building, located on the east side of Fair Street eight (80 parcels south of the intersection of St. James and Fair Streets; • the owner caused the installation of two (2) HVAC mini split systems on the front of the building (one on the ground and one on the 1st-floor roof) and ran lines on the facade of the building that are highly visible from the public right of way in violatio n of FBC ss405.14.I.5 (Screening of Electric and Mechanical Equipment), and that this work was done without permits from the Building Safety Division; • that the applicant shall relocate the existing condensers to front facade, below picture window, behind porch setback; • that the line hides shall be painted to match the exterior of the structure over which they pass; • that the condensers shall be mounted on pads or stands and screened from view by lattice painted to match the basement wall behind the units to obscure their visibility from the public right of way, with added landscaping in front; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 4th day of June 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. items.title: #20 Presidents Pl: Proposed replacement of 32 existing wood windows
items.discussion:
The owner, Rachel Kafka, presented plans to paint the circa 1900 Queen Anne Victorian house
at 20 Presidents Place, which was built as the second (2nd) residence for Conrad Hiltebrant, a locally prominent shipbuilder
in Rondout, using a historically informed color scheme. All four (4) colors are by Benjamin Moore, but only two (2) are
from the historic color collection. Below are the colors and the design scheme:
1) Body/Primary Color: Benjamin Moore Rolling Hills 1497
2) Columns, trim, window casings: Benjamin Moore Market Square Shell CW-30
3) Window Frames: Benjamin Moore Black HC-190
4) Accents including dental moldings, soffits, etc.: Benjamin Moore Forest Floor 1498
The primary entrance and secondary entrance are stained and shall remain stained wood.

R. Kafka explained that the colors she chose came from her research of Victorian era paint design schemes, and while
two of the colors are not drawn from the Benjamin Moore Historic Color Collection, they closely match the historic colors
identified in her paint research. R. Kafka also prepared a rendering of the house with the proposed colors so the HLPC
could see the visual impact of the change.
Commissioners present agreed that although certain color choices were not identified as historic, the research presented
supported using those in combination with the others.

R. Kafka presented the second component of her project  – a proposal to
replace 32 existing wooden windows and their exterior aluminum storm windows at 20 Presidents Place . R. Kafka read
into the record the project overview, which she prefaced as a unique and complex situation:

“So, I would say this is perhaps a unique and somewhat complex situation that I come to you all with tonight. The
short of it is, after becoming aware that many of our original windows are a significant source of blood dust exposure

within our home, we are looking to have 32 of these problem windows replaced. We will be retaining and preserving
13 original windows. I care very deeply about the history and integrity of our home, but nothing is more important to
me than the safety, health, and well-being of my family. So, I have spent the past couple months trying to figure out
how to reconcile the two. I have spent many, many dozens of hours preparing for tonight's meeting, researching,
speaking to contractors, window restorers, window replacement specialists, and the Ulster County Department of
Health. I have left no stone unturned in hopes that we may have a complete discussion on this matter tonight. I've
also prepared a great deal of background information for you all, not only in an effort to share more about the
replacement windows we've selected, but also in an effort to demonstrate the merit of window replacement for our
particular circumstance. I know this commission strongly favors restoration, and that you all have aligned yourselves
with the DOI standards for rehabilitation. I'm also acutely aware that there's been a great deal of very public
discussion in town recently,  debating, replacement versus restoration in regards to another building's window in
Kingston. But 20 President's Place is not a meeting house or institution. It is a private family home that is occupied
100% of the time by myself, my husband, her two cats,  and my young infant son. And while there is no perfect
solution, what I'm about to share with you all tonig ht is what I believe to be the best solution. A commonsense
compromise that balances replacement and preservation, that prioritizes the health, of my family without
compromising the historic integrity of our home or the historic character of the district. And I believe this window
replacement proposal appeals both to the purpose and duties of the HLPC that it is in line with the reasonable
application of the DOI standards with considerations and technical feasibility, and that it follows proven lead safe
guidance and allows us to be compliant with both the EPA's RRP rule, as well as the DOH's post -inspection
requirements. So, I acknowledge that my application and materials are lengthy, as I'm mindful of all of your time, as
well as the other applicants' time, so I'm happy to go through as much or as little of the background information as
needed, depending on what was reviewed prior. “

Planning Director, Suzanne Cahill, noted that  commissioners have notification when applications are submitted on the
system and asked if they had reviewed the materials in advance of the meeting to review and familiarize themselves with
the technical components of the project. S. Cahill asked the commissioners if they had any questions:
• Commissioner Puetz stated “that an analysis was done on some of the windows, but what is the entirety of the
scope of work and the presence of lead across the proposed windows.”
o R. Kafka: “I’ve done my own at home texting with luminosity tests, but I also had the Department of
health come out and tested a single window which confirmed the presence of lead. I’ve prepared my
tests and the DOH analysis for the commission”.
• Commissioner Puetz: “ In your application, you identified the windows proposed for replacement and those
proposed for preservation. It seems like the majority of the ones for replacement are windows that should be
operable.”
o R. Kafka: “Yes – operable or should be….. We hope to preserve six (6) stained glass windows that are
very prominent. The two (2) side lights for the front and side doors. The two (2) eyebrow windows in the
roof, and the one (1) porthole roof window…. We believe these are very important and the most character
defining windows.”
• Commissioner Puetz: “When you had discussions with contractors, was there ever a discussion of a phased
approach.”
o R. Kafka: “Yes – the challenges are not just removing the 32 window (64 sashes) it’s also stripping all
of the jams and associated components, so there is a huge exposure and time component to this type of

approach. The several restorers we spoke with recommended either a phased approach or taking all the
windows out at the same time and installing plexiglass in the fenestration. Right now, we are keeping the
windows closed, but that is not ideal with the summer coming, and the cold weather afterwards further
complicated matters…..”
• Commission Grunblatt: “And present color scheme on the outside of the house requires lead abatement as
well? And how does that impact these windows?”
o R. Kafka: “Yes – so when we initially were exploring painting the metal storms to hide them better – they
are a little unsightly --- Purely because of the time, the windows need your approval. We are looking to
get started as soon as possible with abatement. There is also a 6 –10-week lead time with the window
production, which will likely push the project into August. We also have a timeline placed upon us by the
Department of Health to fix the health situation.”
• Commissioner Grunblatt asked if the lead remediation on the exterior just at the windows?
o R. Kafka: “No, there is lead paint everywhere in and around the house.  The exterior abatement is a
separate project, taking place at the same time. We are factoring them in together, but the windows and
exterior are essentially separate projects.”
• Commissioner Puetz: “You’ve done a lot of research already, but is there any change you looked at the NPS
Technical Brief #37 Appropriate Methods for Reducing Lead- Paint Hazards in Historic Buildings ? Th e NPS
produces a series of briefs that cover everything from top to bottom. Where this commission has some difficulty
in what your advocating for is that the NPS recommends attempting abatement, and there is evidence that it is
possible. I understand your time component in terms of weather. But I am having a hard time understanding why
a phased approach is not possible?”
o R. Kafka: “Yeah – A few reasons: we have an infant at home, and they cannot be in the house during
the abatement. That means leaving the home periodically over the course of many months, which is
something I don’t know how we would do without causing undo harm to our  family. The window
replacement can all be done the vast majority from the outside, while abatement is heavily done on the
inside. We spoke with one abatement specialist and one window restorer, who advised against
restoration and said replacement is the better path forward. In my research I also included another 2012
study that encourages replacement over restoration, and another NPS document that stated that lead
could be a reason for replacement. There certainly are technical and practical reasons to consider.”
• Commissioner Puetz: “Do you think it’s possible that you could get the professionals you spoke with to put their
opinions in writing?”
o R. Kafka: “The one I just had a quick phone call a few months ago, and I wouldn’t feel comfortable
reaching back out to him. I reached out to him with the contractor , I didn’t hear back from him
unfortunately, and I know he is very busy so I would not feel comfortable asking him. But I did actually
include a letter of support submitted in my application from a lead specialist.”
• Commissioner Ricke: “Maybe I missed it in the application, but can you speak to the condition of the casing?”
o R. Kafka: “This is a sampling. We can certainly go through the lengthier document. 15% of the windows
are stuck and do not operate., which we’ve learned to live with.”
• S. Cahill: “Are they not operable because they are painted shut?”
o R. Kafka: “Yes. We have some cracked panes to contend with. There are also chipping paint and rubbing
places. I have personally encapsulated the paint  in an effort to make the home safer , but this is not a
permanent solution because the added layers create additional friction which increases exposure.”
• Commissioner Ricke :”…the folks that you have talked to about abatement and restoration. What is their

strategy? Some said phases and others said take them all? How long does it take to do it?”
o R. Kafka stated that she reached out to 10 people, and that s everal did not respond. Some turned the
whole project down because of the lead issue. One specialist said they are not compliant with EPA lead
safe certification, which is an issue for the Board of Health requirements. Others told me they could begin
in the spring and end in the fall of next year, but that they would take out all windows and put in plexiglass.
The last restorer would do a phased approach, 2-month increment process.
• S. Cahill: Did you have a home inspection, and did it identify lead in the inspection?
o R. Kafka: “We did – we knew there was lead in the home,  which is why I tried encapsulating the paint.
The rooms have all been freshly painted. Its taken several years for us to save up to paint the exterior.
So, yes it was known to us and we thought we dealt with it sufficiently.”

Commissioner Tonner said this is a tough project because you just don’t get old growth windows anymore. Once they are
removed and gone, they are gone for good. It would be appropriate to have them stored on site for potential restoration
and use.
The HPA asked R. Kafka if they consulted with the NY State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) technical services staff
or the homeowner tax credit staff about the project. R. Kafka noted they had used the Homeowner Tax Credit program in
the past but did not consult with them about this project. “ I hope this commission understands I put a lot of thought into
this project and that we love this district and our house –  this is not the decision we came to lightly, but it feels like the
best decision we could make at this time.”
S. Cahill advised the commission to consult with counsel prior to making any final deciding based on current litigation and
recognizing the significant precedent this project could set moving forward. It is important that the commission think
carefully about the decision they may render. Staff also encouraged each commissioner to visit the project site and view
the street, so commissioners  know firsthand what the conditions are for the project. R. Kafka said it was OK for the
commissioners to get closer to the building. S. Cahill added that we will do a poll and let you know when commissioners
are planning to visit.
R. Kafka respectfully asked the timeline for the review as  the Department of Health  has placed a demand and given a
timeframe to remedy the situation. The current review already has them out of compliance in terms of t he DOH 45-day
time frame from the date of the letter, April 23, 2026.
• Commissioner Grunblatt: “Are there worries in the attic?”
o R. Kafka: “There is one finished room in the attic…. There are four (4) operable double- hung wood
windows in the attic dormers.” R. Kafka also clarified that the eyebrow and porthole window are not going
to be replaced because they are not operable.
• S. Cahill: “What is planned for the two diamond style windows that flank the 2nd-story porch door?”
o R. Kafka: “Those are operable. We are looking to replicate those as close as possible and replace them.”
• S. Cahill: “I am not so concerned about the non-street-facing windows, as I am the street facing windows.”
o R. Kafka: “The way our house is situated, all four sides are visible from the public right of way.”

The commission agreed that in terms of detail s, the south and east elevations are the most critical/evocative. R. Kafka
added that the current windows are partially obscured by the exterior storm windows. If new windows are installed, then

no exterior storms will be used. R. Kafka stated that removing the storms will improve the look of the house. R. Kafka
answered Commissioner Grunblatt’s question that the windows have sash weights. She added that the windows will be
inserted, not new construction windows, that will help encapsulate the lead. New construction will be higher costs and will
be disturbed more of the interior and lead paint, which is why they chose the inserts. The HPA asked if the replacement
windows for the diamond windows on the 2nd story porch will be true divided or simulated, and if they are simulated, would
there be a spacer bar inside the windows? R. Kafka said they are not true divided lites and that she is unaware if there is
a spacer bar between the panes.
S. Cahill stated that the next meeting is scheduled for July 2, 2026, but that if the commission feels materials can be
pulled together, then a special meeting could potentially be calendared earlier. R. Kafka agreed to consult with SHPO,
per the HPA’s request, to provide the HLPC with a greater and broader set of experiences in the review of these kinds of
projects. The HPA stated that SHPO opinions have helped the HLPC before with projects. R. Kafka also clarified that the
DOH got involved because of her request after her child tested for elevated lead. The HLPC and Staff stated that a letter
explaining the review process could be provided if that would be helpful.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; KM, MR, RT – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Chairman Grunblatt motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the historic facade repainting project at 20 Presidents Place in the Rondout-West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District (1979), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405 -26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district for the following reasons: • Pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • In accordance with 405.26.L.13.a, the HLPC determined that the proposed project requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • The proposed work is to take place at the 2.5 story Queen Anne/Colonial Revival building located at on the west side of Presidents Place, where the road bends westward, and which is situated on a promontory that is visible from Rondout, the Wurts Street Bridge, and Port Ewen. According to the 1977 New York State, Building Structure Inventory Form (aka blue form), the building is a “…square, hipped roof house; roof of slate with finial at the point; two story tower at the right corner with octagonal, slate roof, surmounted by a finial. Two story bow window on right side with stained glass in upper portion on both floors. Bow window at the left of front on the first floor, which is one story high, balancing that section of tower. Center doorway with oval glass in upper portion, sidelights, and ornamented by Ionic pilasters. A one-story porch across the front has a circular corner at the tower and extends to the bow on right. The porch roof is supported by paired Ionic columns which rest on a cobblestone, bluestone coped, balustrade and foundation. There is a large two story, hipped roof extension at back, surrounded on two sides by a one- story porch with a second single door entrance with sidelights. There is a ki k at junction of first and second floors.” The 1977 BSIF explains the highly ornamented house was built circa 1890, on the former lands of Thomas Cornell’s Estate, “…for Corad Hildebrandt, the owner of the shipyards at Rondout, after he moved from his original house on Spring Street.” (1977.1 NY SHPO, Building Structure Inventory Form, sourced from the NYS, Cultural Resource Information System.) • The HLPC recognizes 20 Presidents Place is within the Rondout -West Strand Local, State, and National Historic District, which has a period of significance which ranges from about 1800s to 1900s, under the following areas of significance: architecture, comm erce, community planning, economics, education, exploration/settlement, industry, landscape architecture, politics/government, religion, and transportation; • Based on the following documents, it is understood that the building is enumerated in the nomination paperwork as a contributing resource to the Rondout-West Strand Local, State, and National Register Historic District: o 1979: Rondout-West Strand National Register Nomination o 1977.1: New York State Historic Preservation Office, Building Structure Inventory Form (aka Blue Form) for 20 Presidents Place. • The applicant may proceed with a lead remediation program for the exterior of their building by their Lead- Safe Certified Contractor, which shall not be physically or chemically aggressive or damaging to the historic building fabric (clapboard, shake, and other historic materials); • The applicant may repaint the facade in the following color scheme: 1) Body/Primary Color: Benjamin Moore Rolling Hills 1497 2) Columns, trim, window casings: Benjamin Moore Market Square Shell CW-30 3) Window Frames: Benjamin Moore Black HC-190 4) Accents including dental moldings, soffits, etc.: Benjamin Moore Forest Floor 1498 • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 4th day of June 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – AP; KM, MR, RT – yes).

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; end – AP; MR, KM, RT – yes
decisions.text: The HLPC voted unanimously to TABLE the matter until the next meeting on July 2, 2026, or to schedule a special meeting if the ability to obtain a quorum and the following issues are able to be addressed: 1) HLPC Commissioners to visit and view the building in-person from the public right of way. 2) Request the property owner consult with SHPO's Homeowner Tax Credit team, and to learn what actions would be considered permissible by SHPO and qualifying for the tax credit opportunity. This would also allow the owners to learn if the tax credits are a v iable option for their proposed work. Any statement from SHPO should be provided to the HLPC in writing. 3) Allow HLPC to confer with Counsel. (Motion – MG; end – AP; MR, KM, RT – yes).

items.title: #330 Wall St: Proposal to install a fixed awning on the Wall Street elevation
items.discussion:
The applicant, Andrew Wright, and Sonia Lemus, of Wright Architects,  presented the project to install a
fixed, non-retractable, awning along the Wall Street ground floor shopfront. Wright Architect’s previously secured a desk
review to install a historically informed retractable awning; however, the property owner prefers a fixed awning to reduce
maintenance and, in an effort, to ensure that the sun is always blocked for the shopfront . The applicants provided the
HLPC with an early 1900s photograph of Wall Street that they believe demonstrate a fixed awning.

The proposed awning will be the same design, size, and color. A. Wright stated that the heat gain from the giant windows
is tremendous. He added that retractable awnings sometimes work and sometimes don’t work. A. Wright said they don’t
have a structure for them, and that the high winds we sometimes get on Wall Street could damage them. S. Lemus added
there are some fixed awnings uptown, as precedents. The awning must still have a clearance of 8 feet over the sidewalk
and cannot encroach within 2 feet of the sidewalk line. The owner must also list the City as co-insured for any projection
over the public right of way.  A. Wright spoke  about exploring the possibility of a 2 nd story awing but decided against it
because of the lack of precedent. Instead, they are researching  the use of internal UV screens, which should provide a
30% reduction in heat gain.

A. Wright answered the HPA’s question, that the proposed awning will not obscure the brick masonry above the shopfront.
S. Lemus added that the rendering is pretty accurate. A. Wright asked the commission about removing the former
windowsills and lintels from the building’s original fenestration (pre-1956). No decision was made on this matter. A. Wright
and S. Lemus shared with the commission that the windows they plan to use on the building to replace the late aluminum
and vinyl windows are by Norwood and utilize Mahogony, producing a high quality and durable window.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – MR; RT, KM, AP
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a conditional negative declaration of environmental significance. Commissioner Puetz motion that the Commissioners present find as fact that the proposed fixed awning above the Wall Street shopfront at 330 Wall Street in the Kingston Stockade Local (1974), State, and National Historic District (1975; 2016), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405- 26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is compatible with the historic character of the district with the following reasons: • pursuant to Sections 405.26.L.11 and 13.a the Historic Landmarks Preservation Commission (HLPC) determined the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the proposed work is to take place at the 3- story row building, located on the east side of Wall Street 3 lots south of the intersection of Wall and North Front Streets, which may have been initially constructed in the 1860s, but received mid-20th-century modifications, and which by 1940 housed Nigent's National Clothing store, and by the 1950s-1960s, housed the Up-to-Date Shop" (SHOP, BSIF, 1987); • the HLPC recognizes that a desk review was authorized for a proposed historically informed and code compliant retractable awning on the Wall St elevation, however, the owner would like to amend the plan to install a fixed awning; • awnings are generally understood to be external fixtures to facades that can be easily removed, without substantial harm to historic building fabric. • the proposed awning may be fixed in nature and must awning conforms with FBC ss405.17, and must not encroach within 2' of the sidewalk's edge, and must maintain a minimum clearance of 8'; • pursuant to City Code § 358- 9 the owner must provide the city with documentation naming the city as additionally insured for any projection over the public right of way and secure a permit for work within the public ROW; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's approval does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 4th day of June 2026, the HLPC grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for the work as described herein and in its application to the HLPC, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion and is valid for one year from this date. (Motion – MG; 2nd – MR; RT, KM, AP).

items.title: #22 W. Pierpont St: Rehabilitating a fire damaged Queen Anne Victorian
items.discussion:
The owner, Luke Interrante and Ciro Interrante, architect presented plans to rehabilitate a Queen Anne

Victorian three (3) unit apartment building at 22 W. Pierpont Street, which suffered a bad fire on April 26, 2025. L.
Interrante stated that the project includes “ Repair of exterior as a result of fire damage and deferred maintenance from
prior ownership. Remove and replace existing shingle siding with clapboard to match original house. Clapboard under
the shingle siding is in poor shape so new siding is proposed. Repair and replace in kind all exterior trim details including
dentals, soffits, gables. Replace windows with new in same size and configuration.” L. Interrante stated that the roof was
mostly caved in and causing the greatest hazard. Under an emergency building permit issued by BSD, they rebuilt the
roof in-kind with n no changes to the design.. The front façade was damaged by the fire but has not been removed or
altered and is mostly covered at this time.

Windows: L. Interrante stated that the goal is to replace the siding and windows, but that they would retain any stained-
glass windows in the building and non- standard-size windows. Any decorative woodwork that is damaged, would be
repaired or reconstructed in-kind. They are asking to replace the double-hung and picture windows.  S. Cahill asked the
percentage of windows that were destroyed. L. Interrante sai d that the windows that were really destroyed were limited
to the front dormer and gable end. T here are 42 windows that are present and damaged. He believes most of these
windows are themselves replacements. C . Interrante said that most of the double hung windows are vinyl, but that the
picture windows are wood. They are looking to do aluminum clad wood windows. S. Cahill asked if the older windows had
a different muntin pattern that they would consider using? L. and C . Interrante stated that older photographs don’t show
multi-light windows. Even the 1956 property record card shows 1/1 double hung windows. L. Interrante stated that the
character defining attic gable windows shall be reconstructed to match their historic design.

SIDING: L. Interrante clarified that the wood siding was former ly a shake siding, but that a professional test revealed it
was not asbestos based. C. Interrante stated that it is a homasote impregnated asphalt siding. The HPA asked if any of
the existing wood clapboards will be saved or will it all be replaced. L. Interrante noted that there is a lot of damage from
the shingles and from bore holes drilled for insultation. In essence, they would remove the current siding and install new
composite siding with the same reveal. The exterior face of the siding would be smooth to match the appearance of wood
clapboard. Diamond and scallop shake wood siding in the gable ends of the building near the roof shall be retained,
restored, or replaced in-kind.
PAINTING: L. Interrante said they are unsure of the final paint scheme for the building. He asked the commission for
suggestions. Staff stated that if colors are chosen from a recognized historic color collection, such as those made by most
major manufacturers, then that component of the project could be reviewed at desk lev el. As for schemes, there are
several examples of Queen Anne designs online that can serve as a basis.
GUTTERS: The HPA asked if there are plans for the gutter system. L. Interrante stated that the building may have some
box gutters, but they will have to return to the commission for any plans to repair or alter.
10YR Tax Abatement Project: The HPA reminded the applicants that the city has a 10 YR graduated rehabilitation tax
abatement program for which this project might qualify. The program allows property owners to increase the value of their
buildings through investment in repairs and renovation without suffering an immediate increase in local property taxes as
a result. It provides for a ten- year window of tax relief following the substantial rehabilitation of a structure. For the first
five (5) years after completion of the project, local property taxes do not increase, except as they may be increased on a
city-wide basis, regardless of the additional value of the property resulting from the project. In the sixth year, only 20% of
the full value of the increase is added to the pre-project tax amount. In the seventh year, 40% of the increase is added,

and so on, until the full value of the property is again taxed in the tenth year after completion of the project. It was
recommended that the applicants reach out to Daniel Baker, the City Assessor. It may also be good to discuss with him
which assessed value today (post fire) versus pre-fire, would be used during the abatement program calculation.
The Commission discussed tabling the project depending on more detailed information which must be delivered by the
applicant by June 18, 2026, for consideration at the July 2, 2026, HLPC meeting.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – MR; KM, RT, AP – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to TABLE the application for the applicant to submit additional materials in accordance with the discussions held at this meeting. (Motion – MG; 2nd – MR; KM, RT, AP – yes).

items.title: Fast-Track Certificate of Appropriateness & City of Kingston, 10YR Graduated Rehabilitation tax Abatement Program
items.discussion:
Staff shared with the commission that as a formality it is advisable for the HLPC to reauthorize/affirm
Staff’s authority to review, evaluate, authorize, and/or elevate to commission level review proposed projects that fall into
the category of in-kind work. Staff stated that the terminology of  such reviews be considered as “Fast-Track Certificates
of Appropriateness (FT-CoA)” going forward, to adequately communicate to the public that staff reviews are expedited in
comparison to Commission level reviews. Staff also stated that because this work is predominantly in- kind, it would be
good to allow property owners to use FT -CoAs in their applications for the city’s 10YR graduated historic rehabilitation
tax abatement program via the City’s Assessor ’s Office. A. Puetz asked if staff have experienced a field change of an y
HLPC approval, that resulted in the need for additional reviews. S. Cahill stated the most visible example is the case at
35 Wurts Street with the front steps from May of 2026. S. Cahill agreed that a minor field change that generally conforms
with the intent of the HLPC’s previous CoA could be done by staff, if the HLPC grants staff that authority.

decisions.vote: Motion - MG; 2nd - MR; AP, KM, RT - yes
decisions.text: The commission voted unanimously to approve the following: 1) Pursuant to the City of Kingston's Form Based Code (FBC) ss405.26.L.6.b.5, the HLPC hereby "Empowers the HLPC staff to evaluate, without public hearing, each application for ordinary maintenance and repair of historic resources, properties or landmarks and; approve, approve with modifications, or deny any such applications." 2) Hereafter, all reviews undertaken by HLPC Staff shall be termed, "Fast -Track Certificate of Appropriateness" or "FT-CoA", and may include minor field changes to reviews for projects approved by the HLPC. 3) The HLPC recognizes that FT-CoAs are equivalent to an approval from the HLPC. 4) The HLPC allows owners to utilize Fast -Tract Certificates of Appropriateness (FT -CoAs) in applications for the City of Kingston's 10YR -Graduated Rehabilitation Tax Abatement program (City Code Chapter 360, Article VI: Exemptions for Historic Properties) and NYS RPTL 444a to expedite and make easier access to the programs benefits for historic property owners who are doing good work to preserve, protect, and save Kingston's special historic properties. (Motion - MG; 2nd - MR; AP, KM, RT - yes)
