#20 Presidents Pl: Proposed replacement of 32 existing wood windows
items.discussion:
The owner, Rachel Kafka, was previously before the HLPC on June 4, 2026, seeking to replace 32 existing
wooden double hung windows with exterior aluminum storm windows at a circa 1900 Queen Anne Victorian house on 20
Presidents Place, which was built as the second residence for Conrad Hiltebrant, a locally prominent shipbuilder in
Rondout. The owner proposes to replace the windows to address a time sensitive lead paint safety matter, caused by
degrading paint, and abrasive rubbing when the windows are operated . The owner has s tated the degraded paint
presented a health matter for their family and the Ulster County Board of Health (BOH) determined the lead is a serious
health concern that must be rectified . In a letter submitted by the owner  from the BOH dated April 23, 2026, the BOH
placed a 45-day timeline for rectifying the lead matter. For an expeditious review, the HLPC and Staff conducted a ground-
only site visit to the property on Tuesday, June 9, 2026, to observe the building, the window conditions, and the potential
effects of the proposed work on the building and district.

Chairman Grunblatt, Esq., began by the review by highlighting that it is a “big project and a big decision” and asked the
commissioners their thoughts and if they had any additional questions of the property owner.

R. Tonner: “So you would like to replace some of the attic windows?”
R. Kafka: “Yes, the attic windows are in particularly bad shape”
R. Tonner: “If no one is living up there, then why couldn’t these windows now be abated and restored?”
R. Kafka: “The issue bigger issue is the removal of lead from all the fixed components of the windows, not just the sashes.
The removal will potentially cause greater exposure when people are going in and out of the house.”
E. Winchell: “So, is the idea to remove the windows from the outside? Will you be leaving the exterior trim to do that?”
R. Kafka: “Yes, a big reason for the inserts is to ensure the existing trim on the inside and outside will be retained.”
E. Winchell: “How will you remove the sashes from the outside?”
A. Puetz: “I can answer that – some of the small sash-stop trim from the outside, then they remove the sashes, and then
they insert the new windows, and then they install trim around the insert frame from the inside.”
E. Winchell: “At that point, what would the difference be between taking the old out and having them restored versus the
use of inserts.”
A. Puetz: “That’s a really good question.”
R. Kafka: “Well the whole issue is how much lead there is on the jams themselves. It is not just taking the sashes out; it
is stripping the jams down and the lead exposure created by that process.”
A. Puetz: “My limited knowledge is that there is a way of installing a metal sliding channel that will reduce friction. I also
have another question regarding your discussion with Frances (Referring to: Frances Stern, NYSDOS). Is she aware that
your proposal is for the use of inserts?”
R. Kafka: “Yes, she is aware that the proposal is for inserts.”
A. Puetz: “My biggest concern with using an insert is that they will not match the design and opening, as they essentially
shrink the opening.”
R. Puetz: “Is there any way to meet in the middle on that?”
M. Morano: “I have a question about restoration. Can they remove the sashes and strip them off site before putting them
back?”
R. Kafka: “Yes, but it is also the restoration of the frames, jams, and trims.”
E. Winchell: “Is the attic a finished space? And is the trim on the inside painted”
R. Kafka: “Yes, it is partially finished space.”
E. Dickerman: “You mentioned you submitted the homeowner rehab tax credit application to the state and that you talked
with Frances Stern at SHPO. Did they ever get back to you?”
R. Kafka: “They have not – it can take up to 30 days. Frances also said SHPO does not get involved with local reviews.”
A. Puetz: “Do you have any plans with the basement windows?”
R. Kafka: “They are all shut so they do not present an issue at this time.”
E. Winchell: “The grilled windows on the 2nd-floor balcony, are they operable?”
R. Kafka. “Yes, they are. Those are windows we would be willing to make as a concession and retain those windows and
install an interior storm window. That is certainly something we can talk about.”
M. Grunblatt: “Alright, we should get a sense of where and how many windows might be in that situation.”
R. Kafka: “So it would be the two diamond grill pattern windows, and the 13 others identified for protection in my
application. Which would leave 30 one over one windows for replacement.”

The commission looked at a table the windows per building elevation, and the proposed treatment of the windows by the

applicant:

Elevation # Proposed for Replacement # Proposed for Preservation
West 12 - 1/1 double hung 0
North 6 - 1/1 double hung 0
East 3 - tower 1/1 double hung 6 - stained glass and curved bay windows.
1 - attic eyebrow window
South 9 - 1/1 double hung windows
2 – quasi-diamond style upper sash over single lite lower
sash, single hung windows that flank the 2 nd-story
balcony door.
1 - attic eyebrow window
1- gable porthole window
2 - ground floor entryway side lites
Totals 32 11

S. Cahill noted that if the two diamond/prismatic windows on the 2nd story balcony are retained, that would mean 30 windows would
be replaced across the four elevations, and 13 would be retained.

N. Morano: “Did you have a restoration expert come in and give you some information?”
R. Kafka: “I’ve talked to about 10 different restores. I didn’t hear back from about 6 or 7 of them. One advised against restoration.
One lead safe contractor also advised me against the project.”
S. Cahill: “Did they give a reason why they advised you against restoration?”
R. Kafka: “If lead is the problem, then this is not your solution to prevent more exposure. We also had two Board of Health inspection,
and they recommended replacement. So, I thought that the idea we came up with was the best compromise, I think there is a perfect
solution. This is why we chose the inserts. I don’t think the new construction is a good option because it disturbs more lead and more
original fabric.”
M. Grunblatt asked R. Kafka “Would you be open to retaining all windows on the south and east primary elevations, while replacing
the windows on the north and west (secondary elevations). These secondary elevations are less visible and critical to the building’s
design integrity.”
E. Dickerman added “between the north and west sides are 18 windows.”
R. Kafka: “Are you suggesting replacing the back and sides but not the south and east sides?”
M. Grunblatt: “Right, what I am looking at is a different variety and that they’re  honestly obscured by the adjacent houses unless
standing within three yards of the sidewalk.”
R. Kafka: “You can see all four sides from the public right of way. The sides you  suggest (South and East restoring) are the sides
where we live almost 80% of the time. We also get into the issue of keeping these white storms on half of the house. I think that
would pose an issue.”

The commission examined the north and west elevation photographs of the building.

N. Morano: “And this is the part of the house that you live on most of the time?”
R. Kafka: “Well, I think the suggestion was that we replace the west and north sides where we spend the least amount of time and
restore the east and south sides where we spend most of the time.”
E. Dickerman: “So if that approach was taken, that would allow for the replacement of 18 windows across the north and west
elevations and restoration of the remaining one over one, attic eyebrows , port hole, entryway door flanking windows, and stained
glass/curved windows on the south and east elevations.”

R. Kafka: “But if the concern is how the house will look from the public right of way, and the entire house is visible from the public
right of way, why are we treating some windows different than others?”
S. Cahill: “It is partially informed by past practices, where the primary elevation is given greatest consideration?”
R. Kafka: “But are you not considering any other components of my application, like the board of health timeline, and the health and
welfare of my family?”
M. Grunblatt: “In part because our charge is the city long after all of us are gone.”
R. Kafka: “Of course, but we are not going to be here is there are hazardous materials in our homes making us sick.”
M. Grunblatt: “This commission and the landmark preservation law are tasked with considering the long- term implications of
changes to the exterior of landmarked buildings and in landmark districts. We must consider decades and centuries, and the law
does not consider health related matters.”

Commissioner Puetz also added that this must also be carefully decided because this is not the only house in the City of King ston
that likely contains lead paint. There are many houses with lead. Any building built before 1978 is generally understood by the EPA
to potentially contain lead paint. Many people have overcome this issue in the past, and certification for lead removal is not a difficult
process.

R. Kafka: “That does not change the reality that many are not certified lead abatement specialists and that I’ve been advise not to
restore. It doesn’t consider what Frances stated, and the potentially long timeline for restoration.”
A. Puetz: “I would have liked to see a statement from one of the restorers that says they won’t take the project on.”

The HPA pulled an email communication up on the screen between the applicant and Ben Brandt of Newburgh Sash, for the
commissioners to view.

Chairman M. Grunblatt noted that another option might be to require anything that is removed be bagged , sealed correctly,  and
retained on site. Commissioner Puetz clarified that only the window sashes would be stored and that the frames would remain i n
place. “Is that preservation for the future?”

A. Puetz: “It is an interesting idea, because you are saving the fabric, enclosing the jam, but slightly reducing the portal with the
insert.”
R. Kafka: “I do not believe this will have a substantial change from the public right of way.”
E. Dickerman: “If I may, I would pose the following question to the commission. You’ve already mentioned the north and west sides.
If you are considering other windows, what role do these windows play in the overall character defining features of the building?
Rachel, you’ve already said that you are open to keeping the diamond and prismatic windows, and that they are clearly character-
defining and unique. You’ve also admitted to retaining the eyebrow and porthole windows in the attic, and the stained class and
curved windows on the east side of the building. Those are certainly character defining. You can also argue that other features, like
the slate roof, the ridge molding, and siding are also critical features to the building that will remain in place. How does the commission
feel when considering the work at this point?”
A. Puetz: “I think if these windows had specific mullion/muntin patterns on them, I would be taking more exception. However, they
are 1 over 1 window, and the proposal may only add another inch or inch and a half to the windows.”
E. Dickerman: “Would that essentially equate to the amount obscured currently by the storms?”
A. Puetz: “Potentially – I think the more distractive feature to not the difference of is if there were more muntin patterns.”
R. Kafka: “I think if we can compromise on the front diamond pattern windows, we can install interior storms on these. Replacement
of the others would allow for the removal of the storms.”
A. Puetz: “Contrary to popular thought, storm windows are actually encouraged and protect windows.”

R. Kafka: “If you keep scrolling in my application, it’s a long document, you can see close-up photographs of what it looks like from
the exterior. You can see current conditions and an example of what it would look like if approved. In my opinion, I do not feel it’s a
significant difference.”
E. Dickerman: “Would there be interior or exterior screens?
R. Kafka: “Exterior screens, like with storms.”
E. Dickerman: “How does the commission feel about the impact of the screens on the aesthetics?”
A. Puetz: “With a black big screen, the effects would be negligible.”
M. Grunblatt: “Okay, so we are talking about a slightly smaller window, with a minimal impact.”

The commissioners examined the specifications and cross section detail on the proposed windows to determine the amount the
portal would shrink. E. Dickerman questioned how the commission feels about the small reduction in size, because of the insert on
the overall integrity of the building. The commissioners reexamined the elevations and felt that the effect is negligible. That t he
existing portal is effectively retained and encapsulated, and that if the sashes are retained on site, that the work could be undone in
the future sometime. Sash weights should be stored. Sash weight gaps may be filled with insulation.

S. Cahill: “Are you agreeable to retaining the existing sashes in bags on site, if they are properly contained?”
R. Kafka: “Its not desirable, and certainly our goal is to get the lead hazards out of the house. But also, one of the inspectors found
trace amounts of asbestos in the window glazing, so that concerns me, but if you can recommend a way to do it safely then we
would be open to it.”
S. Cahill & A. Puetz stated that you would essentially put the sashes into bags and seal them and add in some desiccant bags.
R. Kafka: “Our goal is to make the house safe, so we are happy to compromise on things like this, to get this project done and
moving as quickly as we can.”

M. Grunblatt stated that it appears a consensus of the commissioners would have the attic porthole window, two attic eyebrow
windows, the 2nd-story balcony door diamond windows, the ground floor entryway side lites, and the stained glass/curved windows
retained. No action on the basement windows. The one over one windows elsewhere may be replaced with the proposed units.

The following windows may be replaced:
Elevation Description
West 12 - 1/1 double hung
North 6 - 1/1 double hung
East 3 - tower 1/1 double hung and wall
South 9 - 1/1 double hung windows
Total 30

The following window must be retained and/or restored:
Elevation Description
East 6 - stained glass and curved bay windows.
1 - attic eyebrow window
South 1 - attic eyebrow window
1- gable porthole window
2 - ground floor entryway side lites
2 – quasi-diamond style upper sash over single lite lower sash, single hung windows that
flank the 2nd-story balcony door.
Total 13

R. Tonner: “If we allow lead paint as the reason here, then we would have to allow it in the future. However, for me what
differentiates are the statements from Frances Stern, that these windows are not as critical.”

E. Dickerman: “Yes, essentially you would be saying that the work is permitted because the effect of the proposed work
on these features in not substantial and that these one over one windows are not the critical character defining features
for the overall building. It would be different if the windows in question were more character defining, for example, if the
muntin patterns were more elaborate, wavey glass, old growth wood, manufactured in a unique style, etc.”

A. Puetz: “What if Frances comes back to Rachel and says no? Where do we go from there? Should this be a contingent
approval?”
S. Cahill: “I would recommend that you make that a contingent. That if the state does not approve, then they come back
to the commission for adjustment.”
E. Dickerman: “While anything is possible, it is important to remember that HLPC does not customarily get involved in
SHPO decisions and vice versa.”
M. Grunblatt: “Yes, we don’t want to get into a back and forth with another agency.”
R. Kafka: “We should know from SHPO within 30 days.”
E. Dickerman also informed R. Kafka about the City of Kingston’s 10-year graduated tax abatement program that is run
by the City of Kingston’s assessor’s office.
E. Winchell: “Going forward are we going to be able to consider the difference between one over one and other designs
of windows.”

The full commission agreed that we already do and will continue to because each project and building is unique and
context specific. E. Dickerman stated the commission is not rubber stamping one over one windows and that you must
consider several factors.

items.title: #93 Wall Street (Van Steenburgh House): Proposed remedy for a 2nd-story window replacement windows
items.discussion:
The owner, Martha Dallis,  presented a proposal to remediate the unauthorized window replacement of
historic wood windows which took place during the summer of 2025. Also present with M. Dallis was her contractor Jay
Elsoffler, and Kevin Hoffman from Hilltop Millwork/Lepage Millwork.

Prior to entering involved discussion, S. Cahill noted that Commissioner Ricke had not been a HLPC Member during the
initial reviews with the applicant. Staff provided the background minutes, notes and video links for him to review.  M. Ricke
confirmed he had reviewed and was comfortable in stating that he feels knowledgeable in participating in the review at
this time and able to make a fully informed determination.

The HLPC reviewed a brief history of the project.  In the Summer of 2025, the property owner and their contractor replaced
windows at the landmarked property without HLPC or Staff review. Only four windows that were replaced were publicly
visible: one (1) on the southward facing gable, and three (3) Wall Street-facing dormer windows. The single south-facing
gable window was a six -by-six pane, outward swinging casement, that the owner had replaced with a new window that
matched the operation, design, and material more closely matched the window that had been removed. In November of
2025, the HLPC felt that restoration w ould have been appropriate, but this  window, which was installed matched
sufficiently, and would not have an adverse effect on the landmark. At the same time, the HLPC determined that the three
(3) Wall Street-facing dormer windows were more complicated matters, and the replacement 6/6 double hung aluminum
clad windows differed in design, operation, and had some material differences than the windows that were removed.

Given the significance of the property, the owner requested, in writing, that she be able to have six months to research
replacement windows that the commission might find more suitable than the six over six windows. Since then, the owner
has consulted with staff in good faith, requesting extension on time, to find a replacement window that matches the historic
windows as closely as possible. Presently,  M. Dallis proposes to remedy the current 6/6 double hung dormer windows
by replacing them with two new wood window options by Hilltop Millwork/Lepage Millwork. K. Hoffman presented a sample
of the simulated divided light window to the HLPC.

Option 1 (True Divided Lites) Opt. 2 (Simulated Divided Lites with Black Spacer Bars)
Three (3) 2nd-story Wall Street-facing dormer windows:
The Southern Window: 8 by 8 pane outward swinging
French casement window
The Center Window: 10 by 10 pane outward swinging
French casement window
The Northern Window: 8 by 8 pane outward swinging
French casement window

• All units have double insulated glass with True Divided lite

there is a clear opening with no obstructions

While M. Dallis proposed both True and Simulated Divided lites, she informed the Commission that the True Divided Light
Windows would have muntins that are nearly an inch thick, which is substantially thicker than most historic wood windows.
All windows will be painted white on the exterior. Staff shared with the commission their opinion that of the two options
presented, the simulated divided lites with black internal spacer bars will more appropriately match the historic window’s
design, operation, and materials.

decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to classify the project as Unlisted under SEQR and render a Negative declaration of Environmental Significance. Chairman Grunblatt, Esq., motioned that the Commissioners present find as fact that the 2nd- story window violation remedy project at 93 Wall St (the Tobias Van Steenburgh House), a local landmark (1971) that is also S/NHR listed (1999), if done according to the plans reviewed, the discussions had, and the procedures stipulated in Section 405-26 L, of Kingston's Zoning Code, is appropriate for the historic character of the individual landmark for the following reasons: • pursuant to FBC ss405.26.L.11 & 405.26.L.13.a the Commission determined on July 2, 2026 the application and its supporting materials are complete for formal review, and that the proposed work requires a Certificate of Appropriateness; • the project is located at a 1.5-story Dutch-vernacular (masonry and framed) building/dwelling on the western side of Wall Street at the in intersection of Wall and Franklin Streets dating to the early 18th-century, that served as a home for the Van Steenburgh [Jansen Timmerman], as a Tavern during the American Revolution, and according to oral histories, was one of the only structures to survive the 1777 burning of Kingston by the British army, and which was landmarked by Kingston's HLPC in 1971 and listed on the S/NHR in 1999 under Criterion (C) as the "Property embodies the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or method of construction or represents the work of a master, or possesses high artistic values, or represents a significant and distingui shable entity whose components lack individual distinction." (HLPC, 1971; S/NHR Nomination, 1999); • the HLPC recognizes that the owner understood the Landmark review process, in that they previously worked with the City in July 2024 for an in- kind desk review authorizing the restoration of building's box gutters and roof replacement, which were also reviewed and approved by SHPO for the 20% Homeowner Historic Rehab Tax Credit Program; • the HLPC recognize windows as character defining features of a building, that are both exterior and interior features, which require HLPC review for alterations; • the HLPC recognizes that the owner removed, replaced, and destroyed the pre -2025 2nd- story wood outward swinging French gable and street -facing dormer windows and replaced them with Modern Marvin windows without review or a Building Permit, and that the ow ner subsequently provided photographs of the lost features which documented that they could have been restored; • the HLPC prefers restoration of historic wood windows whenever possible, and finds the loss of these windows regrettable; • in reviewing the before and aftereffects of the violation, the HLPC determined that the new modern Marvin 6 by 6 outward swinging French casement window installed in the south-facing gable is an appropriate replacement that will not adversely impact the integrity and character of the individual landmark; • in reviewing the before and aftereffects of the violation, the HLPC determined that the new modern Marvin Ultimate six over six double hung windows installed in the two (2) Wall Street facing dormers and the one (1) central Wall St - facing gable are of a different design, operation, and material, are inappropriate replacements for the outward swinging casements which were 8 by 8 and 10 by 10 pane designs; • to remedy the violation, the owner has researched and consulted in good faith with Staff, to identify historically appropriate windows for the three Wall Street facing locations, and the owner now proposes to remove the double hung violation windows and replacement them with the following windows by Hilltop Millwork/Lepage Millwork: o Southernmost and Northernmost Wall St -facing dormers: Each with an 8 by 8 pane outward swinging white wood French casement window with double insulated glass and simulated divided lite grill construction with black internal spacer bars. o Central Wall St-facing Gable: A 10 by 10 pane outward swinging white wood French casement window with double insulated glass & simulated divided lite grill construction with black internal spacer bars. • the HLPC closely evaluated the historic casement windows with the proposed windows and determined they closely replicate the historic windows in materials, designs, and operations, and are therefore an appropriate remedy for the violation; • any future changes or additions to the plans and/or work specifically described and outlined in the submitted application are subject to further review by our commission prior to work's start; • the Commission's action does not obviate the need for a Building Permit from the Building Safety Division or any other required approvals from relevant coordinating agencies; Based on the preceding findings of fact, I move that on the 2nd day of July 2026, the Commission grant a Certificate of Appropriateness to the above referenced Applicant, for reasons as described herein and in its application to the Commission, such notice is subject to the conditions contained in the foregoing motion. (Motion – MG; 2nd – EW; MR, NM – yes).

items.title: #22 W. Pierpont St: Rehabilitating a fire damaged Queen Anne Victorian
items.applicant: Luke Inter rante (Interrante Design- Build, LLC)
items.discussion:
Ciro Interrante (co-owner), was present to discuss the plans to rehabilitate a Queen Anne Victorian
building at 22 W. Pierpont Street, which suffered a bad fire on April 26, 2025. L. & C. Interrante were before on the HLPC
on June 4, 2026, with their initial plans and questions for the commission. The HLPC ultimately t abled the project and
requested additional information on the windows, siding, painting, and other components.

The owners have provided the commission with existing condition photographs of the windows and the façade’s siding.
Elevations drawings were submitted showing which portions of the elevations are visible from the public right of way.

With regards to the building’s windows, C. Interrante explained the following:
• 1/1 double hung windows:  that most of the windows are late vinyl and/or aluminum 1/1 replacements and that
the new Weathersheild Aluminum Clad wood windows will match the historic 1/1 windows.
• Stained Glass Windows: These windows will be retained, cleaned, and preserved.
• Attic Windows: These windows will be retained when possible. If damaged from the fire, the windows will be
recreated to their district design.

C. Interrante also explained that there were and are no planned alterations to the roof structure and design as these were
effectively replaced in-kind under emergency work to secure the building. The existing wood clapboard siding is degraded
and riddled with holes from a past blow -particle insulation project, after which the siding was covered over in a type of
fiber shingle siding.  The owners intend to install  James Hardie composite siding with the smooth side exposed with a
5.00-inch reveal.  A photograph of the current siding measure was presented for the dimension.  Attic gable siding on the
front is made of diamond patterned shakes and, on the west-facing attic gable they are scalloped shakes. The goal is to
retain these features and/or repair in- kind. Any decorative soffit and/or fascia elements will be repaired and/or
reconstructed in-kind using the same materials. Chairman Grunblatt asked the applicant if they had made any decisions
on the gutters for the property.  C. Interrante noted that they will be replacing them with half round copper gutters.
Painting: Three different Ben. Moore historic colors schemes for the rehabilitated façade for the commission to consider.
Staff reviewed and found that all 3 are in an appropriate Queen Anne Victorian scheme, and in historic colors. Overall,
the commission was pleased with each option. C. Interrante explained he would personally like option three (3) but would
paint the attic gable in the same attic gable color presented in option two (2). C. & L. Interrante may want to discuss
blending the schemes to meet their preferences. Ultimately, the Commission felt the project could be reviewed by Staff
and authorized via a Fast-Track Certificate of Appropriateness.

items.title: #330 Wall St: Proposal to install a fixed awning on the Wall Street elevation
items.discussion:
Sonia Lemus and Andrew Wright, of Wright Architects,  presented plans for exterior modifications to the
Wall and Fair Street elevations of 330 Wall Street (the former Up-to-Date Company, and later Gargoyles Antiques Shop).
Kevin Hoffman from Hilltop Millwork/Lepage Millwork was also present as a contractor.  The proposals are:
• Wall St: Shaving the “ghost” lintels and sills that partially remain after the building’s original three (3) second story
windows were filled in and the mid- 20th-century façade and fenestration modifications put in place. Only a few
components of the northern and southern window’s sills and lintels remain and primarily are visible in the form of a
textural difference/inconsistency against the surrounding regular brick façade.  The degraded sills of the third floor
will be repaired in-kind with stone material.
• Fair Street: The submitted Fair Street elevation drawing identified 1st, 2nd and 3rd story windows that have brick
lintels. White -painted faux lintels and sills are present to replicate larger more historically proportioned masonry
lintels and sills. S. Lemus and A. Wright propose to replace the existing window true masonry lintels that match the
design, material, texture, and reveal as the adjacent historic lintels on the Fair Street elevation.
• Fair Street Entryway:  S. Lemus proposed replacing the existing ground floor entryway on Fair Street , which is
degraded and has an inappropriate replacement door. The proposed replacement would be by Lepage Millwork in
Mahogony and similarly replicate the existing entryway in design. It would also be made of wood. The primary
difference would be a fixed transom window as opposed to the historic operable transom window. S. Lemus and A.
Wright explained and showed the commission pictures they believe indicated this window was itself a replacement
to an earlier window. The door would have a Stuttgart handle with an  oil rubbed bronze finish also from Lepage
Millwork. The Commission was not opposed to altering the function of the transom.
• Painting & Canopy Colors: S. Lemus and A. Wright proposed painting the building façades in the following colors

and design scheme:
o Body: Benjamin Moore, Van Duesen Blie (HC-156)
o Trim & Architectural Elements: Benjamin Moore, Opaline (Off white) (HC-156)
o Fair St Canopy Color: To match, as closely as possible, Benjamin Moore, Opaline (Off white) (HC-156)
o Wall Street Canopy Color: To match, as closely as possible, Benjamin Moore, Hale Navy (HC -154), and
this canopy shall feature black wrought iron elements, too.

items.title: #10 E. Chestnut St: Construction of a historically informed side porch
items.discussion:
The owner, Annie M. Blasko, and architect, Amy L. Moses, RA, presented the proposed modification for
a new historically informed side porch construction project at 10 E. Chestnut Street (the Newkirk House). A. Blasko & A.
Moses explained that 10 E. Chestnut Street has been altered numerous times over the years, and the HLPC was provided
with the following excerpt from the application:

“…as is evident when comparing the current building to the 1875 image of 10 East Chestnut Street. Porches have
been enclosed, towers removed, windows modified, and chimneys added.  This project proposes the construction
of a new exterior porch designed to match the color, detailing, and architectural character of the existing entry porch
on the East Chestnut Street facade. While the existing porch may not be original to the building,  it has acquired
historic significance through its long- standing association with the property. Adding a matching porch on the
adjacent facade will create a cohesive architectural appearance and restore a sense of continuity to the exterior,
reflecting what may have historically existed.  The scope of work also includes replacing a pair of windows on the
east facade facing Broadway with taller double-hung windows that match the historic window proportions found on
the adjacent facades. In addition, a new entrance door will replace the northern window opening. As shown in the
accompanying documentation, this opening historically functioned as a doorway. The colors, materials, and detailing
of the proposed porch will match the existing entry porch on the East Chestnut Street facade. The only additional
features will be code- compliant wood railings and a stairway connecting the porch to grade. No changes wi ll be
made to the existing wood siding. The proposed porch addition and exterior alterations will not destroy or adversely
affect the historic materials, features, or spatial relationships that characterize the property. No treatments or
construction methods that could damage historic materials will be used.”

A. Moses and A. Blasko explained that the purpose of the porch addition is to provide a more appropriately massed and
designed entrance to the building, as the grand original entrance is on the south- facing elevation which is not as easily
accessible today. At present, the primary entrance is the E. Chestnut Street (back) side and through a thin door into the
old kitchen. For context, A. Moses prepared aerial and street view images showing the proposed porch’s minimal visibility
from Broadway, and greater visibility from E. Chestnut Street. It was explained to the commission that the new porch will
be constructed t o modern code requirements and utilize historic wood materials and design elements from the other
porches present on the building. A. Blasko explained that the north- facing window around the proposed porch was
previously a doorway, which her insurance company required her to enclose when she bought the building as there was
no exterior element to access. Now, she proposes to reopen this portal for access to the porch. A. Moses explained they
would like to modify the current double windows where the porch will be installed to match the fenestration present
elsewhere on the façade. A. Moses explained that she does not believe these to be original windows, and that when she

bought the home the former mid- century kitchen sink was located beneath them in the interior. She added that the new
windows will match the design, operation, and material of the one-over-one windows elsewhere on the building. Overall,
the Commission felt that the visibility and impact of the proposed window modification will not likely cause any adverse
effects to the character of the building and/or district. The commission equally felt that the porch proposal was thoughtful
and historically sensitive.

decisions.vote: Motion – MG; 2nd – NM; MR, EW – yes
decisions.text: The Commission voted unanimously to render the action Type II under SEQR 617.5 c (1) (2) and determined that it will have no significant environmental impact and issued a negative declaration of environmental significance. Chestnut and Stuyvesant Streets, that was likely 'buil t c. 1860 for Edgar B. Newkirk, Cashier of the Rondout National Bank and a land developer in Rondout" (FHK Chestnut St Walking Tour). According to the NY SHPO Building Structure Inventory Form, " Later notable residents were Dr. David Kennedy, who owned a well- known patent medicine company (Dr. Kennedy's Favorite Remedy and others) in Rondout and served as Mayor of Kingston about 1895-96, and Jay Klock, publisher for a number of years of the Kingston Daily Freeman" (SHOP, BSIF, 1982.9.7); • that the applicant provided the HLPC with historical documentation of past features and alterations undertaken to the property after its circa 1860 construction, and that their proposed new porch construction is rooted in a sensitive historically informed design and placement; • the applicant may construct a code compliant side porch (NW corner of the building) facing Broadway and E. items.title: Project Update: FFY24 CLG for the Wilbur State and National Register Nomination:
items.discussion:
Staff informed the commission New York State Historic Review Board meeting was held on June 4, 2026.
SHPO National Register Staff member, Olivia Holland, presented the Wilbur Historic District Nomination to the SRB with
additional commentary from Gregory Dietrich, the City’s grant funded consultant who prepared the nomination. Overall,
the SRB was pleased with the district nomination and the themes, especially that it is the first new district in Kingston
since Chestnut Street in 1985. After the presentation, the SRB voted unanimously to approve the Wilbur Historic District’s
Nomination for the National & State Registers. Here is a link to the State Historic Review Board Meeting Recording:
https://youtu.be/QjlYxPSFErY?si=G4zl2vbUJcmrhLRv SHPO is now likely working to list the district on the state register.
We anticipate SHPO forwarding the SRB’s findings to the Keeper of the National Register in Washington, DC, in the
coming days/weeks for listing. Staff will update the commission when the final NR listing occurs. The HPA is now working
to compile all necessary materials to submit the final report, expense summary, and secure reimbursement of the costs
(effectively 60% total expenditure).

items.title: Project Update: FFY25 CLG for Comprehensive Historic Preservation Plan & City- Wide Historic Design Guidelines:
items.discussion:
The HPA explained to the Commission that the City of Kingston received a $50,000 grant from the New
York State Office of Parks, Recreation, and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) to create a Comprehensive Historic
Preservation Plan & concurrently develop City -Wide Historic Design Guidelines. The City will hire a SOI 36CFR61
accredited consultant to develop these tools in conjunction with a Project Advisory Committee (PAC), City and SHPO
staff. PAC’s are essential parts of community-based projects. Kingston residents with unique knowledge of the community
and/or skills relevant to the project will comprise the PAC. While PACs don't have formal authority to govern the project,
they make critical recommendations and/or provide vital information to the project manager and project consultants. PACs
also serve important public relations roles within the community and provide City Staff with fresh perspectives on
programmatic issues. The City would like to see a diverse mix of applicants from across the city, with different careers,
and representative of all walks of life. PAC membership should include property or business owners in each of the existing
historic districts, architects, contractors, multilingual individuals, and others with relevant knowledge, experiences, and/or
interests. The PAC is expected to have a 12-14 month term, ending on September 30th, 2027. Deadline to apply for the
Comprehensive Historic Preservation Plan PAC is Wednesday, July 15, 2026.

items.title: Historic Window Design Guidance:
items.discussion:
While the FY25 CLG Grant will establish City-Wide Historic Design Guidelines that should help residents,
contractors, developers, and the commission review proposed exterior projects to historic buildings, staff recognizes the
adoption of such guidelines i s likely at least a year from now. Staff stated that the p opular and ever-increasing window
replacement projects make it imperative for the HLPC to develop on its own interim Historic Window Design Guidelines.
Such guidelines could be based on similar guidelines in other NYS CLG communities , and to consider other Federal,
State, and local resources. Staff shared that the following communities have similar examples:
• City of Poughkeepsie, NY: https://www.cityofpoughkeepsie.com/DocumentCenter/View/1775
• City of Binghamton, NY: chrome-extension://efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.binghamton-
